**Couchoud, Goguel and the French quarrel.** In France, the thesis was taken up in the 1920s by a physician and man of letters, Paul-Louis Couchoud (1879-1959), a friend of Anatole France, in *Le Mystère de Jésus* (1924). The book has the merit of clarity. “Jésus n'est pas un homme progressivement divinisé, mais un Dieu progressivement humanisé”, Jesus is not a man progressively divinized, but a God progressively humanized. And again: “Il n'est pas un fondateur religieux mais un Dieu nouveau.[…] Il n'est pas Mahomet, il est Allah”, he is not a religious founder but a new God.[…] He is not Muhammad, he is Allah. The conclusion of this chapter is fine prose: Jesus “n'est pas un personnage historique. Il n'a pas de place dans les générations des hommes. Il n'est pas un homme qui a vécu et qui s'est évanoui dans la mort. Il est un grand rêve des hommes, continuellement vivant”, is not a historical figure; he has no place in the generations of men; he is not a man who lived and vanished into death; he is a great dream of mankind, continually alive. Couchoud makes a prediction that shows the measure of his confidence: “Je crois que vers 1940 Jésus tout entier aura passé du plan des faits matériels dans celui des représentations mentales collectives”, I believe that by about 1940 the whole of Jesus will have passed from the plane of material facts to that of collective mental representations; and he calls Durkheim's sociology to his aid, since “L'histoire de Jésus est une représentation collective de nature sacrée”, the story of Jesus is a collective representation of a sacred nature.

The appeal to Durkheim turns against Couchoud. If the story of Jesus is a sacred collective representation, it can be so, in sound sociology, whether or not a man existed: Durkheim never asked whether the totem had lived. Couchoud confuses two questions, that of the nature of the Christ of believers, which is indeed a collective representation, and that of the existence of the Jesus of history, which is a matter for the sources. The answer came from a Protestant exegete, professor at the Faculté libre de théologie protestante in Paris, Maurice Goguel, in *Jésus de Nazareth : mythe ou histoire ?* (1925), and it is an attested response, addressed by name. Goguel begins by quoting a contributor to the very series Couchoud edited, Albert Houtin, for whom “Without Jesus, the history of Christianity would seem as inexplicable as that of Islam without Mahomet”; then he pays tribute to Couchoud's loyalty and sincerity, which does not prevent him from seeing in his book “the dream of a poet rather than the work of an historian”. Goguel then examines the mythicist arguments source by source and refutes them one by one: Paul's silence is not a silence, the “brother of the Lord” is not the title of a confraternity, the parallels with the gods of the mysteries are remote. Prosper Alfaric, a former priest turned militant rationalist, extended Couchoud's thesis in the 1930s; Michel Onfray prefaced in 2005 the reissue of his *Jésus a-t-il existé ?*. Couchoud had got the date wrong: in 1940, and since, Jesus has not left the plane of facts for that of representations; he has remained, for historians, a poorly known fact that produced an immense representation.

**Carrier, Ehrman and the consensus.** The mythicist thesis enjoyed a revival at the beginning of the twenty-first century, first on the internet, then in a scholarly form, with the American historian Richard Carrier. His *On the Historicity of Jesus* (Sheffield Phoenix Press, 2014), published by an academic house, submits the question to an explicit method, Bayesian probability calculus. Carrier argues there that the probability that Jesus existed cannot reasonably exceed one chance in three, and that with less favourable estimates it falls to one chance in twelve thousand. The most detailed review, that of Daniel Gullotta in the *Journal for the Study of the Historical Jesus* (15, 2017, p. 310-346), acknowledges, according to Carrier himself, the rigour of the undertaking, but judges the mythicist reconstruction implausible, and concludes that the reality of a crucified Jesus, “another failed messianic pretender from Palestine”, “is remarkably more likely than a demonic crucifixion in outer space”, which is Carrier's reconstruction. The irony hits the mark: to account for Paul's letters without a historical Jesus, Carrier must suppose that the first Christians believed in a Christ crucified by demons in a celestial sphere, a myth that the gospels then transposed onto earth. The hypothesis is not absurd in itself; it is simply more costly than the one it seeks to replace.

The most widely read response is that of Bart Ehrman, a New Testament scholar and declared agnostic, in *Did Jesus Exist?* (2012). Ehrman states the finding I make my own: “The view that Jesus existed is held by virtually every expert on the planet”. He makes clear that he has no stake in the matter: “I am not a Christian, and I have no interest in promoting a Christian cause or a Christian agenda”; and he concludes: “a dispassionate consideration of the case makes it quite plain: Jesus did exist”. Ehrman goes further, and here he must be read with reservation: those who deny the existence of Jesus, he writes, do so not because they have considered the evidence “with the dispassionate eye of the historian, but because they have some other agenda that this denial serves”. The argument is ad hominem, and it would be worthless if it replaced the examination of the sources, which Ehrman carries out elsewhere. But the case of Drews shows that it is not without historical foundation: mythicism has often been, from Bauer to Onfray, a weapon more than a hypothesis.

E. P. Sanders, in *Jesus and Judaism* (1985), draws up a list of facts he regards as practically indisputable: Jesus was baptized by John, he preached and healed in Galilee, he called disciples, he was involved in a conflict over the Temple, he was crucified in Jerusalem by the Roman authorities, and his disciples continued to form a movement after his death. John P. Meier, in the volumes of *A Marginal Jew* (1991-2016), and Paula Fredriksen, in *Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews* (1999), reconstruct an apocalyptic Jewish prophet, very close to Schweitzer's, whose crucifixion as “king of the Jews” is explained by Roman fear of unrest during Passover. This Jesus is neither that of the Churches nor that of the mythicists: he is a man of his time, whom his disciples understood, after his death, through the Scriptures, then through the Greek Logos.

**Onfray in the debate.** It is in this landscape that Michel Onfray's thesis must be placed. The *Traité d'athéologie* (2005) already replaced the question of the existence of Jesus with that of “cette construction nommée Jésus”, this construction named Jesus (p. 158). *Théorie de Jésus. Biographie d'une idée* (Bouquins, 2023) radicalizes this point. The thesis is stated bluntly on the back cover: “Jésus a bel et bien existé, mais comme un mythe qui convoque et cristallise les savoirs de l'époque”, Jesus did indeed exist, but as a myth that summons and crystallizes the knowledge of the age, and: “Jésus a bel et bien existé, mais comme concept. Cette Théorie de Jésus propose la biographie de cette immortelle idée”, Jesus did indeed exist, but as a concept; this Theory of Jesus offers the biography of that immortal idea. In an interview, Onfray is blunter still: “Il n'y a pas eu quelqu'un qui s'appelait Jésus”, there was no one called Jesus. The genealogy is the one we have just followed: Bruno Bauer, Arthur Drews, Paul-Louis Couchoud, Prosper Alfaric. The Dominican Renaud Silly, who has examined it, even judges that to call it, as Onfray does, “ultra-minoritaire chez les historiens”, ultra-minority among historians, “c'est complaisance, courtoisie ou euphémisme”, is indulgence, courtesy or euphemism.

One then sees what is original in Onfray's thesis and what is borrowed. It borrows from Couchoud the idea of a humanized God and the fine formula of the great dream; from Bauer and Drews the argument from Paul's silence; from Strauss, without saying so, the vocabulary of the idea: Strauss already made the human species, and not an individual, the subject of the predicates the Church attributes to Christ (Part Five). “Jesus as concept” is not his formula, but it is indeed his gesture. It owes nothing to the research that, from Schweitzer to Sanders, has established what can be known. And it illustrates precisely Schweitzer's first thesis: each age, each individual creates the Jesus he can love or hate. The liberal Jesus was a professor of morals; Onfray's Jesus is a concept, that is to say the object a philosopher can take apart.

**Why the question matters little, and why it matters.** This debate, which so excites public opinion, nonetheless counts for little in our question. Two of the greatest critics of Christianity did not doubt Jesus. Nietzsche, who makes him the only true Christian (Part Seven), takes him for a real man, and the Church for the betrayal of that man. Engels, who thought the historicity doubtful, held the question to be secondary, and said why. He recalled that Bauer had made Philo of Alexandria “der eigentliche Vater des Christentums” and the Stoic Seneca “sozusagen dessen Onkel”, the true father of Christianity and, so to speak, its uncle; but he at once added that philosophers do not found religions: “Religionen werden gestiftet von Leuten, die selbst ein religiöses Bedürfnis empfinden und Sinn haben für das religiöse Bedürfnis der Massen, und das ist in der Regel nicht der Fall bei Schulphilosophen”, religions are founded by people who themselves feel a religious need and have a sense of the religious need of the masses, and as a rule that is not the case with academic philosophers. And the text of 1894, already cited, saw in early Christianity a movement of the oppressed. What explains Christianity, for Engels, is not the existence or nonexistence of a man; it is the need to which it responded, and which the part devoted to the reasons for belief will examine.

The mythicist thesis here shows its true nature. It believes that Christianity would be refuted by proving that its founder did not exist, and thus remains within the first regime of critique, the regime of error, in its most naive form. Yet Feuerbach had shown, as early as 1841, that the truth of religion lies not in the accuracy of its narratives but in what it says about man; Nietzsche, that its strength lies in the values it installs; Durkheim, that its object is a collective representation, which lives independently of its origin. Whether or not Jesus existed changes nothing in the history followed from Philo to Augustine, that of a figure built by the faith of a community and thought through with the concepts of Greek philosophy: a figure that exceeds on every side what the historian can know of the man. My conclusion is therefore twofold. On historical ground, the debate is settled: Jesus existed, and the mythicist thesis does not have the standing of a competing hypothesis. On the ground of this essay, it is instructive: to deny the existence of Jesus is not to leave religion, and that denial served, in Drews, to found another. What matters for our question is not the man from Galilee, whom historians know poorly but do know; it is the way in which a crucified Jewish prophet became, in four centuries, the incarnate Logos of the philosophers. This transformation Celsus denounced as plagiarism, and Origen celebrated as a fulfilment. It is the true mystery of Jesus, and there is nothing mythical about it.

> **En littérature.** Anatole France, “The Procurator of Judea” (1892) ; Mikhail Bulgakov, *The Master and Margarita* (1940)
>
> In Anatole France's tale, Pilate, grown old and retired to Sicily, converses with his friend Lamia about the years in Judea. Lamia recalls a dancer from Jerusalem whom he loved, and who had followed a young miracle worker from Galilee, crucified for some crime, he knows not which. “Pontius Pilatus fronça les sourcils et porta la main à son front comme quelqu'un qui cherche dans sa mémoire. Puis, après quelques instants de silence : Jésus ? murmura-t-il, Jésus, de Nazareth ? Je ne me rappelle pas”, Pontius Pilate frowned and raised his hand to his forehead like someone searching his memory. Then, after a few moments of silence: Jesus? he murmured, Jesus of Nazareth? I do not remember.
>
> Why here: the tale's ending says in one sentence the result of the historical inquiry, a Galilean prophet crucified among others, of whom the Roman world retained nothing. This is not the mythicist thesis, it is its opposite: Jesus existed, and his existence did not count; what counted is what the faith of a community made of him. Tacitus and Josephus, whom the section draws on, say nothing different.
>
> Bulgakov opens *The Master and Margarita* with a conversation at the Patriarch's Ponds, in Moscow: Berlioz, chairman of a writers' association, explains to the poet Bezdomny that Jesus never existed and that the Gospels are late inventions; a foreigner, Woland, sits down beside them and assures them that Jesus existed, that no proof is needed and that he himself was on Pilate's balcony; there follow the chapters on Pilate and Yeshua Ha-Notsri. Mythicism is here the doctrine of a State that needs the nonexistence of Jesus as the Inquisitor needed his silence: the novel shows that denying the founder does not lead out of religion, and that the devil himself knows it.
>
> Sources: Anatole France, “Le Procurateur de Judée”, *L'Étui de nacre* (1892) ; Mikhail Bulgakov, *Мастер и Маргарита* (*The Master and Margarita*, written 1928-1940, published 1966-1967), ch. 1-3.
### Transition: from the Cross to the God of the philosophers

The religion that the Moderns will seek to leave has now received its form: the faith of a messianic Jewish community, thought through with the instruments of Greek philosophy. The God of the Bible, who speaks, chooses, grows angry and repents, has become in Philo a Being of whom we know only that he exists, and whose Logos secures the link with the world. The Christ of the first communities, a crucified prophet whom his disciples saw alive, has become in Justin the Logos itself, which the philosophers had glimpsed, and in Augustine the Word that the books of the Platonists announced without knowing it incarnate. Celsus was right, against the Christians, to say that their theology owes much to Plato, and wrong to see plagiarism in it: it was a translation, perhaps the most fruitful in the whole intellectual history of Europe.

This translation has a price, which the following centuries will pay. In receiving the God of the philosophers, Christianity also received his demands: a God who must be demonstrated, who must be coherent, who must account for the world and its evil. As long as the Church guaranteed the agreement of faith and reason, the demand remained under control; scholasticism had settled it by distinguishing what reason can prove from what revelation alone teaches. The classical age will set it free, and when Pascal sets the God of Abraham, of Isaac and of Jacob against the God of the philosophers, it is precisely to the God from before the Greek translation that he will appeal.
## Part Three: the classical age, the God of the philosophers

Between the Wars of Religion and the Enlightenment, the question changes shape. The Reformation shattered the unity of Christendom, and Renaissance scepticism, nourished on Sextus Empiricus, shook confidence in reason. Montaigne uses this double shock to humble reason before received faith, and he leaves it to his readers to decide whether he is defending faith or reducing it to a custom. Descartes builds against doubt a metaphysics with God as its keystone, and Pascal rejects it in the name of faith. Spinoza thinks God as nature itself. Bayle draws from the quarrel a conclusion that will scandalize: morality does not depend on belief. Leibniz, finally, answers him by making God the sufficient reason of everything that exists, called upon to account for evil. This is the age in which the God of the philosophers takes shape, and in which, by the same stroke, the weapons of its critique are forged.

### Montaigne (1533-1592): received religion as a custom

The longest chapter of the *Essays* is a filial commission that went wrong. Pierre Bunel, a humanist passing through the château, had left Montaigne's father a fifteenth-century book, the *Theologia naturalis* of the Catalan Raymond Sebond, a professor at Toulouse, who claimed to establish all the truths of the faith by reason alone, by reading the “book of creatures”. The father asked the son to translate it; Montaigne did, and the translation appeared in 1569. Then, to defend the book against its critics, he wrote the *Apology for Raymond Sebond* (*Essays* II, 12), published with the first two books in 1580 and enlarged up to the posthumous edition of 1595. The story of its origins is in the chapter itself: Bunel made his father a present “d'un livre qui s'intitule Theologia naturalis ; sive, Liber creaturarum magistri Raimondi de Sebonde”, of a book entitled Theologia naturalis, or Book of Creatures, by Master Raymond Sebond.

The paradox of the *Apology* fits into one sentence: Montaigne defends a rational theology by ruining reason. To the critics who reproach Sebond for the weakness of his arguments, he does not reply that they are strong; he replies that the contrary arguments are no better, and that human reason, looked at without indulgence, is worth nothing at all. The two hundred pages that follow are the most systematic inventory of human impotence the Renaissance produced. The thesis is laid down at once: “La presomption est nostre maladie naturelle et originelle. La plus calamiteuse et fragile de toutes les creatures c'est l'homme, et quant et quant, la plus orgueilleuse”, presumption is our natural and original disease; the most wretched and frail of all creatures is man, and at the same time the proudest. Man believes himself master of the world and does not even know what his cat thinks: “Quand je me jouë à ma chatte, qui sçait, si elle passe son temps de moy plus que je ne fay d'elle ?”, when I play with my cat, who knows whether she is not passing her time with me more than I am with her? The privilege theology granted to man, created in the image of God and king of creation, is dismantled piece by piece through a comparison with the beasts that always turns to the beasts' advantage.

Then comes reason, and Pyrrhonian scepticism, which Montaigne had read in Sextus Empiricus, serves as the instrument of demolition. The philosophers contradict one another on everything, the senses deceive us, judgment varies with mood and health. Montaigne draws a motto from it, which he says he bears with the emblem of a pair of scales: “Cette fantasie est plus seurement conceuë par interrogation : Que sçay-je ? comme je la porte à la devise d'une balance”, this idea is more surely conceived in the form of a question: what do I know? as I bear it as a motto with a pair of scales. The interrogative form matters: it avoids the negative dogmatism of the sceptic who asserts that nothing is known, and who, in so doing, still knows something.

The weapon then turns around. If reason can do nothing, it can do nothing for religion either, and the only thing that distinguishes one religion from another is the place where one was born. The passage, the most famous in the chapter, is of an audacity that is poorly measured because it is quoted out of context. Montaigne observes that Christians live no better than others, and he concludes: “Tout cela c'est un signe tres-evident que nous ne recevons nostre religion qu'à nostre façon et par nos mains, et non autrement que comme les autres religions se reçoivent”, all this is a very evident sign that we receive our religion only in our own fashion and by our own hands, and in no other way than other religions are received. Then, after listing the human reasons that bind us to ours (antiquity, authority, fear of threats), he adds: “Une autre region, d'autres tesmoings, pareilles promesses et menasses, nous pourroyent imprimer par mesme voye une creance contraire. Nous sommes Chrestiens à mesme tiltre que nous sommes ou Perigordins ou Alemans”, another region, other witnesses, similar promises and threats could imprint on us by the same path a contrary belief. We are Christians by the same title as we are Perigordians or Germans. What makes us Christians is not the truth of Christianity but custom, just as what makes us Perigordians is geography.

The same logic extends to the gods themselves. Montaigne, who had read Lucretius and Cicero, is ironic about the human manufacture of divinities: “L'homme est bien insensé : Il ne sçauroit forger un ciron, et forge des Dieux à douzaines”, man is truly mad: he could not make a mite, and he makes gods by the dozen. The sentence has the air of a maxim of Epicurus or a fragment of Xenophanes, and one understands why the seventeenth-century libertines made the *Apology* their breviary.

Must we then read Montaigne as an atheist in disguise, defending Sebond the better to undermine faith? That is the libertine reading, which has had great champions. I do not think it right, and the conclusion of the chapter says why. Montaigne there quotes a saying of Seneca, whom he calls a pagan “tesmoing”, a witness: “O la vile chose, dict-il, et abjecte, que l'homme, s'il ne s'esleve au dessus de l'humanité !”, oh what a vile and abject thing, he says, is man, if he does not raise himself above humanity! And he replies: the wish is good, but absurd, for man can see only with his own eyes and grasp only with his own hold. “Il s'eslevera si Dieu lui preste extraordinairement la main ; il s'eslevera, abandonnant et renonçant à ses propres moyens, et se laissant hausser et soubslever par les moyens purement celestes. C'est à nostre foy Chrestienne, non à sa vertu Stoique, de pretendre à cette divine et miraculeuse metamorphose”, he will rise if God extraordinarily lends him a hand; he will rise by abandoning and renouncing his own means, and letting himself be raised and lifted up by purely heavenly means. It is for our Christian faith, not for his Stoic virtue, to aspire to that divine and miraculous metamorphosis. The structure is that of fideism: reason is humbled so that grace alone can raise. The humbling of reason is not the negation of faith; it is, in Montaigne as later in Pascal and in Bayle, its condition.

This structure nonetheless has an effect its author does not control, and that is what matters here. By placing faith entirely outside reason, Montaigne leaves reason a single explanation of religion as it exists in the world: custom. He has no need to deny grace; it is enough for him to observe that it cannot be seen, and that people believe what they have been taught to believe. The sincerity of the Catholic Montaigne, who died, according to the account given by Étienne Pasquier, while mass was being said in his room, is beyond question and in any case undecidable; what is not undecidable is that his book already contains, two centuries before Hume, the thesis of *The Natural History of Religion*: people's religion is explained by their nature and their history, not by its truth. Without being a critic of religion in the sense that d'Holbach is, Montaigne brackets religion: without denying it, he suspends judgment on its truth and describes its reality. This is a new form, descriptive rather than legislative, of what I have called the regime of social function, and it is born from the pen of a believer.

Pascal's response is attested, and it is twofold. In the *Conversation with M. de Sacy*, dated to 1655 and known to us only through the account left by Nicolas Fontaine, Sacy's secretary, Pascal sets Epictetus and Montaigne against each other as the two philosophers who saw most clearly, the one the greatness of man, the other his wretchedness; each is right against the other, and only Christianity reconciles the two truths. Montaigne thus serves Pascal as an instrument: he brings down the pride of reason and prepares the place of faith. But the *Pensées* also show what Pascal does not forgive him, and it is not his scepticism, it is his way of dying. Fragment 62 of the Brunschvicg edition attacks the “sot projet qu'il a de se peindre”, the foolish project he has of portraying himself, and fragment 63 something graver: “on ne peut excuser ses sentiments tout païens sur la mort ; car il faut renoncer à toute piété, si on ne veut au moins mourir chrétiennement ; or, il ne pense qu'à mourir lâchement et mollement par tout son livre”, one cannot excuse his wholly pagan feelings about death; for one must renounce all piety if one does not at least wish to die as a Christian; yet throughout his book he thinks only of dying cowardly and softly. And the next fragment says in a word what Montaigne was for him: “Ce n'est pas dans Montaigne, mais dans moi, que je trouve tout ce que j'y vois”, it is not in Montaigne but in myself that I find everything I see there (fr. 64).

Pascal's reproach hits the mark, and it opens the second side of Montaigne, the one that concerns spirituality. The first book contained a chapter with a Ciceronian title, “Que philosopher, c'est apprendre à mourir”, that to philosophize is to learn to die (I, 20), where Montaigne takes up the Stoic meditation on death: “La premeditation de la mort est premeditation de la liberté. Qui a apris à mourir, il a desapris à servir”, the premeditation of death is the premeditation of freedom. Whoever has learned to die has unlearned how to serve. But he already slips in a wish that announces the book's evolution: “Je veux qu'on agisse, et qu'on allonge les offices de la vie tant qu'on peut, et que la mort me treuve plantant mes chous, mais nonchalant d'elle, et encore plus de mon jardin imparfait”, I want us to act, and to prolong the tasks of life as long as we can, and I want death to find me planting my cabbages, but unconcerned about it, and even more so about my unfinished garden. It is this nonchalance that Pascal calls dying softly. And the last chapter of the *Essays*, “De l'expérience”, “Of experience” (III, 13), completes the movement by explicitly refusing any elevation above the human. There Montaigne says of those who want to get outside themselves: “C'est folie : au lieu de se transformer en anges, ils se transforment en bestes ; au lieu de se hausser, ils s'abattent. Ces humeurs transcendentes m'effrayent, comme les lieux hautains et inaccessibles”, it is folly: instead of transforming themselves into angels, they transform themselves into beasts; instead of raising themselves, they bring themselves down. These transcendent humours frighten me, like lofty and inaccessible places. Wisdom lies elsewhere: “C'est une absolue perfection, et comme divine, de scavoyr jouyr loiallement de son estre”, it is an absolute perfection, and as it were divine, to know how to enjoy one's being loyally. And the book almost closes on a sentence that could serve as an epigraph to the whole of Part Twelve of this essay: “Les plus belles vies sont, à mon gré, celles qui se rangent au modelle commun et humain, avec ordre, mais sans miracle et sans extravagance”, the finest lives are, to my mind, those that conform to the common human pattern, with order, but without miracle and without extravagance.

Between the conclusion of the *Apology* and that of the *Essays*, something has tipped over. In the *Apology*, man can rise only if God lends him a hand. In “Of experience”, he no longer has to rise at all: elevation has become a danger, and perfection “as it were divine” consists in inhabiting one's condition loyally. Montaigne does not deny salvation; he stops talking about it. This silence is a spirituality, in the sense in which Hadot and Foucault will take the word, a way of transforming oneself through the exercise of writing and judgment; and it is a spirituality without salvation, which promises nothing after death. Long before modern wisdoms argued over whether they should remain immanent or keep a transcendence (Part Twelve), Montaigne chose immanence, and he did so without polemic, as a practising Catholic. That is why he enters none of the refoundations this essay records: he proposes no absolute, he asks no one to sacrifice themselves to it, and his motto is a question.

> **En littérature.** William Shakespeare, *The Tempest* (1611) ; William Shakespeare, *Hamlet* (1601)
>
> In *The Tempest*, the old counsellor Gonzalo dreams aloud of what he would do with the island: “I' th' commonwealth I would by contraries / Execute all things; for no kind of traffic / Would I admit; no name of magistrate; / Letters should not be known; riches, poverty, / And use of service, none”; no sovereignty, no metal, no corn, no wine; “All things in common nature should produce / Without sweat or endeavour”. The passage copies, through Florio's translation, Montaigne's description of the Cannibals (*Essays* I, 31); Sebastian and Antonio sneer that Gonzalo would be king of it all the same.
>
> Why here: Shakespeare read Montaigne, and laughs at him tenderly. The relativism of customs, “chacun appelle barbarie ce qui n'est pas de son usage”, each calls barbarism whatever is not his own usage, becomes in Gonzalo a utopia, and in his mockers a proof that man cannot do without a master. This is the very movement of the *Apology*: custom explains everything, and founds nothing.
>
> *Hamlet* gives the inner version. To Rosencrantz, who finds that Denmark is not a prison, Hamlet replies: “Why, then 'tis none to you; for there is nothing either good or bad but thinking makes it so. To me it is a prison” (II, 2). Montaigne's “Que sçay-je ?”, put into the mouth of a prince who must act, ceases to be a peace: doubt about custom becomes doubt about oneself, and it is with that doubt that Pascal will reproach Montaigne for “mourir mollement”, dying softly.
>
> Sources: William Shakespeare, *The Tempest*, II, 1 (1611); *Hamlet*, II, 2 (c. 1601).

### Descartes (1596-1650): the idea of the infinite and the guarantor God

The *Meditationes de prima philosophia* (*Meditations on First Philosophy*) appeared in Latin in Paris in 1641, followed by the objections of several learned men and the author's replies, then in Amsterdam in 1642; the French translation by the duc de Luynes, revised by Descartes, appeared in 1647. The book opens with a dedicatory letter to the Faculty of Theology of Paris, the Sorbonne, and this letter states the project in so many words: “Semper existimavi duas quaestiones, de Deo & de Animâ, praecipuas esse ex iis quae Philosophiae potius quàm Theologiae ope sunt demonstrandae”, I have always thought that these two questions, of God and of the soul, were the chief among those that ought to be demonstrated by the aid of philosophy rather than of theology.

The rest of the sentence gives the reason, political as much as philosophical. For the faithful, faith suffices; but infidels can be persuaded of no religion, and of hardly any moral virtue, unless one first proves these two things to them by natural reason, for, says Descartes, “pauci rectum utili praeferrent, si nec Deum timerent, nec aliam vitam expectarent”, few would prefer the right to the useful if they neither feared God nor expected another life. Descartes takes it for granted that human morality hangs on the fear of God and the hope of the hereafter, a thesis that Bayle, forty years later, will set about demolishing in the *Various Thoughts on the Occasion of a Comet*. The comparison is constructed, since Bayle is not aiming at Descartes here; the fact remains that the philosopher who founds modern science shares, on religion, the oldest prejudice of all, that of Polybius and Critias. Descartes even adds, in the same letter, that proving God by Scripture and Scripture by God would seem to infidels a circle. The irony is that his readers, beginning with Antoine Arnauld in the Fourth Objections, will accuse him of committing another circle, by guaranteeing through God the clear and distinct ideas he uses to prove God.

Descartes's gesture is understood by contrast with the tradition he rejects. Thomas Aquinas, in the *Summa theologiae* (I, q. 2, a. 3), had given five ways of proving God, all *a posteriori*, all starting from the world: motion, causality, contingency, degrees of perfection, order; and he had rejected, in the first article of the same question, Anselm's argument, which claimed to conclude from the idea of God to his existence. Descartes reverses the order. He does not start from the world, which he has just doubted to the point of supposing that an evil genius deceives him about everything; he starts from the only point that resists doubt, the *cogito*, “Ego sum, ego existo”, and he looks for God in thought.

The Third Meditation finds in me an idea that cannot come from me: that of the infinite. I do not perceive the infinite by negating the finite, as I perceive rest by negating motion; on the contrary, “manifeste intelligo plus realitatis esse in substantiâ infinitâ quàm in finitâ, ac proinde priorem quodammodo in me esse perceptionem infiniti quàm finiti, hoc est Dei quàm meî ipsius”, I clearly understand that there is more reality in an infinite substance than in a finite one, and hence that my perception of the infinite is in some way prior to my perception of the finite, that is, my perception of God prior to that of myself. How would I know that I doubt, that I desire, that I lack something, if I had no idea of a being more perfect than myself? This idea cannot have been produced by a finite being; it must therefore have been placed in me by God himself, “tanquam nota artificis operi suo impressa”, like the mark of the craftsman stamped on his work. The Fifth Meditation adds the proof known as ontological, a name Kant will give it: existence belongs to the essence of the supremely perfect being, so that it is no less contradictory to think of God without existence “quàm cogitare montem cui desit vallis”, than to think of a mountain without a valley. This is the argument of Anselm of Canterbury, who in chapter 2 of the *Proslogion* defined God as “aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit”, something than which nothing greater can be thought, recast in the language of clear and distinct ideas.

But Descartes's God is not only proved; he works. His function in the system is to guarantee truth. God being perfect, he cannot be a deceiver, for “proculdubio velle fallere, vel malitiam vel imbecillitatem testatur”, the will to deceive undoubtedly bears witness either to malice or to weakness. He therefore guarantees that what I conceive clearly and distinctly is true, and the Fifth Meditation draws the conclusion that makes him the keystone of science: “Atque ita plane video omnis scientiae certitudinem & veritatem ab unâ veri Dei cognitione pendere”, and so I see plainly that the certainty and truth of all knowledge depend on the knowledge of the true God alone.

It is this God that Pascal does not forgive Descartes. Fragment 77, which opens with “Je ne puis pardonner à Descartes”, I cannot forgive Descartes, goes on: Descartes “n'a pu s'empêcher de lui faire donner une chiquenaude, pour mettre le monde en mouvement ; après cela, il n'a plus que faire de Dieu”, could not help making him give a flick of the finger to set the world in motion; after that, he has no further use for God. The Cartesian God is indispensable, but he is so as a foundation: he guarantees mathematics and physics, then withdraws and leaves science to work on its own. He has no history, no covenant, no people; he has spoken to no one. Heidegger, who will make Descartes the moment when the being of beings becomes the certain representation of a subject, will see in this God the accomplished figure of onto-theology, and his reproach joins Pascal's: a God who serves to found is not a God before whom one prays.

Two features nonetheless complicate this picture, and they bear on our question. The first is the doctrine of the creation of the eternal truths. In a letter to Mersenne of 15 April 1630, Descartes maintains that mathematical truths, which are called eternal, were established by God and depend on him like the rest of his creatures, so that God “a été aussi libre de faire qu'il ne fût pas vrai que toutes lignes tirées du centre à la circonférence fussent égales, comme de ne pas créer le monde”, was as free to make it untrue that all lines drawn from the centre to the circumference are equal as he was free not to create the world. The God who guarantees reason is thus also a God above reason, with a freedom that exceeds anything we can understand. Leibniz will see a danger in this. For our purpose, the doctrine shows that the God of the philosophers, in the very thinker who constructed him best, is not wholly reducible to a function: there remains in him an abyss of will that Duns Scotus and Ockham would recognize.

The second feature is the very form of the book. The *Meditationes* are not a treatise. They are six meditations, spread out like six days, written in the first person, which ask the reader to retrace with the author the path from doubt to certainty, and which warn him that he must sometimes dwell for a long time on a single thought to make it familiar. And the Third Meditation, at the moment when God has just been found, breaks off for a contemplation: Descartes says he now wishes “in ipsius Dei contemplatione immorari, ejus attributa apud me expendere, & immensi hujus luminis pulchritudinem, quantum caligantis ingenii mei acies ferre poterit, intueri, admirari, adorare”, to dwell for a while in the contemplation of God himself, to weigh his attributes within myself, and to gaze upon, admire and adore the beauty of this immense light, so far as the eye of my darkened mind can bear it. He adds that, just as faith teaches us that the supreme happiness of the next life consists in this contemplation, so we experience even now that a similar contemplation, though less perfect, gives us the greatest contentment of which we are capable in this life.

This passage creates a difficulty for Foucault's thesis, examined in Part Twelve, of a “Cartesian moment” in which philosophy supposedly separated itself from spirituality: the book that performs this separation keeps the form of the exercise and culminates in adoration. This is my reading, and I offer it as such: the Cartesian moment is not a clean break, it is a conversion of spirituality into metaphysics, in which the contemplation of God remains the summit, but a summit reached by demonstration and not by purification. Descartes is the last great philosopher for whom the knowledge of God is at the same time a joy, and the first for whom that joy is no longer necessary to science. Spinoza, his reader, will take up both ends, the geometrical method and the intellectual love of God, and will try to weld them together.

Descartes therefore does not leave religion. He does more and less: he takes away from theology the task of proving God and entrusts it to philosophy, and he makes God a component of reason. This is at once the triumph of the God of the philosophers and the beginning of his fragility, for a God who is a component of reason can be dismantled by reason. Kant will do so, by showing that existence is not a predicate that can be drawn from a concept, and the ontological proof, after him, will hardly be defended except as an exercise in logic.

> **En littérature.** Paul Valéry, *La Soirée avec monsieur Teste* (1896)
>
> Monsieur Teste is the man who pushed method to its limit: “La bêtise n'est pas mon fort. J'ai vu beaucoup d'individus, j'ai visité quelques nations, j'ai pris ma part d'entreprises diverses sans les aimer, j'ai mangé presque tous les jours, j'ai touché à des femmes. Je revois maintenant quelques centaines de visages, deux ou trois grands spectacles, et peut-être la substance de vingt livres”, stupidity is not my strong point. I have seen many individuals, I have visited a few nations, I have taken my part in various undertakings without loving them, I have eaten almost every day, I have touched women. I now see again a few hundred faces, two or three great spectacles, and perhaps the substance of twenty books. The narrator follows him to the theatre and to his bare room, where he falls asleep observing his own thought: “Je suis étant, et me voyant ; me voyant me voir, et ainsi de suite… Pensons de tout près. Bah ! on s'endort sur n'importe quel sujet…”, I am being, and seeing myself; seeing myself see myself, and so on… Let us think very closely. Bah! one falls asleep on any subject…
>
> Why here: Valéry wrote his tale in the year he was rereading Descartes, and Teste is a cogito turned into a character, a consciousness that keeps of the world only what it has been able to make of it. He lacks precisely what the essay notes in the Third *Meditation*: the idea of the infinite and the adoration that crowns it. Teste adores nothing, and his method leads to no guarantor God. He illustrates by default what Foucault calls the Cartesian moment: the spirituality of exercise converted into a pure discipline of the mind, without an object, an ascetic without transcendence.
>
> Sources: Paul Valéry, *La Soirée avec monsieur Teste* (1896; 1919 edition).

### Pascal (1623-1662): the God of Abraham against the God of the philosophers

On the night of Monday 23 November 1654, from about half past ten in the evening until about half past midnight, Blaise Pascal lived through an experience that he recorded on a sheet of paper, copied onto a piece of parchment, and sewed into the lining of his coat, where it was found after his death. This text, known as the *Memorial*, bears after the date a single isolated word, “Feu”, fire, and continues thus: “Dieu d'Abraham, Dieu d'Isaac, Dieu de Jacob, / non des philosophes et des savants. / Certitude. Certitude. Sentiment. Joie. Paix.”, God of Abraham, God of Isaac, God of Jacob, / not of the philosophers and the scholars. / Certainty. Certainty. Feeling. Joy. Peace.

These two lines contain a critique of religion that is never ranked among the critiques of religion, because it is made in the name of faith. The God “of the philosophers and the scholars” is the God of Descartes, whom Pascal knew, and whom he did not forgive Descartes for having wanted to do without (fr. 77, quoted above): a demonstrated God, guarantor of the eternal truths, first mover, cause of himself. This God Pascal does not deny; he declares him useless for salvation. The true God is the God of a history, that of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the God who reveals himself to persons and not to reasonings. Heidegger will say the same thing of the *causa sui* (Part Ten); Pascal had said it, without the concept of onto-theology, on that night in 1654. And Jean-Luc Marion, a reader of both Pascal and Heidegger, will make this opposition the centre of *God Without Being*.

The *Pensées*, published in 1670 by Port-Royal from the bundles of papers Pascal left (the order of the fragments is a reconstruction by the editors, and the Léon Brunschvicg edition I quote proposes one among others), develop this critique in three directions.

The first is the primacy of the heart. “Le cœur a ses raisons, que la raison ne connaît point”, the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know (fr. 277); and the next fragment: “C'est le cœur qui sent Dieu, et non la raison : voilà ce que c'est que la foi : Dieu sensible au cœur, non à la raison”, it is the heart that feels God, and not reason: that is what faith is: God perceptible to the heart, not to reason (fr. 278). The Pascalian “heart” is not feeling in the Romantic sense; it is the faculty that grasps first principles, immediate intuition. But the formula opens a path that Schleiermacher will take, and that leads to religion as experience.

The second is the hidden God. Pascal takes up the verse of Isaiah, “Vere tu es Deus absconditus” (Is 45, 15), and makes it a thesis: Scripture “dit au contraire que Dieu est un Dieu caché”, says on the contrary that God is a hidden God (fr. 242). One must therefore not seek to prove God from nature, as the apologists do; nature proves nothing, or rather it shows both the presence and the absence of God. Modern man, in the infinite universe, first experiences the void: “Le silence éternel de ces espaces infinis m'effraie”, the eternal silence of these infinite spaces frightens me (fr. 206). Pascal is one of the first Christian thinkers to take the experience of God's absence seriously as a religious experience. Nietzsche, who said he did not read him but loved him, will see in him “das lehrreichste Opfer des Christentums”, the most instructive victim of Christianity (*Ecce homo*, “Warum ich so klug bin”, § 3); Simone Weil will take up the idea of a God who withdraws.

The third is the wager, fragment 233, the most famous and the most misread. It is presented as a calculation of interest, and it is one; but the essential lies elsewhere. “Dieu est, ou il n'est pas”, God is, or he is not: reason cannot decide. Yet one cannot not choose: “il faut parier ; cela n'est pas volontaire, vous êtes embarqué”, you must wager; it is not optional, you are embarked. And when the interlocutor objects that he is so made that he cannot believe, Pascal gives him a method: do as those who believe do, “en prenant de l'eau bénite, en faisant dire des messes, etc. Naturellement même cela vous fera croire et vous abêtira”, taking holy water, having masses said, and so on. Quite naturally this will make you believe and will make you like the beasts.

This “vous abêtira” does not mean “will make you stupid” but “will make you like the beasts”, that is, will submit the machine, the automaton, habit, in place of proud reason. But it says something that all of modern critique will rediscover: belief is acquired through practice, and practice precedes belief. Durkheim will show that rite makes belief and not the reverse; Pascal, for his part, had prescribed it. One sees here how thin the line is between the apologist and the sociologist: the same proposition, that belief is born of habit, serves Pascal to convert and Hume to explain.

Pascal is therefore not a critic of religion in the sense that Spinoza is, but he radically separates the God of faith from the God of reason, and it is this separation that will make possible, on the one hand, the rational critique of theology (if the God of the philosophers is not the true God, he can be demolished without touching faith), and on the other, a religion of the heart that no longer owes anything to proofs. Kierkegaard, two centuries later, will take up his fight against an overly reasonable Christendom.

> **En littérature.** Charles Baudelaire, “Le Gouffre” (1862) ; Jean Racine, *Phèdre* (1677)
>
> “Pascal avait son gouffre, avec lui se mouvant”, Pascal had his abyss, moving with him: the first line of Baudelaire's “Le Gouffre” turns the anecdote of the abyss that Pascal is said to have seen open at his side into the very name of modern anguish, which now finds in the sky only a window open onto nothingness.
>
> Why here: Baudelaire keeps from Pascal the eternal silence of the infinite spaces and loses the God of Abraham who filled it. The abyss without the wager is what fragment 206 becomes when the heart no longer feels anything: the dread remains, the addressee is missing. The poem measures what the essay calls an exit from above, and what happens when the above empties.
>
> *Phèdre* is the tragedy of the hidden God as Lucien Goldmann read it in 1955, in the book that bears that title and that places Racine among the writers of Port-Royal: the dominant reading in its day, now disputed, and which I give for what it is. Phèdre, granddaughter of the Sun, lives under the gaze of a heaven that sees everything and never answers: “Soleil, je te viens voir pour la dernière fois !”, Sun, I come to see you for the last time! (I, 3); then, when the sin is consummated, “J'ai pour aïeul le père et le maître des dieux ; / Le ciel, tout l'univers est plein de mes aïeux : / Où me cacher ? Fuyons dans la nuit infernale”, my forebear is the father and master of the gods; / heaven, the whole universe is full of my forebears: / where can I hide? Let us flee into the infernal night (IV, 6). Grace does not come; the heroine is judged by a God who keeps silent. This is the world of the *Memorial* seen from the side of those who did not have the night of 23 November.
>
> Sources: Charles Baudelaire, “Le Gouffre”, *Les Fleurs du mal*, 1868 ed. (poem of 1862); Jean Racine, *Phèdre*, I, 3 and IV, 6 (1677); Lucien Goldmann, *The Hidden God* (*Le Dieu caché*, 1955), for the reading.
### Spinoza (1632-1677): God is not someone

The *Tractatus theologico-politicus* (*Theological-Political Treatise*) appeared in 1670, anonymously, under a false publisher's imprint; the *Ethica* (*Ethics*) appeared only after Spinoza's death, in the *Opera posthuma* of 1677. This gap between what Spinoza published in his lifetime and what he held back matters: the TTP is a book of political combat, the *Ethics* a system. The critique of religion does not have the same function in the one and in the other, and confusing them produces the most widespread misreading of Spinoza, the one that makes him a masked atheist.

His fundamental thought is contained in a formula from the preface to the fourth part of the *Ethics*: “Deus seu Natura”, God, that is, Nature. The full sentence reads: “Ratio igitur, seu causa, cur Deus seu Natura agit, et cur existit, una eademque est”, the reason, or cause, why God, that is, Nature, acts and why he exists is one and the same. The formula does not abolish God; it displaces him. God is not a being separate from the world who wants something for himself; he is the single substance of which all things are modes, and he acts by the sole necessity of his nature. He therefore has neither design, nor anger, nor favour. What is false in religion is not God; it is the image of a God who resembles a king. One recognizes the gesture of Epicurus, but radicalized: the gods of Epicurus were indifferent, the God of Spinoza is impersonal.

The appendix to the first part dismantles the mechanism of this image. Men are born ignorant of the causes of things and conscious of their desires; they believe themselves free because they do not know what determines them, and they imagine that nature, like them, acts for ends. Hence finalism, and from finalism a God who supposedly arranged everything for man. When such a mind is pressed with questions about the cause of an accident, it goes back from cause to cause “donec ad Dei voluntatem, hoc est ignorantiæ asylum, confugeris”, until you take refuge in the will of God, that is, the asylum of ignorance. The will of God, in vulgar theology, is not an explanation: it is the name that explanation takes when it comes to a halt.

The TTP adds to this analysis an affective genesis and a political thesis. The preface opens on superstition: if men could manage all their affairs by a sure plan, or if fortune were always favourable to them, they would not be superstitious; but they waver between hope and fear. And Spinoza concludes: “The true cause of superstition, what preserves and sustains it, is therefore fear”. This is the thesis of Lucretius, transposed from physics to the psychology of the passions, and Hume will take it up. As for the political thesis, it lies in the radical separation of faith and philosophy. Philosophy aims at truth; faith “requires not so much truth in its doctrines as piety, that is, what moves the mind to obedience” (ch. XIV). Between the two, “there is no commerce and no affinity” (ch. XIV).

Here lies Spinoza's originality: he does not ask for religion to disappear. He asks that it cease to lay claim to truth and content itself with what it actually does: securing obedience to a few precepts of justice and charity. Religion becomes a social practice without theoretical content, which the State can regulate and which the philosopher has no need to combat. Spinoza therefore does not leave religion: he *puts it in its place*. Religion so placed closely resembles Cicero's *religio*, civic observance without metaphysics, and what Durkheim will call the social function of the sacred. Spinoza thinks of religion, after Polybius and Machiavelli but with another rigour, as a useful institution whose truth matters little.

For Spinoza keeps, for himself, the name of God, charged with a meaning the vulgar do not suspect, and here the question of spirituality changes the reading. The fifth part of the *Ethics* culminates in a notion that hasty readers treat as a rhetorical concession and that is the summit of the system: the intellectual love of God. “Mentis Amor intellectualis erga Deum est ipse Dei Amor, quo Deus se ipsum amat”, the mind's intellectual love of God is the very love with which God loves himself (V, prop. 36). This love expects nothing in return, since God loves no one in the human sense; it is the joy that accompanies the knowledge of things in their necessity, *sub specie aeternitatis*. It affords an experience that Spinoza does not hesitate to describe in terms of eternity: “At nihilominus sentimus experimurque, nos æternos esse”, and nevertheless we feel and experience that we are eternal (V, prop. 23, scholium). And it is not the reward of a virtuous life: “Beatitudo non est virtutis præmium, sed ipsa virtus”, blessedness is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself (V, prop. 42).

This last proposition is Spinoza's deepest answer to religion, deeper than the critique of finalism. Every religion of salvation promises a reward: a paradise, an eternal life, a retribution. Spinoza abolishes the reward by interiorizing it: there is no other salvation than the present joy of understanding. This is what Foucault will call a spirituality: a transformation of the subject that gives it access to the true. And this is why the *Ethics* can end on a sentence that sounds like a word of wisdom rather than a theorem: “Sed omnia præclara tam difficilia quam rara sunt”, but all things excellent are as difficult as they are rare. The free man, the fourth part says again, “de nulla re minus quam de morte cogitat; et ejus sapientia non mortis, sed vitæ meditatio est”, thinks of nothing less than of death, and his wisdom is a meditation not on death but on life (IV, prop. 67).

The libertine tradition, and later part of Marxist criticism, read the retention of the name of God as prudence. I believe this reading is wrong. The God of the *Ethics* is not a pseudonym for Nature meant to deceive the censors; he is what allows Spinoza to think Nature as infinite, necessary and perfect, and to ground a blessedness upon it. What is preserved out of prudence is not the name of God; what is preserved, out of conviction, is the structure of the blessed life. Spinoza is a philosopher of the exit from superstition, not of the exit from the divine. Novalis, in a fragment published after his death by Friedrich Schlegel and Ludwig Tieck, called him “ein Gott-trunkener Mensch”, a God-intoxicated man (*Novalis Schriften*, vol. II, Berlin, 1802, p. 487).

This is precisely what his successors will hold against him, and their objections already form a debate. Hegel, in his lectures on the history of philosophy, will say that Spinozism is not an atheism but an acosmism, “Der Spinozismus ist also Akosmismus”, and that there is in him not too little but “zu viel Gott”, too much God (*Vorlesungen über die Geschichte der Philosophie*, Suhrkamp ed., vol. 20, p. 162-163): far from denying God, he denies the world, which is now no more than a set of modes without consistency. Feuerbach and the Hegelian left, conversely, will read Deus seu Natura as an elegant way of saying that only Nature exists. The real objection, the one that will tell, is a different one: Spinoza explains the illusion by ignorance and fear; he does not explain why man clings to it even when it is shown to him. He describes the error; he does not account for the *need* for the error. That need will be the object of Feuerbach, Marx and Freud. Nietzsche, finally, who will recognize in Spinoza a precursor, will also mock the “Hocuspocus von mathematischer Form” with which he armours his philosophy (*Jenseits von Gut und Böse*, § 5): the geometrical form itself will seem to him a mask of the will.

> **En littérature.** Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, *Dichtung und Wahrheit* (1814) ; Isaac Bashevis Singer, “The Spinoza of Market Street” (1961) ; Jorge Luis Borges, “Spinoza” (1964)
>
> In book XIV of *Poetry and Truth* (*Dichtung und Wahrheit*), Goethe recounts his encounter with the *Ethics*: “ich fand hier eine Beruhigung meiner Leidenschaften, es schien sich mir eine große und freie Aussicht über die sinnliche und sittliche Welt aufzutun”, here I found a calming of my passions; a great and free view over the sensible and moral world seemed to open before me. What binds him above all is “die grenzenlose Uneigennützigkeit, die aus jedem Satze hervorleuchtete”, the boundless disinterestedness that shone forth from every proposition, and “jenes wunderliche Wort: „Wer Gott recht liebt, muß nicht verlangen, daß Gott ihn wieder liebe“”, that strange saying: whoever truly loves God must not demand that God love him in return.
>
> Why here: the “strange saying” is proposition 19 of the fifth part, and Goethe makes of it exactly what the essay reads in *Ethics* V, 42: not a doctrine but a way of living, “meine Maxime, meine Ausübung”, my maxim, my practice. The poet confirms through use that Spinoza's God is kept out of conviction: no one finds peace with a pseudonym.
>
> In Singer's story, Dr Fischelson, an old Warsaw scholar who has been rereading the *Ethics* for thirty years in his garret and believes himself dying, marries his neighbour Dobbe, an illiterate old maid; the wedding night gives him back strength he thought lost, and he murmurs before the stars an apology to the divine Spinoza for having become a fool again. Borges, in a sonnet, shows the lens grinder building God in the half-light with the words of his geometry. Both say what the essay says: blessedness is not a reward, and the sage who loses it by loving someone has betrayed nothing.
>
> Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, *Aus meinem Leben. Dichtung und Wahrheit*, part three, book XIV (1814) ; Isaac Bashevis Singer, “The Spinoza of Market Street” (1961) ; Jorge Luis Borges, “Spinoza”, *El otro, el mismo* (1964).

### Bayle (1647-1706): a society of atheists is possible

Pierre Bayle, a French Protestant who took refuge in Rotterdam in 1681 after the suppression of the Protestant Academy of Sedan, published in 1682 a *Lettre sur la comète*, which became the following year the *Pensées diverses sur la comète*. The pretext was the passage of the comet of 1680, which popular belief held to be an omen. Bayle first demonstrates that a comet portends nothing; then he arrives at an unexpected argument. If comets were omens sent by God to warn men, they could only strengthen the idolatry of the pagans, who interpreted them as signs from their gods. God would thus have worked a miracle to fortify idolatry. Now is idolatry, Bayle asks, less grave than atheism? And he answers, in the very title of a section: “Que l'Athéisme n'est pas un plus grand mal que l'Idolâtrie”, that atheism is not a greater evil than idolatry (§ CXIV).

The scandal was immediate, and it provoked an immediate attested response. The pastor Pierre Jurieu, a former friend turned enemy, attacked him precisely on this point; the modern editor quotes his complaint: “On lit le dangereux paradoxe, que l'Athéisme n'est pas un plus grand mal que l'idolâtrie”, one reads the dangerous paradox that atheism is not a greater evil than idolatry. What troubles Jurieu is not so much the theological proposition as its practical consequence: if the atheist is no worse than the idolater, why punish him?

Bayle goes further, and this is the heart of the matter: he maintains that men act not according to their principles but according to their passions, their temperament and their habits; that belief in God therefore does not prevent Christians from being as vicious as anyone else; and that, conversely, the absence of belief does not prevent one from being virtuous. Hence the conjecture, in § CLXI of the 1749 edition: as regards morals and civil actions, a society of atheists “seroit toute semblable à une société de Paiens. Il y faudroit à la vérité des loix fort severes, et fort bien exécutées pour la punition des criminels. Mais n'en faut-il pas par tout ?”, would be quite like a society of pagans; it would indeed need very severe laws, very well enforced, for the punishment of criminals; but are they not needed everywhere? And Bayle concludes with a sentence that would delight a sociologist: “la Justice humaine fait la vertu de la plus grande partie du monde”, human justice makes the virtue of the greater part of the world.

Bayle's argument is therefore not an apology for the atheist; it is a sociology before the term existed: men's virtue does not depend on their belief in immortality, it depends on laws, honour, opinion, temperament. Durkheim will draw the opposite consequence: if morality depends on society, and if religion is society worshipping itself, then religion did not die with God. The confrontation with the thesis that posterity attributed to Ivan Karamazov will be conducted in Part Seven.

Bayle was not an atheist but a sceptical Calvinist, convinced that reason is powerless to establish the truths of faith and that faith must therefore do without reason, which brings him close, by an entirely different path, to Pascal. His defence of the virtuous atheist is a defence of tolerance: if the atheist can be an honest man, the State has no reason to persecute him, and all the less reason to persecute the Protestant or the Jew. The exit from religion he sketches is not an exit from faith; it is an exit from religion as *political cement*. In this sense he is one of the first to think the exit from religion as the end of a structure of society, not of a belief held by individuals.

> **En littérature.** Montesquieu, *Persian Letters* (1721) ; Jonathan Swift, *Gulliver's Travels* (1726)
>
> The story of the Troglodytes, which Usbek tells Mirza in letters XI to XIV, is Bayle's society of atheists turned into a fable, and turned around. A first people, without justice or gods, perishes “par leur méchanceté même”, through their very wickedness; two virtuous families rebuild a happy people whose virtue owes nothing to a Church; then this people, grown numerous, wants a king, and the old man they choose weeps: “Je vois bien ce que c'est, ô Troglodytes ! votre vertu commence à vous peser”, I see well what this is, O Troglodytes! your virtue is beginning to weigh on you; without a ruler, “il faut que vous soyez vertueux, malgré vous”, you must be virtuous in spite of yourselves, but “ce joug vous paroît trop dur”, this yoke seems too hard to you.
>
> Why here: Montesquieu grants Bayle that a society can be virtuous without religion, and answers him that this virtue does not last, because it is tiring: one gives oneself a king as one gives oneself a god, so as no longer to have to be just by oneself. It is Bayle's “la Justice humaine fait la vertu”, seen from the side of those who ask for its yoke.
>
> In Swift, the empire of Lilliput has been torn for three generations by the war of the Big-Endians and the Little-Endians: an emperor having cut his finger while opening his egg at the big end, an edict commanded that eggs be broken at the small end, and “it is computed that eleven thousand persons have at several times suffered death, rather than submit to break their eggs at the smaller end”. This is the war of religions reduced to its cause, a rite, and to its effect, the sacrifice demanded of dissenters: Bayle's critique of political cement, in a single paragraph.
>
> Sources: Montesquieu, *Persian Letters*, XI-XIV (1721) ; Jonathan Swift, *Gulliver's Travels*, I, 4 (1726).

### Leibniz (1646-1716): why something rather than nothing

Leibniz wrote about God all his life, but the two texts in which his thought is summed up are two brief expositions from 1714, written in French during a stay in Vienna: the *Principes de la nature et de la grâce fondés en raison*, published in 1718 in *L'Europe savante*, and the *Monadology*, first published in German translation in 1720, whose French text appeared only in 1840. The only major philosophical work he published in his lifetime is of another kind: the *Theodicy: Essays on the Goodness of God, the Freedom of Man and the Origin of Evil*, published in Amsterdam in 1710 and born of a controversy with a dead man, Pierre Bayle, who had died four years earlier.

Leibniz's thought about God comes down to a question, the most famous in modern metaphysics. It is posed in § 7 of the *Principes de la nature et de la grâce*: “maintenant il faut s'élever à la métaphysique, en nous servant du grand principe, peu employé communément, qui porte que rien ne se fait sans raison suffisante ; c'est-à-dire que rien n'arrive sans qu'il soit possible à celui qui connaîtrait assez les choses de rendre une raison qui suffise pour déterminer pourquoi il en est ainsi, et non pas autrement. Ce principe posé, la première question qu'on a droit de faire sera : Pourquoi il y a plutôt quelque chose que rien ? Car le rien est plus simple et plus facile que quelque chose”, now we must rise to metaphysics, making use of the great principle, little employed as a rule, which holds that nothing happens without a sufficient reason; that is, that nothing happens without its being possible for one who knew things well enough to give a reason sufficient to determine why it is so and not otherwise. This principle laid down, the first question we have the right to ask will be: Why is there something rather than nothing? For nothing is simpler and easier than something.

Everything hinges on the “for” of the last sentence: nothingness needs no explanation, since it is the simplest state; it is existence that demands one. And this explanation cannot be found in the sequence of contingent things, for each refers to another, to infinity, without any of them accounting for the whole series. The *Monadology* formulates the principle (“aucun fait ne saurait se trouver vrai ou existant, aucune énonciation véritable, sans qu'il y ait une raison suffisante, pourquoi il en soit ainsi et non pas autrement”, no fact can be true or existent, no statement true, unless there is a sufficient reason why it is so and not otherwise, § 32) and draws the conclusion: “la dernière raison des choses doit être dans une substance nécessaire, dans laquelle le détail des changements ne soit qu'éminemment, comme dans la source, et c'est ce que nous appelons Dieu”, the ultimate reason of things must lie in a necessary substance, in which the detail of changes exists only eminently, as in its source, and this is what we call God (§ 38). It also takes up Descartes' argument and completes it: the ontological proof is valid only if one first shows that the idea of God is possible, that is, non-contradictory, and Leibniz concludes that “Dieu seul ou l'Être nécessaire a ce privilège, qu'il faut qu'il existe, s'il est possible”, God alone, or the necessary Being, has this privilege, that he must exist if he is possible (§ 45).

The next paragraph contains an attested response to Descartes, and it illuminates the whole difference between the two theologies. “Cependant il ne faut point s'imaginer avec quelques-uns, que les vérités éternelles, étant dépendantes de Dieu, sont arbitraires et dépendent de sa volonté, comme Descartes paraît l'avoir pris et puis M. Poiret”, yet one must not imagine, with some, that the eternal truths, being dependent on God, are arbitrary and depend on his will, as Descartes seems to have taken it, and after him M. Poiret (§ 46). Only contingent truths depend on God's choice; necessary truths depend on his understanding. Leibniz's God does not have the abyss of freedom of the Cartesian God: he is bound by logic, and he chooses according to reasons. He is reason itself become a person. One cannot go further in the rationalization of the divine, and that is why Heidegger, who in 1955-1956 devoted an entire lecture course to the principle of reason, published in 1957 under the title *Der Satz vom Grund* (*The Principle of Reason*), will see in Leibniz the thinker in whom onto-theology speaks its name most clearly: in it God is the sufficient reason of beings, the supreme being that grounds all the others.

This God-as-reason must have reasons for creating this world rather than another, and they can lie only in his goodness. Hence the thesis that made Leibniz famous and ridiculous. Among all possible worlds, God chose the best, for “s'il n'y avait pas le meilleur (optimum) parmi tous les mondes possibles, Dieu n'en aurait produit aucun”, if there were not a best (optimum) among all possible worlds, God would have produced none (*Theodicy*, I, § 8). Evil is not denied: it is classified, and its presence is justified by the whole. “On peut prendre le mal métaphysiquement, physiquement et moralement. Le mal métaphysique consiste dans la simple imperfection, le mal physique dans la souffrance, et le mal moral dans le péché”, evil may be taken metaphysically, physically and morally; metaphysical evil consists in mere imperfection, physical evil in suffering, and moral evil in sin (I, § 21). Metaphysical evil is inevitable, since every creature is finite; physical evil and moral evil are not necessary, but they are possible, and God permits them because the world that contains them is better, taken as a whole, than any world that would not contain them.

The *Theodicy* is an attested response, and its target is named from the preface onwards. Bayle, in his *Historical and Critical Dictionary*, had maintained that the Manichaeans' objections against the goodness of God were rationally unanswerable, and that one must therefore believe against reason. Leibniz replies that faith and reason cannot contradict each other, since two truths do not contradict each other, and he judges his adversary's position severely: “M. Bayle paraît l'avoir pris tout autrement : il se déclare contre la raison, lorsqu'il se pouvait contenter d'en blâmer l'abus”, M. Bayle seems to have taken it quite otherwise: he declares himself against reason, when he could have contented himself with censuring its abuse (“Discourse on the Conformity of Faith with Reason”, § 46). The debate on religion, at the dawn of the Enlightenment, thus does not run between believers and unbelievers: it runs between two believers, one who separates faith from reason to save faith, the other who unites them to save both. The same preliminary discourse counts among the adversaries of this union an Italian “secte de philosophes”, sect of philosophers, who were called “Averroïstes”, Averroists (§ 7), and we saw in Part One what was really the case with Averroes.

The meeting with Spinoza belongs to the same picture, and it calls for caution, for Leibniz himself recounted it in a way that minimized its significance. In November 1676, returning from Paris by way of London, Leibniz stopped at The Hague and visited Spinoza, who would die three months later. The *Theodicy*, thirty-four years afterwards, speaks of it in one offhand sentence: “Je vis M. de la Court, aussi bien que Spinosa, à mon retour de France par l'Angleterre et par la Hollande, et j'appris d'eux quelques bonnes anecdotes sur les affaires de ce temps-là”, I saw M. de la Court, as well as Spinoza, on my return from France by way of England and Holland, and I learned from them some good anecdotes about the affairs of that time (III, § 376). Political anecdotes, then; Leibniz's papers show something else: a note from the same period records that he presented Spinoza with his demonstration of the possibility of the supremely perfect being, and that Spinoza read it. What Leibniz thought at bottom of Spinozism, the preface to the *Theodicy* states bluntly: Spinoza holds that everything came from the first cause “par une nécessité aveugle et toute géométrique, sans que ce premier principe des choses soit capable de choix, de bonté et d'entendement”, by a blind and wholly geometrical necessity, without this first principle of things being capable of choice, goodness and understanding. The whole of Leibnizian theology can be read as the effort to save the God of reason from the God of necessity: to keep Spinoza's rigour, but to give back to God an understanding, a will and a goodness, that is, everything Spinoza had taken from him.

This God is not only a principle; he is also the object of a love, and Leibniz has his spirituality, which is that of the optimist. The *Principes de la nature et de la grâce* end with it: “On peut même dire que dès à présent l'amour de Dieu nous fait jouir d'un avant-goût de la félicité future”, one may even say that even now the love of God gives us a foretaste of future happiness; and this love, though disinterested, produces “une véritable tranquillité de l'esprit ; non pas comme les stoïciens résolus à une patience par force, mais par un contentement présent”, a true tranquillity of mind, not like the Stoics resolved upon a forced patience, but through a present contentment (§ 18). The difference from Stoicism is carefully marked: the Stoic resigns himself to the order, the Leibnizian approves it, because he knows the order is the best. Minds, § 15 says further, are members of the “cité de Dieu”, the city of God, governed by the best of monarchs, “où il n'y a point de crime sans châtiment, point de bonnes actions sans récompense proportionnée”, where there is no crime without punishment, no good action without proportionate reward. The same man spent years, in the last decade of the century, negotiating by letter with Bossuet a project for reuniting the Catholic and Protestant Churches: Leibniz's religion is a religion of reason and concord, which would have the confessions reconciled as truths agree.

The most famous response to Leibniz is not by a professional philosopher, and it is attested. After the Lisbon earthquake of 1 November 1755, Voltaire wrote a poem on the disaster, then, in 1759, *Candide, or Optimism*, whose tutor Pangloss teaches “la métaphysico-théologo-cosmolonigologie”, metaphysico-theologo-cosmolonigology, and proves “que, dans ce meilleur des mondes possibles, le château de monseigneur le baron était le plus beau des châteaux”, that in this best of all possible worlds, my lord the baron's castle was the finest of castles (ch. I). After the earthquake and the auto-da-fé that follows it, Candide, flogged and bleeding, wonders: “Si c'est ici le meilleur des mondes possibles, que sont donc les autres ?”, if this is the best of all possible worlds, what then are the others? (ch. VI). And the tale ends on the answer that dismisses metaphysics: “il faut cultiver notre jardin”, we must cultivate our garden (ch. XXX). Rousseau, in a letter to Voltaire of 1756 that we shall meet again, will on the contrary take up the defence of Providence.

Voltaire caricatures, but he touches a point that the caricature must not make us forget. Theodicy justifies each particular evil by the good of the whole. The criterion asks whether one installs an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded; now theodicy is, in the strict sense, a thought that accepts the sacrifice of the individual to the harmony of the whole, even if it is God, and not man, who decides it. Hegel will transpose theodicy into history, making world history the tribunal where individuals are judged and crushed so that Spirit may advance; and Ivan Karamazov, in Part Seven, will refuse the final harmony if it must be paid for with the tears of a single tortured child. This refusal, a constructed comparison with Leibniz, is the moral response to the *Theodicy*, as *Candide* is its ironic response. I believe it strikes truer: what is refused is not the best of worlds, it is the idea that an individual could be counted as a part of the best.

It would be a mistake to abandon the question of § 7 along with theodicy. Leibniz answered it with God; but the question can outlive the answer. Schelling will take it up in his lectures on the philosophy of revelation, Heidegger will make it the first question of his *Introduction to Metaphysics*, Bergson will hold it to be a false problem, and Wittgenstein will shift the wonder it expresses towards the very fact that the world is. The last part will gather them around this single question, perhaps the purest form of what may be called a spirituality without religion: wonder before existence, which asks for neither cult, nor dogma, nor sacrifice, and which Leibniz, the most rationalist of philosophers, formulated with the greatest clarity.

> **En littérature.** Voltaire, *Zadig* (1747) ; Alexander Pope, *An Essay on Man* (1734) ; George Gordon Byron, *Cain* (1821)
>
> The penultimate chapter of *Zadig* turns the *Theodicy* into a tale. A hermit sets fire to the house of the host who received him and drowns the child of a charitable widow; then he reveals himself to be an angel, Jesrad, and explains: “il n'y a point de mal dont il ne naisse un bien”, there is no evil from which some good is not born, “il n'y a point de hasard ; tout est épreuve, ou punition, ou récompense, ou prévoyance”, there is no chance; all is trial, or punishment, or reward, or foresight. Zadig objects a first time, “s'il n'y avait que du bien, et point de mal ?”, what if there were only good, and no evil?, and a second: “Mais, dit Zadig…”, But, said Zadig…; “Comme il disait *mais*, l'ange prenait déjà son vol vers la dixième sphère. Zadig, à genoux, adora la Providence, et se soumit”, as he was saying *but*, the angel was already taking flight towards the tenth sphere; Zadig, on his knees, worshipped Providence, and submitted.
>
> Why here: twelve years before *Candide*, Voltaire has already found the answer that matters. It is not Jesrad's argument that is refuted; it is the *but* that is prevented from finishing: theodicy asks the individual to sacrifice his complaint, and the tale shows the angel flying off at the precise moment the complaint was about to be spoken. Pope, whom Voltaire will target in the *Poem on the Lisbon Disaster*, had given the same doctrine its most serene formula: “All partial evil, universal good: / And, spite of pride in erring reason's spite, / One truth is clear, whatever is, is right”.
>
> Byron's *Cain* gives Zadig's *but* its tragic form. Cain refuses the inherited fault: “The snake spoke truth; it was the Tree of Knowledge; / It was the Tree of Life: knowledge is good, / And Life is good; and how can both be evil?”; Lucifer, who leads him through the abyss of worlds, says of the Creator: “He is great / But, in his greatness, is no happier than / We in our conflict!”; and before Abel's altar Cain declares: “I will build no more altars, / Nor suffer any”, then kills his brother in the anger the accepted sacrifice arouses in him. This is Ivan Karamazov half a century before Ivan: not the denial of God, but the refusal to count the innocent as a part of the best.
>
