To the children who ask whether they have no father: “Wir sind alle Waisen, ich und ihr, wir sind ohne Vater”, we are all orphans, I and you, we are without a father. Then the sleeper wakes: “Meine Seele weinte vor Freude, daß sie wieder Gott anbeten konnte”, my soul wept for joy that it could worship God again. Mme de Staël freely translated the dream in *De l'Allemagne*, under the title “Un Songe” (A Dream): “les morts s'écrièrent : Ô Christ ! n'est-il point de Dieu ? Il répondit : Il n'en est point.[…] j'ai regardé dans l'abîme et je me suis écrié : Père, où es-tu ? mais je n'ai entendu que la pluie qui tomboit goutte à goutte dans l'abîme, et l'éternelle tempête, que nul ordre ne régit, m'a seule répondu”, the dead cried out: O Christ! is there no God? He answered: There is none; I looked into the abyss and cried out: Father, where are you? but I heard only the rain falling drop by drop into the abyss, and the eternal storm, which no order rules, alone answered me; to the dead children who ask whether they have no father, Christ answers: “Nous sommes tous orphelins, moi et vous nous n'avons point de père”, we are all orphans, I and you, we have no father, and the world collapses. She stops there, without the awakening, and comments: it seems to her beautiful “de transporter ainsi au-delà de la tombe l'horrible effroi que doit éprouver la créature privée de Dieu”, thus to carry beyond the grave the horrible dread that the creature deprived of God must feel.
>
> Why here: six years before “Gott selbst ist tot”, a novelist had put the death of God into the mouth of Christ, and it was through Mme de Staël that the image passed into France, to Nerval, to Vigny, to Musset. The difference between the two versions is the whole stake of the section: in Jean Paul, the dream ends with an awakening and a God regained, as the speculative Good Friday ends with a resurrection; in Mme de Staël, the dream remains without awakening, and it is this version that Nietzsche will keep. The death of God with sublation or without sublation: Hegel and his left, already, in two translations of the same dream.
>
> Sources: Jean Paul, *Siebenkäs*, “Erstes Blumenstück” (1796) ; Germaine de Staël, *De l'Allemagne*, part two, ch. XXVIII (1813).
### David Friedrich Strauss (1808-1874) and Bruno Bauer (1809-1882): myth and imposture

In 1835 and 1836 the two volumes of *Das Leben Jesu, kritisch bearbeitet* (*The Life of Jesus, Critically Examined*) appeared in Tübingen. Their author, twenty-seven years old, who had heard Hegel in Berlin shortly before his death, would lose his post at the Tübingen seminary because of the book, and a professorship in Zurich would be withdrawn from him in 1839 under popular pressure. Rarely has a work of scholarship caused such a scandal, and rightly so: it raises, with all the resources of philology, the question that runs all the way to Onfray, that of the historical value of the gospel narratives.

Strauss's answer comes down to one notion: myth. Before him, two readings were at odds. The supernaturalist reading took the miracles as facts; the rationalist reading, that of a Paulus, also took them as facts, but natural and misunderstood ones: Jesus did not walk on the water, he walked along the shore, and the disciples saw wrongly. Strauss dismisses both readings alike, because both assume that the Gospels report events. He proposes a third way: the gospel narratives are myths, that is, according to the definition he gives in the introduction, “nichts Andres, als geschichtartige Einkleidungen urchristlicher Ideen, gebildet in der absichtslos dichtenden Sage”, nothing other than history-like clothings of early Christian ideas, formed in legend that composes without intention.

Everything hangs on the adverb *absichtslos*, without intention. Myth is not a lie: it has no author who knows he is inventing. It arises in a community that awaits a Messiah and that, convinced Jesus was he, tells his life according to the features the Scriptures attributed to the Messiah: birth in Bethlehem, descent from David, the healings foretold by Isaiah. The narrative is not fabricated to deceive; it is produced by faith itself, which cannot picture the Messiah otherwise. This notion ruins at a stroke the old Enlightenment hypothesis of priestly imposture, found in the clandestine treatise of the *Three Impostors* and which Voltaire only half shook off. The evangelists are not forgers; they are believers who think in images.

But Strauss does not stop there, and this is what makes him more than a philologist. In the preface he asserts that his critique leaves the heart of faith intact: “Den inneren Kern des christlichen Glaubens weiss der Verfasser von seinen kritischen Untersuchungen völlig unabhängig”, the author knows the inner core of the Christian faith to be entirely independent of his critical inquiries. The supernatural birth, the miracles, the resurrection and the ascension, he adds, “bleiben ewige Wahrheiten, so sehr ihre Wirklichkeit als historischer Fakta angezweifelt werden mag”, remain eternal truths, however much their reality as historical facts may be doubted. One recognizes the Hegelian structure: the narrative is the representation, the eternal truth is the concept.

And what is this concept? The *Schlussabhandlung*, the concluding dissertation, states it in pages that are, in my view, the true starting point of Feuerbach. Strauss asks whether the idea of the unity of divine and human nature must have been realized once, in one individual, and never again. He answers that this is not how the idea realizes itself: it does not like to pour all its fullness into a single specimen; it unfolds in a multiplicity of individuals. Then comes the thesis: “Das ist der Schlüssel der ganzen Christologie, dass als Subjekt der Prädikate, welche die Kirche Christo beilegt, statt eines Individuums eine Idee, aber eine reale, nicht Kantisch unwirkliche, gesetzt wird”, this is the key to the whole of Christology: as the subject of the predicates the Church assigns to Christ, one posits, instead of an individual, an idea, but a real one, not unreal in the Kantian manner. And the idea is named: “Die Menschheit ist die Vereinigung der beiden Naturen, der menschgewordene Gott”, humanity is the union of the two natures, God become man. Strauss goes on: humanity is the worker of miracles, since spirit subdues nature ever more; it is the sinless one, it is the one that dies, rises again and ascends to heaven.

We can see what has happened. Strauss has performed the operation Feuerbach will theorize six years later: he has transferred the predicates of Christ to the human species, to the *Gattung*. The very word *Gattung* appears in his text: the properties the Church attributes to Christ contradict one another in an individual; they agree “in der Idee der Gattung”, in the idea of the species. Feuerbach's divinized Man is already there, in 1836, from the pen of a Hegelian who believes he is saving Christianity. The most radical historical criticism of its time thus ends, not in the abolition of the divine, but in its transfer onto humanity. The English reception confirms it in its own way: Strauss's first English translator (1846) would also be Feuerbach's translator in 1854, Marian Evans, who was to become George Eliot. The title of her translation of Feuerbach presents her precisely as “Translator of "Strauss's Life of Jesus"”.

Bruno Bauer goes further, and in another direction. First a theologian of the Hegelian right, he moved to the extreme left at the end of the 1830s, lost his *venia legendi* in Bonn in 1842, and argued in his *Kritik der evangelischen Geschichte der Synoptiker* (1841-1842) that the Gospels are not the product of a collective legend, as Strauss held, but the conscious literary work of one author, the evangelist Mark, on whom the others depend. Against Strauss's *absichtslos*, then, there is an author, an intention, a creation; hence, in the late Bauer, doubts about the historical existence of Jesus himself. Engels, who had known Bauer in his Berlin days, paid him a qualified tribute in 1882 in “Bruno Bauer und das Urchristentum”. He judges the dependence of the Gospels on one another irrefutably demonstrated, and concedes that, since the content of the Gospels proves almost entirely unverifiable historically, “so daß man selbst die geschichtliche Existenz eines Jesus Christus für fraglich erklären kann”, one may even declare the historical existence of a Jesus Christ doubtful. But Engels rejects the Enlightenment conclusion that Bauer comes close to: one is not done with a religion that subjugated the Roman Empire “indem man sie einfach für von Betrügern zusammengestoppelten Unsinn erklärt”, by simply declaring it nonsense patched together by impostors. It must be explained by its historical conditions.

Strauss and Bauer thus trace, as early as the 1840s, the two paths between which the whole historical criticism of Christianity will oscillate, down to Onfray. For Strauss, the narratives are myths born of a community's faith, and their kernel of truth is an idea; for Bauer, they are a literary creation behind which there may be no one at all. The first path leads to a religion of humanity, the second to a thesis of non-existence, and neither leaves religion: the first transfers it, the second reduces it to a fiction whose power remains to be explained, which Bauer does not do and for which Engels reproaches him. As we saw in Part Two, Michel Onfray's *Théorie de Jésus* takes up, without always knowing it, Bauer's path while lending it Strauss's vocabulary: Jesus “as a concept”.

Strauss's story has an epilogue, which prompts an attested response from Nietzsche. Nearly forty years after *Das Leben Jesu*, Strauss published *Der alte und der neue Glaube* (*The Old Faith and the New*, 1872). In it he asks four questions: are we still Christians? do we still have a religion? how do we conceive the world? how do we order our life? To the first he answers no. To the second he answers “ja oder nein, je nachdem man es verstehen will”, yes or no, depending on how one wishes to understand it: there remains a piety towards the universe, “dieselbe Pietät, wie der Fromme alten Stils für seinen Gott”, the same piety as the old-style believer feels for his God, a feeling of dependence on the All, which the Darwinian science expounded in the next chapter does not abolish but orients. The most feared critic of Christianity ends by proposing a religion of the universe, bourgeois and comfortable, in which Beethoven and Haydn take the place of liturgy. In 1873 the young Nietzsche devoted to him the first of his *Unzeitgemäße Betrachtungen*, *David Strauss, der Bekenner und der Schriftsteller* (*David Strauss, the Confessor and the Writer*), in which he makes him the type of the “Bildungsphilister”, the cultivated philistine. Nietzsche does not reproach Strauss for being too critical, but for not being critical enough: he has done away with the Christian God and kept Christian morality intact, without seeing that the one does not stand without the other, the first statement of the objection that *The Gay Science* will make famous. Strauss thus travels in a single lifetime the movement I describe over a century: from the critique of dogma to a substitute religion.

> **En littérature.** George Eliot, *Middlemarch* (1871-1872) ; Alfred Tennyson, *In Memoriam A. H. H.* (1850)
>
> Marian Evans was twenty-six when she completed, in 1846, the English translation of Strauss's *Leben Jesu*, followed by that of Feuerbach in 1854; having become George Eliot, she put into *Middlemarch* a scholar who is the reverse of Strauss. Mr Casaubon devotes his life to “the Key to all Mythologies”, a work meant to trace all the myths of the world back to a corrupted primitive revelation; he dies without having written it, because he knows no German and the Germans have already made his project obsolete.
>
> Why here: Casaubon looks beneath the myths for a revelation, Strauss finds in them a community that believes; the novel makes pre-critical erudition into a domestic tragedy, and German criticism into a rumour arriving from abroad. Dorothea, who marries Casaubon to serve this Key, is the reader of Strauss that George Eliot had been, and the novel leads her to what the essay calls the religion of humanity, without God and without a Key.
>
> Tennyson, in *In Memoriam*, gave Victorian England the formula of its crisis, just as Strauss was reaching it in English: “There lives more faith in honest doubt, / Believe me, than in half the creeds” (XCVI). The line is the exact contemporary of the transfer Strauss performs: faith leaves the dogmas, and it must go somewhere; in Tennyson, into doubt itself; in Strauss, into humanity; in both cases the place does not remain empty.
>
> Sources: George Eliot, *Middlemarch* (1871-1872) ; Alfred Tennyson, *In Memoriam A. H. H.*, XCVI (1850).

### Ernest Renan (1823-1892): the god become an incomparable man

The *Vie de Jésus* (*The Life of Jesus*) appeared in Paris in 1863. Its author had left the seminary of Saint-Sulpice in 1845; he was a philologist of the Semitic languages, and he had just been suspended from his chair at the Collège de France for having, in his inaugural lecture of 1862, called Jesus “un homme incomparable”, an incomparable man. A great publishing success, the book sold tens of thousands of copies within a few months, was translated throughout Europe and provoked hundreds of refutations.

Renan does three things at once, and they must be told apart to understand why Nietzsche would hate him and Dostoevsky would fight him.

The first is a principle of method, laid down in the introduction with a clarity the Germans had lacked. Renan imagines a wonder-worker presenting himself, and a commission of scholars checking his miracle under controlled, repeatable conditions. Never, he observes, has a miracle occurred under such conditions; the wonder-worker has always chosen his subject, his setting, his audience; and most often it is the people themselves, “par suite de l'invincible besoin qu'il a de voir dans les grands événements et les grands hommes quelque chose de divin”, owing to their invincible need to see something divine in great events and great men, who create the legends after the fact. Hence the principle: “un récit surnaturel ne peut être admis comme tel, qu'il implique toujours crédulité ou imposture, que le devoir de l'historien est de l'interpréter et de rechercher quelle part de vérité, quelle part d'erreur il peut receler”, a supernatural narrative cannot be accepted as such, it always implies credulity or imposture, and the historian's duty is to interpret it and to seek out what share of truth and what share of error it may conceal. Renan, like Strauss, looks for the truth behind the narrative, but his method is positivist, not Hegelian: the supernatural is excluded on principle, not by dialectic. And the word “imposture” reappears, alongside “credulity”.

The second is an experience, which Renan recounts with an emotion that did much for the book's success. In 1860-1861 he travelled in Galilee on an archaeological mission. The agreement of texts and places, the harmony of the gospel ideal with the landscape, were for him “comme une révélation”, like a revelation. He goes on: “J'eus devant les yeux un cinquième évangile, lacéré, mais lisible encore, et désormais, à travers les récits de Matthieu et de Marc, au lieu d'un être abstrait, qu'on dirait n'avoir jamais existé, je vis une admirable figure humaine”, I had before my eyes a fifth gospel, torn but still legible, and from then on, through the narratives of Matthew and Mark, instead of an abstract being one would say had never existed, I saw an admirable human figure. The sentence is aimed at Bauer's thesis: against the abstract being one would say had never existed, Renan sets the human figure recovered in Galilee, and he is thus the anticipated adversary of all the mythicists.

The third is a cult. The *Vie de Jésus* is not a cold book: it ends in a genuine doxology. Having said that we moderns labour without reaping, Renan concludes: “Mais quels que puissent être les phénomènes inattendus de l'avenir, Jésus ne sera pas surpassé. Son culte se rajeunira sans cesse; sa légende provoquera des larmes sans fin; ses souffrances attendriront les meilleurs coeurs; tous les siècles proclameront qu'entre les fils des hommes, il n'en est pas né de plus grand que Jésus”, but whatever the unexpected phenomena of the future may be, Jesus will not be surpassed. His cult will renew its youth unceasingly; his legend will draw tears without end; his sufferings will move the best hearts; every century will proclaim that among the sons of men there has been born none greater than Jesus. Christ ceases to be God; he becomes the greatest of men; and his cult is declared eternal. Renan is a pure example of an exit from religion that preserves it in the form of admiration. It is Christianity minus the supernatural, that is, a religion of the great man.

Two attested responses measure what is at stake. The first is Nietzsche's, who read Renan with growing hostility. In *Der Antichrist* (written in 1888, published in 1895), he writes: “Herr Renan, dieser Hanswurst in psychologicis, hat die zwei ungehörigsten Begriffe zu seiner Erklärung des Typus Jesus hinzugebracht, die es hierfür geben kann: den Begriff Genie und den Begriff Held”, Monsieur Renan, that buffoon *in psychologicis*, has brought to his explanation of the type of Jesus the two most unfitting concepts there could be: the concept of genius and the concept of hero. And in *Götzen-Dämmerung* (completed in 1888, published in January 1889), he goes further: what is the use of all the free thought, modernity and mockery, “wenn man mit seinen Eingeweiden Christ, Katholik und sogar Priester geblieben ist!”, when one has remained, in one's entrails, a Christian, a Catholic and even a priest! Renan believes he has left the Church; he has merely changed altars.

The second response is Dostoevsky's. In *A Writer's Diary* of 1873, he recalls Renan, who, unlike Belinsky, stopped before the figure of Christ, proclaiming in his book “полной безверия”, full of unbelief, the *Vie de Jésus*, that Christ nonetheless remains “идеал красоты человеческой”, the ideal of human beauty. The connection with Renan is attested, and we know that the figure of a too human Christ, reduced to morality and admiration, is one of Dostoevsky's constant targets.

Renan opens a possibility that what follows will take up again and again: that of a spirituality without the supernatural, centred on an exemplary figure. Jesus becomes a master of life, like Socrates or the Buddha. The contemporary spiritualities that make Christ a sage, of which Frédéric Lenoir gave a popular version at the beginning of the twenty-first century under the title *Le Christ philosophe* (2007), are the direct heirs of Renan. Nietzsche's objection reaches them all: to admire Jesus as a genius or a hero is to misunderstand him twice, as God and as man. Between Renan and Nietzsche lies the whole difference between an exit that preserves religion as a cult of the great man and a genealogy that refuses every cult.

> **En littérature.** Marcel Proust, *Pastiches et mélanges* (1919)
>
> In *L'Affaire Lemoine*, Proust tells the same swindle, an engineer claiming to manufacture diamonds, in the manner of nine writers. The Renan pastiche lends the author of the *Vie de Jésus* his indulgence towards the impostor and his lyricism of the future: “Patience donc ! Humanité, patience. Rallume encore demain le four éteint mille fois déjà d'où sortira peut-être un jour le diamant ! Perfectionne, avec une bonne humeur que peut t'envier l'Éternel, le creuset où tu porteras le carbone à des températures inconnues de Lemoine et de Berthelot. Répète inlassablement le sto ad ostium et pulso, sans savoir si jamais une voix te répondra : ‘Veni, veni, coronaberis’”, patience then! Humanity, patience. Light again tomorrow the furnace already put out a thousand times, from which the diamond will perhaps one day come forth! Perfect, with a good humour the Eternal may envy you, the crucible in which you will bring carbon to temperatures unknown to Lemoine and Berthelot. Repeat tirelessly the sto ad ostium et pulso, without knowing whether a voice will ever answer you: ‘Veni, veni, coronaberis’.
>
> Why here: Proust caught with a perfect ear what Nietzsche aimed at in a word, the priest “in one's entrails”. The art of pastiche is to keep the music while changing the object: Renan applying to a stock-market affair the fervour, the patience and the Latin quotations he reserved for Humanity is the cult of the great man become style, and style become cult. Humanity is addressed there with the familiar “thou”, as Nature was by d'Holbach, and promised a coronation.
>
> Sources: Marcel Proust, *Pastiches et mélanges*, “L'Affaire Lemoine”, VIII, “par Ernest Renan” (1919; the first pastiches appeared in *Le Figaro* in 1908).

### Transition: from a quarrel of schools to the break

Schleiermacher shifted religion towards experience, to the point of admitting a religion without God; Hegel towards the concept, to the point of making philosophy its truth. Strauss transferred the predicates of Christ to humanity; Renan made Christ the greatest of men and declared his cult eternal. None of them wants to destroy religion; all want to save it by transforming it, and all transform it into something that keeps the place of the absolute: the universe, Spirit, Humanity, the great man.

Against this caution there rises, from 1841 onwards, the generation of the Young Hegelians, who take Hegel's *Aufhebung* and Strauss's transfer at their word and draw the consequence their masters did not dare to draw: if God is man, then one must say so, and stop worshipping him under another name. But in saying so, they merely displace worship once more.
## Part Six: the Hegelian left and its adversaries

In 1840 Frederick William III of Prussia died; his son, Frederick William IV, a pietist romantic, brought Schelling to Berlin to combat “die Drachensaat des Hegelschen Pantheismus”, the dragon's seed of Hegelian pantheism. The Young Hegelians lost their posts, their journals were banned, and the critique of religion became for them the necessary form of political critique in a state that called itself Christian. This is the context of the German texts in this part, published between 1841 and 1845 in a climate of censorship and exile. At the same moment, in Copenhagen and in Paris, two authors who could not be more opposed, Kierkegaard and Comte, answered the same question by opposite routes, one by returning to faith against Christendom, the other by founding a religion without God. And in Frankfurt an old philosopher ignored for thirty years, Schopenhauer, proposed a mysticism without God that would shape Nietzsche's youth.

### Ludwig Feuerbach (1804-1872): the secret of theology

This whole debate pivots on Feuerbach, who must be followed at greater length than is usually done. He is reduced to a formula, theology is anthropology, and to a book, *Das Wesen des Christentums*. But his thinking about religion extends over twenty years, from 1830 to 1851, and it moves: it starts from death, passes through Christianity, takes on Hegel, defends itself against Stirner and ends in nature. At every stage our question returns: did the man who dissolved God into man abolish religion, or did he displace it?

The first book, published anonymously, cost its author his career. The *Gedanken über Tod und Unsterblichkeit* (*Thoughts on Death and Immortality*) appeared in Nuremberg in 1830. Feuerbach, then a *Privatdozent* at Erlangen, denies personal immortality in it: the individual is finite, and what is infinite in him, reason, love, spirit, does not belong to him as his own; death is the act by which the individual returns to the infinite what was not his. The author was quickly identified, and he would never be appointed professor. This starting point sheds light on everything else: the first object of Feuerbach's critique is not God but the beyond, and his first gesture is not to deny the infinite but to take it away from the individual and give it to the species. The young Hegelian of 1830 is still a pantheist of spirit, and it will take him ten years to make the species no longer Spirit, but man.

*Das Wesen des Christentums* (*The Essence of Christianity*) appeared in Leipzig, published by Otto Wigand, in 1841. It struck a whole generation as a liberation, and Engels still remembered it in 1886 in his *Ludwig Feuerbach und der Ausgang der klassischen deutschen Philosophie*: “Die Begeisterung war allgemein: Wir waren alle momentan Feuerbachianer”, the enthusiasm was general: we were all Feuerbachians for the moment. The words “for the moment” already tell what followed.

The thesis is stated in the preface to the first edition: the book means to show “daß das Geheimniß der Theologie die Anthropologie ist”, that the secret of theology is anthropology. The abridged formula of the textbooks, “die Theologie ist Anthropologie”, is not in the first edition in that form, and the difference is no small one: the word *Geheimnis* says that theology *hides* what it is and must be deciphered. George Eliot, in her 1854 translation made from the second German edition, keeps the word: “the secret of theology is anthropology”.

The deciphering rests on a theory of consciousness. Man differs from the animal because he is conscious not only of himself as an individual but of his species, his *Gattung*, that is, of the infinity of his essence: reason, will, love. This infinite essence the finite individual cannot recognize as his own: he projects it outside himself and worships it under the name of God. Hence the central formula: “Das Bewußtsein Gottes ist das Selbstbewußtsein des Menschen”, the consciousness of God is the self-consciousness of man. The mechanism is precise: man, and this for Feuerbach is the secret of religion, objectifies his essence, then makes himself the object of this objectified essence transformed into a subject; he thinks of himself as an object, but as the object of an object, of another being. All the divine predicates are human predicates raised to infinity: God is love, and it is human love that is worshipped without knowing it.

The book tests the thesis dogma by dogma, and it was this testing, more than the thesis, that made its success. The first part, entitled “Die Religion in ihrer Uebereinstimmung mit dem Wesen des Menschen”, religion in its agreement with the essence of man, reads each mystery as the secret of a human reality. The incarnation is the secret of love: God becomes man because love drives him to it, and the love that commands God is higher than he is, which Feuerbach writes with a boldness that announces the conclusion: “Die Liebe ist Gott selbst und außer ihr ist kein Gott”, love is God himself and apart from it there is no God. Prayer is the secret of the heart that knows no limits: “Das Gebet ist die Selbsttheilung des Menschen in zwei Wesen”, prayer is the self-division of man into two beings, a dialogue of man with himself, with his heart. The miracle is the secret of desire: “Das Wunder ist eine Creatio ex nihilo”, the miracle is a creation out of nothing, for whoever makes wine from water makes wine from nothing; and its truth is simple: “Aber was ist das Wunder? Ein realisirter supranaturalistischer Wunsch”, but what is the miracle? A supernaturalist wish fulfilled.

The second part reverses the lighting: “Die Religion in ihrem Widerspruch mit dem Wesen des Menschen”, religion in its contradiction with the essence of man. For the projection is not innocent: placed outside man, his essence escapes his criticism and turns against him. The central chapter, the last before the conclusion, is “Der Widerspruch von Glaube und Liebe”. Love, says Feuerbach, is universal and unites all men; faith is particular and separates those who believe from those who do not. “Der Glaube ist also wesentlich parteiisch”, faith is therefore essentially partisan; “Der Glaube kennt nur Feinde oder Freunde, keine Unparteilichkeit”; and the consequence is necessary: “Der Glaube ist wesentlich intolerant”, faith is essentially intolerant. The flames of hell, he adds, are only the sparks of the furious glance that faith casts on unbelievers. This chapter is the real point of the book: Feuerbach does not reproach Christianity for being false, but for betraying its own heart, love, for the sake of faith, from which love must be wrested.

The second edition, in 1843, adds a preface containing Feuerbach's most quoted sentence in the twentieth century, because Guy Debord made it the epigraph of *The Society of the Spectacle* (1967). I give it in Eliot's translation, made from that edition: the present age “prefers the sign to the thing signified, the copy to the original, fancy to reality, the appearance to the essence”; and for that age, the criticism that dispels illusion is a profanation, “for in these days illusion only is sacred, truth profane”. The sentence says that Feuerbach knew himself to be a profaner and held profanation to be a duty of truth.

Feuerbach owes to Strauss the transfer of the predicates to the species, but he does away with the Hegelian Spirit of which Strauss's humanity was the realization: there is only man, sensuous and natural. He owes to Schleiermacher the idea that religion has its seat in feeling, but where Schleiermacher saw the place where the infinite gives itself, he sees the place where man gives himself the infinite. The reduction Hegel feared is accomplished.

There remained Hegel, with whom Feuerbach settles accounts in two short texts that are perhaps more important than the great book. The *Vorläufige Thesen zur Reform der Philosophie* (*Provisional Theses for the Reform of Philosophy*), written in 1842 and published in 1843 in Switzerland, because of Prussian censorship, in Arnold Ruge's *Anekdota*, open with a sentence that extends the diagnosis of 1841: “Das Geheimnis der Theologie ist die Anthropologie, das Geheimnis aber der spekulativen Philosophie die Theologie”, the secret of theology is anthropology, but the secret of speculative philosophy is theology. Hegel did not go beyond religion, he rationalized it. “Die Hegelsche Philosophie ist der letzte Zufluchtsort, die letzte rationelle Stütze der Theologie”, Hegelian philosophy is the last refuge, the last rational support of theology, and Feuerbach adds with biting irony that, just as Catholic theologians once became Aristotelians to fight Protestantism, Protestant theologians will have to become Hegelians to fight atheism. Hence the method, which fits in one line: “Wir dürfen nur immer das Prädikat zum Subjekt, und so als Subjekt zum Objekt und Prinzip machen”, we need only ever make the predicate the subject, and thus, as subject, the object and the principle. Hegel says: Spirit thinks; Feuerbach: man thinks, and Spirit is only his thought. This is the inversion that Marx, thirty years later, would still claim in the afterword to *Capital*, by setting back on its feet a dialectic that was standing on its head.

The *Grundsätze der Philosophie der Zukunft* (*Principles of the Philosophy of the Future*), of 1843, give the positive version. The first paragraph states the meaning of the whole modern age: “Die Aufgabe der neueren Zeit war die Verwirklichung und Vermenschlichung Gottes”, the task of the modern age was the realization and humanization of God. The philosophy of the future will be sensualist: real being is sensuous being, and truth lies not in the thinking self but in the relation between two sensuous beings, the I and the Thou. “Der natürliche Standpunkt des Menschen, der Standpunkt der Unterscheidung in Ich und Du, Subjekt und Objekt ist der wahre, der absolute Standpunkt”. Here one recognizes, eighty years before Buber's *Ich und Du* (1923), the philosophy of dialogue; Buber acknowledged this debt, which I note without quoting it, not having checked the passage.

Paragraph 60 states plainly what the book of 1841 implied. “Einsamkeit ist Endlichkeit und Beschränktheit, Gemeinschaftlichkeit ist Freiheit und Unendlichkeit”, solitude is finitude and limitation, community is freedom and infinity; and Feuerbach concludes: man by himself is man, in the ordinary sense; man with man, “die Einheit von Ich und Du ist Gott”, the unity of I and Thou is God. This is not a metaphor. The *Theses* had said it of the new philosophy: it has made the attribute the substance, the predicate the subject, and thereby “die neue Philosophie ist die realisierte Idee, die Wahrheit des Christentums”, the new philosophy is the realized idea, the truth of Christianity; and Feuerbach specifies: “Aber eben weil sie das Wesen des Christentums in sich hat, gibt sie den Namen des Christentums auf”, but precisely because it has the essence of Christianity within it, it gives up the name of Christianity. This sentence is the centre of our question: Feuerbach does not claim to abolish Christianity, but to keep its essence and give up its name.

Criticism therefore has a positive task: not to destroy religion, but to *retranslate* it, to give back to man what he has alienated. The necessary turning point of history, says the last chapter of 1841, is the avowal “daß das Bewußtsein Gottes nichts andres ist als das Bewußtsein der Gattung”, that the consciousness of God is nothing other than the consciousness of the species. And he draws the practical rule from it: if the essence of man is the supreme being of man, then the first and highest law must be the love of man for man. “Homo homini Deus est”, man is a God to man, “dieß ist der oberste praktische Grundsatz”, this is the supreme practical principle, and it is the “Wendepunkt der Weltgeschichte”, the turning point of world history. The formula reverses the *homo homini lupus* of the Hobbesian tradition.

Hasty readers miss the essential point: Feuerbach does not merely say that human relations are good, he says that they are *holy*. The relations between child and parents, between spouses, between brothers, between friends, in a word moral relations, are “per se wahrhaft religiöse Verhältnisse”, in themselves truly religious relations; life is, in its essential relations, “durchaus göttlicher Natur”, of a wholly divine nature; it does not receive its consecration from the priest's blessing. Marriage, as the free union of love, is “durch sich selbst” holy. Religion is not abolished but moved from the church to the home, from heaven to the relation between I and Thou. Feuerbach does not desacralize the world, he resacralizes the whole of it.

There is a greatness in this undertaking that what came after has caused to be forgotten. Feuerbach is one of the first to have taken religion seriously *as human truth*: Spinoza put it in its place, Feuerbach listens to it, not as a web of errors but as the deepest expression of man, misunderstood by man himself. Hence, in *Das Wesen des Christentums*, pages of almost religious fervour on love, suffering, the incarnation: Feuerbach does not refute Christianity, he *realizes* it, and theologians have been able to read him as an ally. Karl Barth, in 1927, would declare him entirely right in his interpretation of *religion*, with one restriction: in so far as it bears on religion as the experience of evil and mortal man; and this would be the better to withdraw *revelation* from his critique (see Part Ten).

The first objection, which came almost at once, forced Feuerbach to define himself. In 1844 Stirner accused him, in *Der Einzige und sein Eigentum*, of having achieved no more than a theological liberation from theology: he had done away with the subject, God, but left intact the predicates, love, reason, Man, before which one must still kneel. Feuerbach replied in 1845, in *Wigands Vierteljahrsschrift*, with an article entitled “Über das *Wesen des Christentums* in Beziehung auf den *Einzigen und sein Eigentum*”. The response is attested, and stronger than is usually said.

First, on the predicates: to let them remain is not to let them remain divine. “Werden sie aus Gott in den Menschen versetzt, so verlieren sie eben den Charakter der Göttlichkeit”, transferred from God into man, they lose precisely the character of divinity. A political image: the majesty of the king rests only on the opinion that he is a being apart; let me see him as a man among others, and it vanishes; the same holds for heavenly majesty. Then he turns Stirner's own weapon against him: the Unique One declares that he has founded his cause on nothing, but nothing too is a predicate of God, as mysticism has said a hundred times. “So hat also der »Egoist« doch auch noch seine Sache auf Gott gestellt! So gehört also auch er noch zu den »frommen Atheisten!«”, so the egoist too has founded his cause on God after all! so he too still belongs among the pious atheists! Stirner's formula comes straight back in his face.

Next, on substance, the formula “man is the God of man” deifies nothing. “Der Satz: der Mensch ist der Gott, das höchste Wesen des Menschen, ist daher identisch mit dem Satz: es ist kein Gott, kein höchstes Wesen im Sinne der Theologie”, the proposition ‘man is the God, the supreme being of man’ is therefore identical with the proposition ‘there is no God, no supreme being in the sense of theology’; the first is only the positive, practical, religious expression of what the second expresses negatively. He had written just before, for anyone who might think to take him at his word: “Religion ist Affekt, ist Poesie; voilà tout”, religion is affect, it is poetry, that is all. Finally, he rejects the charge of having sacrificed the individual to the species, since his book makes the sensuous individual, who eats and drinks, the last word of the mystery, and he refuses the heavenly Unique One as well as the earthly one: “Schlage Dir den »Einzigen« im Himmel, aber schlage Dir auch den »Einzigen« auf Erden aus dem Kopfe!”, get the Unique One in heaven out of your head, but get the Unique One on earth out of your head too! The article closes on a self-definition that would become famous: Feuerbach is neither materialist, nor idealist, nor philosopher of identity; he is a man, or rather, since he places the essence of man in community, “Gemeinmensch, Kommunist”, a communal man, a communist. Stirner replied once more the same year, and the quarrel ended there.

Who prevails? Feuerbach's reply seems to me right on one point and weak on the other. Right when it shows that the Unique One, founded on nothing, rejoins negative theology: this is the objection I make to Stirner myself, and Feuerbach saw it as early as 1845. Weak when it claims that the proposition “man is God to man” is purely negative. If it were, why say it in the language of religion? Why call human relations “divine”, marriage “holy”, the unity of I and Thou “God”? It is, Feuerbach replies, the positive, practical, religious way of saying the same thing. But that is the whole question: whoever keeps only the positive expression of a negation keeps religion. His distinction between the name and the thing turns against him: he gives up the name of God, but keeps the thing, that is, worship.

The last works, the ones the textbooks ignore most, confirm this. In 1846 *Das Wesen der Religion* (*The Essence of Religion*) appeared; then, having given thirty public lectures in Heidelberg during the winter of 1848-1849, at the students' invitation and in the fever of revolution, Feuerbach published them in 1851 under the title *Vorlesungen über das Wesen der Religion*. The shift is twofold. Feuerbach widens the object: Christianity was only a religion of man, and there is an older religion, which worships nature. And he changes the principle of explanation, through an avowed borrowing from Schleiermacher. “Das Abhängigkeitsgefühl des Menschen ist der Grund der Religion; der Gegenstand dieses Abhängigkeitsgefühles, Das, wovon der Mensch abhängig ist und abhängig sich fühlt, ist aber ursprünglich nichts andres, als die Natur”, man's feeling of dependence is the ground of religion; but the object of this feeling, that on which man depends and feels himself dependent, is originally nothing other than nature.

Feuerbach takes up Schleiermacher's *schlechthinniges Abhängigkeitsgefühl* and himself recalls, in the *Vorlesungen*, Hegel's gibe: the expression has had a bad reputation among speculative philosophers ever since Hegel, against Schleiermacher, made the witticism that the dog too ought to have a religion, since it feels dependent on its master. He takes the side of feeling against the concept, but turns this feeling towards nature: what man depends on is not a personal God, it is air, water, light, earth, and religion is the affective and imaginary translation of this real relation. The response to Schleiermacher is attested: Feuerbach does not deny the phenomenon described, he shifts its object.

*Das Wesen der Religion* even touches, without knowing it, on the criterion of this essay. In paragraph 29 Feuerbach writes: “Im Opfer versinnlicht und concentrirt sich das ganze Wesen der Religion”, in sacrifice the whole essence of religion is made sensible and concentrated; the ground of sacrifice is the feeling of dependence, fear, uncertainty; but its result and its aim are self-feeling, courage, enjoyment. Feuerbach thus sees that religion is concentrated in sacrifice; he concludes that man sacrifices to reassure himself, I conclude that a religion is recognized by its demand that sacrifices be made to it. It remains to be seen whether his religion of humanity escapes this demand.

The last Heidelberg lecture answers unambiguously. Feuerbach calls on his listeners to will a better life rather than believe in one, and to will it together. But for this, he says, “müssen wir an die Stelle der Gottesliebe die Menschenliebe als die einzige, wahre Religion setzen”, we must put in place of the love of God the love of man as the only, the true religion, and in place of faith in God man's faith in himself, the faith that the destiny of humanity depends on humanity alone, that “der einzige Teufel des Menschen der Mensch[…], aber auch der einzige Gott des Menschen der Mensch selbst ist”, that the only devil of man is man, but also that the only God of man is man himself. Then, by way of farewell, the aim of all his teaching: to turn his listeners “aus Gottesfreunden zu Menschenfreunden, aus Gläubigen zu Denkern, aus Betern zu Arbeitern, aus Candidaten des Jenseits zu Studenten des Diesseits”, from friends of God into friends of men, from believers into thinkers, from people who pray into workers, from candidates for the beyond into students of the here and now. The first lecture had announced the same programme, in almost the same terms: to turn men from theologians into anthropologists, and from theophiles into philanthropists.

I admire this programme, but it must be read to the end: Feuerbach's last word is not that religion is an illusion to be dispelled, it is that the love of man is “the only, the true religion”. He himself supplied Engels with the material for his objection.

Engels formulated the objection in 1886, in what is in my view the best page of his book. Feuerbach, he writes, “will die Religion keineswegs abschaffen, er will sie vollenden. Die Philosophie selbst soll aufgehn in Religion”, by no means wants to abolish religion, he wants to complete it; philosophy itself is to be absorbed into religion. Engels describes the mechanism as I have done from the start: Feuerbach does not accept that love, friendship, compassion, sacrifice are worth something in themselves; he asserts that they reach their full value only if they are given a higher consecration by being called religion. “Sie sollen für voll gelten, erst wenn sie religiös abgestempelt sind”, they are to count fully only once they have been stamped as religious. Then comes an etymological remark that takes us back to the prologue: “Religion kommt her von religare und heißt ursprünglich Verbindung. Also ist jede Verbindung zweier Menschen eine Religion”, religion comes from *religare* and originally means bond; therefore every bond between two people is a religion. Engels mocks: “Solche etymologische Kunststücke bilden das letzte Auskunftsmittel der idealistischen Philosophie”, such etymological tricks are the last resort of idealist philosophy. To this he adds a historical argument: from 1793 to 1798 the Christian religion had so thoroughly disappeared from France that Napoleon had difficulty restoring it, without there appearing, in that interval, the slightest need for a substitute in Feuerbach's sense. And, more harshly, a social remark: in Feuerbach, “die Liebe ist überall und immer der Zaubergott, der bei Feuerbach über alle Schwierigkeiten des praktischen Lebens hinweghelfen soll”, love is everywhere and always the magic god who is supposed to help one over all the difficulties of practical life, and this in a society divided into classes with diametrically opposed interests.

The argument is very powerful. Engels does not reproach Feuerbach for loving human beings, but for needing to call this love “religion”. Refoundation does not lie in the content of what one loves, but in the need to *sacralize* it, which sharpens the criterion set out in the prologue: one refounds a religion not when one preserves values that religion carried, but when one feels the need to consecrate them as absolute and to give them the name of sacred. From here on two degrees must be distinguished: soft refoundation, which consecrates without demanding, and refoundation in the strict sense, which installs an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded, and criticism of which becomes sacrilege; self-offering freely consented to belongs to neither.

Must Feuerbach then be ranked among the refounders, alongside Rousseau and Comte? I believe so, with a nuance that the comparison brings out. Rousseau sacralizes the city, and his civil religion has dogmas, a Sovereign who fixes them, a penalty for whoever betrays them: it demands sacrifice and says so. Comte would sacralize Humanity, with a calendar, temples and a high priest. Feuerbach, for his part, sacralizes the relation: love, marriage, friendship, the unity of I and Thou. His religion has neither dogmas, nor priests, nor penalties, and demands of no one that he immolate himself: it belongs to soft refoundation, the need to consecrate, and not to refoundation in the strict sense, the absolute that can demand the sacrifice of the individual. It is the softest of refoundations, and that is why it has been so fertile: it nourished the “true socialism” that Engels mocked, the religion of humanity of George Eliot, who translated it and made it the morality of her novels, and the philosophy of dialogue in the twentieth century. But it also opened the way to less gentle refoundations: for if man is God to man, someone will end up asking which man, and in the name of which humanity. Stirner asked the question as early as 1844, and the answers of Marx, of Comte and of the political religions of the twentieth century would show that Man, once installed in the place of God, can demand as much as he did.

Feuerbach is thus the textbook case of the need to consecrate. It remains to hear Stirner's objection in its original form, the one given it in 1844 by a former regular of the “Freien”, the circle of Berlin Young Hegelians, with a brutality that Feuerbach's reply did not disarm.

> **En littérature.** Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Das Göttliche” (1783) ; John Steinbeck, *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939) ; George Eliot, *Adam Bede* (1859)
>
> “Edel sey der Mensch, / Hülfreich und gut! / Denn das allein / Unterscheidet ihn / Von allen Wesen, / Die wir kennen”, let man be noble, helpful and good, for that alone distinguishes him from all the beings we know: so opens “Das Göttliche” (*The Divine*). Nature is unfeeling, the sun shines on the good and the wicked alike; “Nur allein der Mensch / Vermag das Unmögliche: / Er unterscheidet, / Wählet und richtet”, man alone can do the impossible: he distinguishes, chooses and judges; and of the “unknown higher beings” we sense, the poem says only: “Sein Beyspiel lehr' uns / Jene glauben”, may his example, that of the good man, teach us to believe in them.
>
> Why here: sixty years before *The Essence of Christianity*, the poem makes exactly the gesture Feuerbach would theorize, making the predicate the subject. The gods are now no more than what the good man allows us to believe; the divine attributes, goodness, justice, help, are transferred to “der Mensch”, man in general, that is, the *Gattung*. Goethe does not sacralize a cult; he consecrates the human, and this is soft refoundation before the term existed.
>
> Jim Casy, the former preacher of *The Grapes of Wrath*, tells Tom Joad that he stopped preaching because he no longer knew what the Holy Spirit was, and that he came to think it is perhaps all the men and all the women we love, and that this is the Holy Spirit, the human spirit. It is the “love of man as the only, the true religion” of the *Heidelberg Lectures*, spoken by an Oklahoma preacher; Casy will die organizing a strike. George Eliot, who had translated Feuerbach in 1854, made it five years later the morality of her first novel, in which the Methodist preacher Dinah Morris has no theology other than sympathy.
>
> Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, “Das Göttliche” (1783) ; John Steinbeck, *The Grapes of Wrath*, ch. 4 (1939) ; George Eliot, *Adam Bede* (1859).
### Max Stirner (1806-1856): Man is a ghost

*Der Einzige und sein Eigentum* (*The Ego and Its Own*) appeared from the same publisher as Feuerbach, Otto Wigand, in the autumn of 1844, dated 1845. Its author, Johann Caspar Schmidt, a teacher at a school for young ladies in Berlin, signed himself Max Stirner. The book opens and closes on the same line, borrowed from Goethe: “Ich hab' mein' Sach' auf Nichts gestellt”, I have set my cause on nothing. Everything lies in this framing: the Unique One rests on no cause that surpasses him, neither God, nor Man, nor Truth, nor the People.

The preface sets out the argument with an irony of great precision. Everyone wants me to serve a cause: the cause of God, of humanity, of truth, of freedom, of the fatherland. But God serves only his own cause, he is perfectly egoistic, and so is humanity. Hence the conclusion: “Gott und die Menschheit haben ihre Sache auf Nichts gestellt, auf nichts als auf Sich. Stelle Ich denn meine Sache gleichfalls auf Mich, der Ich so gut wie Gott das Nichts von allem Andern, der Ich mein Alles, der Ich der Einzige bin”, God and humanity have set their cause on nothing, on nothing but themselves. Let me then likewise set my cause on myself, I who am, just as much as God, the nothing of everything else, I who am my all, I who am the Unique One. And Stirner at once specifies that this nothing is not a void: “Ich bin Nichts im Sinne der Leerheit, sondern das schöpferische Nichts, das Nichts, aus welchem Ich selbst als Schöpfer Alles schaffe”, I am nothing, not in the sense of emptiness, but the creative nothing, the nothing out of which I myself, as creator, create everything.

Stirner's thought generalizes the critique of projection. Feuerbach had shown that God was the alienated human essence. Stirner shows that the human essence is *itself* an alienation. Every instance one places above oneself and to which one must sacrifice oneself is a ghost, a *Spuk*, and whoever believes in it has “einen Sparren zu viel”, a screw loose: “Mensch, es spukt in Deinem Kopfe; Du hast einen Sparren zu viel!” Political liberalism, socialism, the humanism of Feuerbach and of Bruno Bauer are stages of this haunting.

From the first pages of the first part, Stirner sets side by side the two formulas of the moment: “Der Mensch ist dem Menschen das höchste Wesen, sagt Feuerbach. / Der Mensch ist nun erst gefunden, sagt Bruno Bauer”. He concludes, in the second part, that humanism has merely changed the object of fear: “Menschenfurcht” is “bloß eine veränderte Gestalt der Gottesfurcht”, the fear of Man is only a modified form of the fear of God. And then comes the sentence that sums up the whole book and that I have taken as the thread of this essay: “Unsere Atheisten sind fromme Leute”, our atheists are pious people. The feudal analogy follows: in the feudal age, we held everything from God as a fief; in the liberal age, the same relation of vassalage exists with Man; God was the lord, now it is Man; God was the mediator, now it is Man; God was the Spirit, now it is Man. The rights of man themselves are a power received from a superior, which for that reason we call “right” and not “might”.

Stirner goes further still, to the point of turning the language of Christian demonology against humanism: “Der Mensch ist der letzte böse Geist oder Spuk, der täuschendste oder vertrauteste, der schlaueste Lügner mit ehrlicher Miene, der Vater der Lügen”, Man is the last evil spirit or ghost, the most deceptive or the most familiar, the craftiest liar with an honest face, the father of lies. The “father of lies” is the name of the devil in the Gospel of John (8, 44): Feuerbach's Man, the idol of the humanists, is the egoist's devil. And in its place Stirner claims what he calls an “Entheiligung”, a desecration without measure: “Nichts ist ihm heilig!”, nothing is sacred to him.

Stirner formulated as a programme a complete desecration, and he saw that all the critiques of religion of his time were “theologische Insurrectionen”, theological insurrections: revolts against God waged with the weapons and within the categories of theology. The diagnosis is astonishingly accurate.

The objection that strikes him comes from two sides, and it is a sign of his strength that his two main adversaries, Marx and Nietzsche, are also those who profited most from him. On Marx's side, *Die deutsche Ideologie* (written in 1845-1846 with Engels, published in 1932) devotes its longest section to “Saint Max”, a commentary of ferocious irony. The argument fits in a line: the Unique One is an abstraction, who believes he has freed himself from all essences but ignores the material conditions that make him what he is, and his “ego” is the ideological reflection of the isolated individual of commodity society. That the shock of Stirner was decisive in Marx's break with Feuerbach is a widespread interpretation; it is plausible, it is not proven.

On Nietzsche's side, the objection is more subterranean, and I believe it is deeper. Nietzsche may not have read Stirner, we have only indirect testimony of it, but his critique of the subject strikes the Unique One head on. The “I” is for him a grammatical fiction, supposed behind the action because language imposes a subject on every verb; the Unique One, a fixed point that consumes everything without being consumed, is still a substratum, a substance. Worse, Stirner's preface says so itself: the Ego rests on nothing “so gut wie Gott”, just as much as God. The Unique One has not abolished the place of God, he has settled into it. This is the objection Camus will take up in *The Rebel* (1951), one chapter of which is precisely devoted to “The Unique One”: revolt that refuses every limit ends by deifying itself (see Part Ten). Stirner stated the law of the whole series without escaping it himself.

> **En littérature.** George Gordon Byron, *Manfred* (1817) ; Ivan Turgenev, *Fathers and Sons* (1862) ; Flannery O'Connor, *Wise Blood* (1952)
>
> Manfred, alone in his Alpine castle, has summoned the spirits and dismissed them; to the abbot who comes to offer him reconciliation with the Church, then to the demons who come for him at the hour of his death, he replies: “The mind which is immortal makes itself / Requital for its good or evil thoughts, / Is its own origin of ill and end, / And its own place and time”; “I have not been thy dupe nor am thy prey, / But was my own destroyer, and will be / My own hereafter”. Why here: this is the Unique One before Stirner, an Ego that recognizes neither God nor Devil nor Man, and whose only property is itself. But Manfred dies of this sovereignty, and Byron saw what Stirner does not: the Ego set on nothing ends with nothing left to consume but itself.
>
> In Turgenev, Arkady defines his friend Bazarov for his scandalized uncle: “A nihilist is a man who does not bow down before any authority, who does not take any principle on faith, whatever reverence that principle may be enshrined in”. Bazarov dissects frogs, denies art and love, and dies of a cut while dissecting a typhus victim, without having founded anything: Stirner as a novel, and one sees there, as Marx says of “Saint Max”, that the individual without essences holds together only through isolation.
>
> Hazel Motes, in *Wise Blood*, founds in Taulkinham the “Church Without Christ”, where the blind do not see, the lame do not walk and the dead stay dead; he preaches the absence of sin from the hood of his car and ends by blinding himself with quicklime. O'Connor, a Catholic, wrote Feuerbach's demonstration against Stirner: the atheist who founds a Church is a pious man, and knows it to the point of punishing himself.
>
> Sources: George Gordon Byron, *Manfred*, III, 4 (1817) ; Ivan Turgenev, *Отцы и дети* (*Fathers and Sons*), ch. 5 (1862) ; Flannery O'Connor, *Wise Blood* (1952).

### Karl Marx (1818-1883) and Friedrich Engels (1820-1895): religion as symptom

The introduction to *Zur Kritik der Hegelschen Rechtsphilosophie* (*Critique of Hegel's Philosophy of Right*) appeared in Paris in the *Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher* of 1844. It opens with an observation that is at the same time a farewell: “Für Deutschland ist die Kritik der Religion im wesentlichen beendigt, und die Kritik der Religion ist die Voraussetzung aller Kritik”, for Germany, the critique of religion is essentially complete, and the critique of religion is the premise of all critique. Marx does not extend Feuerbach, he closes him: the work of translation is done; what remains is to ask why men needed this upside-down translation.

Marx's most famous text on religion is also the most badly quoted: only its end is remembered, read as an insult. Here it is in full: “Das religiöse Elend ist in einem der Ausdruck des wirklichen Elendes und in einem die Protestation gegen das wirkliche Elend. Die Religion ist der Seufzer der bedrängten Kreatur, das Gemüt einer herzlosen Welt, wie sie der Geist geistloser Zustände ist. Sie ist das Opium des Volkes.” Religious misery is at once the expression of real misery and the protest against real misery; religion is the sigh of the oppressed creature, the heart of a heartless world, as it is the spirit of spiritless conditions; it is the opium of the people.

Everything hangs on this word *Protestation*, which hurried readers forget: religion is not only a consolation that lulls, it is also a complaint that accuses. And opium, in 1844, is not first of all the drug of the underworld: it is the remedy, the painkiller. Marx does not despise the believer: he takes his pain and his revolt seriously, and says only that they mistake their object. Hence the consequence, which absolutely distinguishes the regime of the symptom from the regime of error: “Die Forderung, die Illusionen über seinen Zustand aufzugeben, ist die Forderung, einen Zustand aufzugeben, der der Illusionen bedarf”, to call on the people to give up their illusions about their condition is to call on them to give up a condition that requires illusions. One does not refute a symptom, one treats the disease. Marx has an image of great beauty to say so: criticism has plucked the imaginary flowers from the chain, “nicht damit der Mensch die phantasielose, trostlose Kette trage, sondern damit er die Kette abwerfe und die lebendige Blume breche”, not so that man may wear the chain without fantasy and without consolation, but so that he may cast off the chain and pluck the living flower. And again: “Die Religion ist nur die illusorische Sonne, die sich um den Menschen bewegt, solange er sich nicht um sich selbst bewegt”, religion is only the illusory sun that revolves around man as long as he does not revolve around himself. The programme follows: “Die Kritik des Himmels verwandelt sich damit in die Kritik der Erde, die Kritik der Religion in die Kritik des Rechts, die Kritik der Theologie in die Kritik der Politik”.

The image of the sun betrays something. Religion is the illusory sun; man must revolve around himself, around “seine wirkliche Sonne”, his real sun. The centre changes, but the structure remains: there is still a centre, and it is now man. Marx, in 1844, is still a Feuerbachian; he breaks a year later.

The *Thesen über Feuerbach* (*Theses on Feuerbach*), jotted down in the spring of 1845 and published by Engels in 1888 in a revised version (I quote here Marx's manuscript, MEW 3, p. 5-7), give this shift its theoretical form. The fourth thesis is its heart: Feuerbach dissolves the religious world into its secular basis, but the fact that this basis “sich von sich selbst abhebt und sich ein selbständiges Reich in den Wolken fixiert”, detaches itself from itself and establishes an independent realm in the clouds, “ist nur aus der Selbstzerrissenheit und Sichselbstwidersprechen dieser weltlichen Grundlage zu erklären”, can only be explained by the inner cleavage and self-contradiction of this secular basis. The sixth thesis turns Feuerbach's own concept of species against him: Feuerbach dissolves the religious essence into the human essence, but the human essence “ist kein dem einzelnen Individuum inwohnendes Abstraktum. In seiner Wirklichkeit ist es das ensemble der gesellschaftlichen Verhältnisse”, is no abstraction inherent in the single individual; in its reality, it is the ensemble of social relations. The seventh adds that the “religiöse Gemüt” is “selbst ein gesellschaftliches Produkt”. And the eleventh draws the conclusion for philosophy as a whole: “Die Philosophen haben die Welt nur verschieden interpretiert, es kömmt drauf an, sie zu verändern”.

The sixth thesis is Marx's attested response to Feuerbach, and it bears on the point isolated above. Feuerbach's Man, the species, the *Gattung*, is an abstraction, a mute “Allgemeinheit”, a generality that binds individuals together naturally. This is Stirner's objection turned around: for Stirner, Man is a ghost and only the Ego is real; for Marx, Man and the Ego are two abstractions, and only social relations are real. Marx took from Stirner his critique of Man in order to turn it against him, and one understands why *Die deutsche Ideologie* devotes so many pages to “Saint Max”: Stirner was the most dangerous adversary, because he had seen before Marx what Marx also saw.

Twenty years later, *Das Kapital* (1867) rediscovers the religious structure where one no longer expected it: to understand the fetishism of the commodity, “müssen wir in die Nebelregion der religiösen Welt flüchten”, we must take flight into the misty region of the religious world, where the products of the human head appear endowed with a life of their own. The first chapter goes further and establishes a correspondence between economic form and religious form. For a society of commodity producers, who relate their private labours to one another as abstract human labour, “ist das Christenthum, mit seinem Kultus des abstrakten Menschen, namentlich in seiner bürgerlichen Entwicklung, dem Protestantismus, Deismus u. s. w., die entsprechendste Religionsform”, Christianity, with its cult of abstract man, especially in its bourgeois development, Protestantism, Deism and so on, is the most fitting form of religion. The remark reaches far: the “cult of abstract man” is what Feuerbach proposed as the religion of the future, and Marx suggests that Feuerbachian humanism is not the exit from Christianity, but its purest bourgeois form. And he announces the condition of its real disappearance: “Der religiöse Wiederschein der wirklichen Welt kann nur verschwinden, sobald die Verhältnisse des praktischen Werkeltagslebens den Menschen tagtäglich durchsichtig vernünftige Beziehungen zu einander und zur Natur darstellen”, the religious reflection of the real world can only vanish when the relations of practical everyday life present to men, day after day, transparently rational relations with one another and with nature. The process of social life will strip off its “mystischen Nebelschleier”, its mystical veil of mist, only when it is the product of freely associated men, under their conscious and planned control.

Engels extends Marx in a direction that tends to be neglected. We have seen that, in connection with Bauer, he set aside the explanation by imposture (Part Five). In “Zur Geschichte des Urchristentums” (1894-1895), he goes further and likens early Christianity to the workers' movement: “Wie diese, war das Christentum im Ursprung eine Bewegung Unterdrückter: es trat zuerst auf als Religion der Sklaven und Freigelassenen, der Armen und Rechtlosen, der von Rom unterjochten oder zersprengten Völker”, like the latter, Christianity was originally a movement of the oppressed: it first appeared as the religion of slaves and freedmen, of the poor and those without rights, of the peoples subjugated or dispersed by Rome.

Hence the objection that Marxism invites, and that has been made to it a hundred times without always being well formulated. It is not that communism is “a religion” in the vague sense in which this is said of any enthusiasm; it is more precise. If religion is the protest of the oppressed against a misery whose cause he does not see, and if Engels himself recognizes in early Christianity a movement of the oppressed analogous to the workers' movement, then revolutionary emancipation inherits the *function* of religion. It promises the end of suffering, the reconciliation of man with his essence, a history that has a meaning and an end, a “transparent” society in which nothing will any longer be hidden. Marx can abolish the need for opium only by promising a world in which that need will have disappeared, and this promise has the form of salvation. This is the thesis Karl Löwith will develop in 1949 and Hans Blumenberg will contest in 1966; I discuss it in Part Eleven, because Blumenberg raises against it a serious objection that forces one to specify what it means to “inherit” from a religion.

Marx must be given his best defence. He does not deify humanity in Feuerbach's sense, since he precisely refuses abstract Man; he founds no cult, asks for no veneration, and mocks the “true socialists” who made a religion of love. The critique Engels addresses to Feuerbach holds against all sacralization. If Marxism produced cults, it was his heirs who produced them. I find this defence admissible as far as the texts are concerned, insufficient as far as the structure is concerned. The real sun of 1844 around which man must revolve, the transparent society of 1867, keep the form of an eschatological promise. Marx dismissed the sacred; he did not dismiss salvation.

> **En littérature.** Heinrich Heine, *Deutschland. Ein Wintermärchen* (1844) ; Émile Zola, *Germinal* (1885) ; Bertolt Brecht, *Die heilige Johanna der Schlachthöfe* (1932)
>
> Heine, Marx's friend in Paris in 1844, opens *Germany: A Winter's Tale* with a little harp-girl singing at the border the old hymn of renunciation, and replies: “Ich kenne die Weise, ich kenne den Text, / Ich kenn auch die Herren Verfasser; / Ich weiß, sie tranken heimlich Wein / Und predigten öffentlich Wasser. // Ein neues Lied, ein besseres Lied, / O Freunde, will ich euch dichten! / Wir wollen hier auf Erden schon / Das Himmelreich errichten”, I know the tune, I know the words, I know the gentlemen authors too; I know they drank wine in secret and preached water in public. A new song, a better song, O friends, I will compose for you: here on earth already we mean to build the kingdom of heaven.
>
> Why here: this is the 1844 *Introduction* in verse, written the same year and in the same city: the opium unmasked, then the kingdom carried down to earth. Heine says in four lines what the essay reproaches Marx with: the new song keeps the word kingdom, and the real sun of the earth is still a sun.
>
> *Germinal* shows what this transfer becomes in a strike. Abbé Ranvier, the new parish priest of Montsou, preaches to the miners that deliverance will come from the country priests and the wretched rising together to restore the kingdom of Christ, “en révolutionnaire de l'Évangile”, as a revolutionary of the Gospel, and the poor people no longer understand him; the novel ends with Étienne walking away, hearing beneath his feet his comrades tapping: “Des hommes poussaient, une armée noire, vengeresse, qui germait lentement dans les sillons, grandissant pour les récoltes du siècle futur, et dont la germination allait faire bientôt éclater la terre”, men were springing up, a black avenging army, germinating slowly in the furrows, growing for the harvests of the coming century, and its germination would soon burst the earth apart. Engels would have recognized the priest and the germination: early Christianity and the workers' movement, on the same page, with the same expectation. Brecht, finally, in *Saint Joan of the Stockyards*, has Joan Dark, a lieutenant of the Black Straw Hats, discover that the Salvation Army's soup is the opium that keeps the workers of Chicago quiet; she dies renouncing her God, and the Black Straw Hats at once canonize her to drown out her last words: the Protestation and the opium in the same woman, nearly a century after the 1844 *Introduction*.
>
> Sources: Heinrich Heine, *Deutschland. Ein Wintermärchen*, Caput I (1844) ; Émile Zola, *Germinal*, VI, 2 and VII, 6 (1885) ; Bertolt Brecht, *Die heilige Johanna der Schlachthöfe* (1932).

### Søren Kierkegaard (1813-1855): Christendom against Christianity

While the Hegelian left criticizes religion in the name of man, a Dane criticizes it in the name of God. A contemporary of Feuerbach and Marx, Kierkegaard heard Schelling in Berlin in 1841-1842, in the same lecture halls as Bakunin and Engels, and he read Feuerbach. His conclusion, opposed to theirs, strangely joins their diagnosis: the Christianity of his time is not Christianity.

Two moments must be distinguished. The first is philosophical, and it culminates in the *Afsluttende uvidenskabelig Efterskrift til de philosophiske Smuler* (*Concluding Unscientific Postscript to Philosophical Fragments*, 1846), published under the pseudonym Johannes Climacus. Against Hegel, who claims to understand Christianity by sublating it into the concept, Kierkegaard maintains that Christianity is not a doctrine to be understood but an existence to be lived, and that Christian truth is not objective but subjective. The formula is famous: “Subjektiviteten er Sandheden”, subjectivity is truth. It does not mean that everyone has his own truth, but that religious truth is possessed only in the passionate relation of the existing individual to what surpasses him. Kierkegaard defines faith with paradoxical precision: “Tro er netop Modsigelsen mellem Inderlighedens uendelige Lidenskab og den objektive Uvished”, faith is precisely the contradiction between the infinite passion of inwardness and objective uncertainty. And again: inwardness is so great because it embraces objective uncertainty “med Uendelighedens hele Lidenskab”, with the whole passion of the infinite.

This is a radical response to Hegel: Christianity is a paradox that offends reason, and every attempt to understand it destroys it. It is also a response to Schleiermacher, faith being not a feeling for the universe but a passionate decision before a paradox. And it is a response to Feuerbach. Kierkegaard read *The Essence of Christianity* and, according to a study devoted to this reading, found in Feuerbach a paradoxically useful witness: in his papers of 1844, he judges him consistent, and illuminating by contrast; elsewhere, he says that he sets out Christianity so honestly that it is a pleasure to read him. It is also reported that he said Christianity needed more “traitors” of this kind; I have found this formula only in English translation in an anthology, without a Danish original, and I regard it as unsourced. The logic of this esteem is clear: Feuerbach saw that the Christianity of Christendom is a human religion, all too human; he was merely wrong to believe that it was Christianity.

The second moment, polemical, occupies the last months of Kierkegaard's life. From May to September 1855, he published at his own expense a series of pamphlets, *Øieblikket* (*The Moment*), in which he attacked the official Church of Denmark with unprecedented violence. The thesis is simple: Christendom has abolished Christianity. Kierkegaard says so in a parable about the cunning of mankind: unable to reject Christianity by force, it found a ruse, “vi ere alle Christne, saa er eo ipso Christendommen afskaffet”, we are all Christians, so Christianity is eo ipso abolished. And elsewhere: it is perhaps without analogy in history that a religion should have been abolished in this way, “ved at florere”, by flourishing; the religion of suffering has become the religion of the joy of living, “men har beholdt Navnet uforandret”, but has kept its name unchanged. Kierkegaard piles up the sarcasms: the two thousand churches of the kingdom are, Christianly speaking, a swindle, and so are the thousand priests in velvet and silk.

Kierkegaard's contribution comes down to this. He demonstrates from inside faith what Stirner demonstrated from outside, that established religion is not what it claims to be, but he reverses the conclusion. For Stirner, humanism is a religion in disguise; for Kierkegaard, established religion is a humanism in disguise, a “paganism” living under the name of Christianity: “og saa leve vi (under Navn af Christendom) Hedenskabet”, and so we live (under the name of Christianity) paganism. Both see a sacralization of the human under a divine name; the one concludes that all the sacred must be abolished, the other that true transcendence must be recovered. And Kierkegaard adds an idea that Barth and Bonhoeffer will take up in the twentieth century: authentic Christianity is inversely related to numbers; a single true Christian is enough for Christianity to exist, and when all have become Christians, the concept of Christian is abolished.

Kierkegaard is therefore a critic of religion, and one of the most radical, if by religion one means the institution, the socially reassuring cult, the piety that grounds order; he is not one if one means faith. His position takes up, against established Christendom, the exit *from above* that Pascal had opened: leaving religion in the name of a faith that religion betrays. We shall find it again in Barth (“Religion ist Unglaube”), in Bonhoeffer (a Christianity without religion), in Simone Weil (atheism as purification). But the objection is immediate, and Hegel would have made it: a faith defined by the infinite passion of inwardness before objective uncertainty has, no more than Schleiermacher's feeling, an internal criterion for distinguishing the true God from the idol. Kierkegaard knows it and accepts it: it is the risk of faith. But this risk makes his position a limit case, which one may admire without making it a general answer.

> **En littérature.** Henrik Ibsen, *Brand* (1866) ; Franz Kafka, “Letter to Robert Klopstock” (1921)
>
> Pastor Brand, in Ibsen's drama, demands all or nothing of himself and of those close to him: he refuses the sacraments to his dying mother because she will not give up all her wealth, lets his child die rather than leave his frozen parish, then his wife Agnes, whom he has made give away the dead little boy's clothes; at last he leads his people up the mountain, is stoned, and dies beneath the avalanche. A phantom with Agnes's features has wrung from him the word of his sickness: “Nought or all”; and a voice answers through the thunder: “He is the God of Love”.
>
> Why here: Ibsen denied having read much Kierkegaard; since Brandes, however, *Brand* has been read as the “all or nothing” of the *Postscript* and of *The Moment* carried onto the stage, the infinite passion before objective uncertainty, turned against the lukewarm Christendom of pastors and burgomasters. The play makes visible what the essay calls the limit case: a faith without an internal criterion between God and the idol, which demands the sacrifice of the child and the wife, that is to say, of others. The final voice, *deus caritatis*, judges Brand in the name of love; the sacrifice criterion says nothing else.
>
> Kafka, in a letter to Robert Klopstock of June 1921, imagines other Abrahams: one, ready to obey like a waiter, cannot set out because his house is not in order; another fears that the call is not meant for him and that he will be ridiculous, like the bad pupil who stands up when the top of the class is called. This is *Fear and Trembling* reread by a man who does not have faith: the leap remains, the addressee is missing.
>
> Sources: Henrik Ibsen, *Brand*, act V, English trans. C. H. Herford (1866) ; Franz Kafka, letter to Robert Klopstock, June 1921.
### Auguste Comte (1798-1857): the proof by fact

If every exit from religion tends to refound one, there must be a case in which refoundation is not a hidden symptom but an avowed programme. That case exists. Auguste Comte, founder of positivism, the man who had decreed the end of the theological age and of the metaphysical age, founded a religion.

The starting doctrine is well known. The *Cours de philosophie positive* (1830-1842) sets out the law of the three states: the human mind passes through the theological state, in which it explains phenomena by supernatural wills, then through the metaphysical state, in which it explains them by abstract entities, and finally through the positive state, in which it gives up the search for first causes and confines itself to discovering laws; each branch of our knowledge, says the first lesson, “passe successivement par trois états théoriques différents : l'état théologique, ou fictif ; l'état métaphysique, ou abstrait ; l'état scientifique, ou positif”, passes successively through three different theoretical states: the theological or fictitious state, the metaphysical or abstract state, the scientific or positive state. Religion therefore belongs to the childhood of humanity, and one would expect from Comte a pure and simple exit from religion.

Yet from 1845 onwards, after his meeting with Clotilde de Vaux (October 1844), who died in April 1846, Comte carried out what he himself called a subjective turn, and he founded the Religion of Humanity. The *Système de politique positive* (1851-1854) gives its doctrine, the *Catéchisme positiviste* (1852) its popular exposition, in the form of a dialogue between a priest of Humanity and a woman. The text, perfectly clear, carries out point by point what Feuerbach had announced and what Stirner had denounced.

Religion, first of all, is redefined without God: “La religion consiste donc à régler chaque nature individuelle et à rallier toutes les individualités”, religion therefore consists in regulating each individual nature and in rallying all individualities.
