> For *Answer to Job*, Melville had already written the character. Ahab, in chapter 36, answers Starbuck, who accuses him of blasphemy: “To me, the white whale is that wall, shoved near to me. Sometimes I think there's naught beyond. But 'tis enough. He tasks me; he heaps me; I see in him outrageous strength, with an inscrutable malice sinewing it.[…] Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I'd strike the sun if it insulted me”. Jung would say that Job is morally superior to the God who crushes him; Ahab had thought it, and he had made of this superiority a hunt. Jung's book is an *Answer to Job*; *Moby-Dick* is Ahab's answer, and it ends at the bottom of the sea.
>
> Sources: Hermann Hesse, *Demian. Die Geschichte von Emil Sinclairs Jugend* (1919) ; Herman Melville, *Moby-Dick*, ch. 36, “The Quarter-Deck” (1851).
### Girard (1923-2015): the sacred is born of sacrifice

René Girard is the author in this part who bears most directly on the thesis. Trained at the École des chartes, he left in 1947 to teach in the United States, where he spent his whole career, notably at Johns Hopkins, at Buffalo and then at Stanford, and he came to anthropology through literature. His first book, *Deceit, Desire and the Novel* (1961), starts from an observation about the great novelists, Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust and Dostoevsky: their characters never desire an object directly; they desire it because someone else desires it. Don Quixote wants to be a knight because Amadis was one; Emma Bovary loves through the novels she has read. Human desire is not a straight line between a subject and an object but a triangle whose apex is a model. Girard calls this desire **mimetic**.

Girard recounted that while writing the last page of *Deceit, Desire and the Novel*, on the final conversion of the heroes who renounce desire according to the other, he himself underwent, at the end of the 1950s, a conversion that brought him back to the Catholicism of his Avignon childhood. The biography does not explain the thesis, but it says where the author speaks from: Girard speaks as a believer. Elected to the Académie française in 2005, he remained admired by theologians, debated by anthropologists, and more or less ignored by the philosophers of the French university.

The discovery would have remained a thesis of literary criticism without its consequence. When the model is distant, like Amadis for Don Quixote, imitation is harmless. When the model is close, desiring the same object in the same world, he becomes a rival, the rival an obstacle, and the obstacle an even more fascinating model. Mimetic desire breeds rivalry, and rivalry too spreads by imitation: each imitates the other's violence, differences fade, and the whole community slides towards what Girard calls the **mimetic crisis**, a war of all against all in which nothing any longer distinguishes the adversaries. This is the hypothesis of his second book, *Violence and the Sacred* (1972), and it is there that Girard encounters religion.

How does a community get out of it? Girard answers with a hypothesis that nothing allows us to observe, but which he believes he can read in myths the world over. The violence of all against all, because it is mimetic, can suddenly turn into the violence of all against one. It is enough for an individual, singled out by some trait or other, an infirmity, a strangeness, a royal position, to draw the accusations upon himself; imitation does the rest, and the unanimous community turns against him and kills him. This collective murder has a miraculous effect: peace returns, since all the violence has been discharged onto a single victim. The community, which does not understand what has happened, attributes the return of peace to the victim itself. The victim was guilty, since it was killed; it is beneficent, since its death saved everyone. It becomes sacred, that is, at once accursed and divine. Girard sums up the thesis in a sentence that has become famous, which makes violence the true heart and secret soul of the sacred.

All archaic religion proceeds, according to Girard, from this **victimage mechanism**. Myth is the story of the lynching told from the point of view of the lynchers, who do not know that they have killed an innocent: the god in it is always guilty of something, of incest like Oedipus, of a fault like the Pharmakos. Rite is the controlled repetition of the founding murder, on a substitute victim, human or animal, so as to reproduce its pacifying effects: this is **sacrifice**. Prohibitions are the measures taken to prevent the return of the crisis, by separating what mimetic desire tends to confuse. The gods, finally, are deified victims. Girard here takes up all of Frazer's material, his sacrificed kings and his scapegoats, but he reverses its interpretation: where Frazer saw an error of reasoning, Girard sees a necessary misrecognition, without which the mechanism would not work. If the lynchers knew that their victim was innocent, peace would not return.

Girard builds his demonstration on *Oedipus the King*, which shows how he reads a myth. Thebes is ravaged by plague, the image of the crisis in which differences fade; the city looks for the culprit; Oedipus and Tiresias, then Oedipus and Creon, accuse each other in a series of symmetrical exchanges in which each becomes the double of the other. And the city at last finds its culprit, the lame stranger who became king, who has committed the two undifferentiating crimes par excellence, parricide and incest, the crimes that confuse generations and places. Oedipus is driven out, the plague ceases. For Girard, Sophocles' tragedy is half lucid: it shows the symmetry of the accusations and lets us suspect that Oedipus's guilt might be a collective verdict rather than a fact; but in the end it confirms it, and the myth it takes up never doubts it for a moment. The case of Oedipus throws light, by contrast, on that of Socrates, whom the trial for impiety likewise singles out to the unanimity of a city in crisis; and Plato, as we have seen, wrote the law that would have condemned him a second time. The comparison is constructed: the city of the philosophers was not safe from the mechanism it believed it had mastered.

Ten years later, *The Scapegoat* (1982) applies the same grid to texts that no one takes for myths. Girard starts from a poem by Guillaume de Machaut, which tells how, in the middle of the fourteenth century, the Jews were accused of poisoning the wells during the Black Death and were massacred. The modern reader does not hesitate for a second: the plague is real, the accusation false, the massacre real. From this Girard draws what he calls the “stereotypes of persecution”: a crisis that effaces differences, undifferentiating crimes imputed to the victims, signs that single them out, minorities, the infirm, foreigners, and the collective violence itself. If we know how to read these stereotypes in a medieval text, he asks, why not in myths, which display all of them? The strength of the argument is methodological: it does not ask us to invent an original murder; it asks us to treat myths as we treat chronicles of persecution, by taking the side of the victim. The last great book, *I See Satan Fall Like Lightning* (1999), gives this reversal its biblical name: Satan, in the Gospels, is the accuser, the principle of mimetic desire and of the unanimous crowd, and his fall is the end of his power to accuse without being unmasked.

One can see why Girard matters to this essay. The criterion I have proposed says that a religion is refounded when an absolute is installed in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded. Girard says more: religion is **born** of the sacrifice of an individual to the unanimity of the group. What the essay described as a symptom of refoundation would be the birth certificate of every religion. If the sacred is collective violence transfigured, then each time an exit from religion singles out a victim, Plato's impious man, the citizen who violates Rousseau's civil religion, the class enemy, the traitor to the Nation, it reproduces the founding gesture and refounds, literally, a religion. Dostoevsky's Grand Inquisitor is not only a parable of power; he is, in Girardian terms, the priest who manages the victimage mechanism and who protects the crowd from the truth.

But Girard also reverses the thesis, and it is there that he becomes truly original. There are, according to him, texts that tell the lynching from the point of view of the victim, and that proclaim its innocence: those of the Bible. Joseph, sold by his brothers, is innocent; Job, accused by his friends, is innocent; Isaiah's suffering servant is innocent; the Psalms give voice to the man whom the crowd assails. The Gospels complete this unveiling: the Passion is a unanimous lynching, in which even the disciples fail, but it is told by those who know that the victim is innocent, and who proclaim it. Christianity, for Girard, is therefore not one more sacrificial religion; it is the revelation of the sacrificial mechanism, the revelation of “things hidden since the foundation of the world” (Mt 13, 35), which give their title to the book of 1978, written in dialogue with two psychiatrists, Jean-Michel Oughourlian and Guy Lefort. This revelation has a historical consequence: once unveiled, the mechanism no longer works, since it required misrecognition. The societies that have received the Gospels can no longer reconcile themselves at the expense of a victim without knowing, at least dimly, that they are committing an injustice. Hence the modern concern for victims, which Girard regards as the deepest legacy of Christianity, and hence also, for want of a regulating mechanism, the rise of a violence that nothing any longer contains, the theme of his last book, *Battling to the End* (2007).

For a long time Girard refused to call the Passion a sacrifice, precisely because it unveiled sacrifice; at the end of a long exchange with the Jesuit theologian Raymund Schwager, he finally accepted the word in a new sense, that of the gift of self that refuses violence instead of undergoing it. This dispute over vocabulary is not secondary: it means that Christianity, for Girard, is at once the exit from sacrificial religion and a religion, which is the very thesis of Marcel Gauchet, whom we shall read in the part on secularization: Christianity as the religion of the exit from religion. The comparison is constructed, for the paths differ, Gauchet starting from political history and Girard from the anthropology of desire; yet the two bodies of thought share the same weakness, which is to make Christianity the end point of the religious history of humanity.

Girard responded, in attested fashion, to several authors in this essay. Against Freud, he takes up in *Violence and the Sacred* the hypothesis of *Totem und Tabu* (1912-1913), the original murder of the father by the horde of sons, and he pays tribute to him for having glimpsed the founding murder; but he reproaches him for having tied it to sexual desire and to the father, instead of to mimetic rivalry and to the arbitrary victim. Against Durkheim, he accepts that the sacred is social, but he refuses the idea that society worships itself in it: what the community worships is its own violence transfigured, and the reverse side of Durkheimian unanimity is a corpse. It is against Nietzsche that his response goes furthest. Nietzsche had ended *Ecce homo* with the formula “Dionysos gegen den Gekreuzigten”, Dionysus against the Crucified. Girard takes up the formula as the title of an essay and agrees with Nietzsche on the diagnosis: the difference between Dionysus and Christ does not lie in the story, for both die under the blows of a crowd; it lies in the point of view, since the Dionysian myth takes the side of the lynchers and the Gospel that of the victim. Nietzsche saw this better than the theologians, and he chose Dionysus, that is to say the crowd. From this Girard draws a grave charge against Nietzsche: the will to power that despises compassion for the weak is the return, in philosophy, of the persecutors' point of view.

There remain the objections of the anthropologists. The first concerns method: a founding mechanism that leaves traces only in the myths that conceal it is, by construction, unverifiable, and any absence of a victim in a myth can be read as further proof of concealment. The second concerns universality: many societies practise sacrifice as an exchange, a gift, a meal shared with the gods, without the lynching scene being found in it, and field ethnologists have often reproached Girard for treating the ethnographic material as Frazer did, by selective comparisons. The third concerns closure: a theory that makes its own religion the key to all the others lays itself open to the suspicion of having been constructed to lead there. These objections are strong, and Girard has not, I believe, entirely answered them.

In this immense construction two storeys must be separated, one of which carries my conviction and the other not. The first is anthropological: mimetic desire, the crisis, the singling out of a scapegoat, the misrecognition that allows the crowd to believe itself innocent. It is a hypothesis, unverifiable in its originary version, but of considerable descriptive power, and the history of the twentieth century, with its designated victims and its unanimous crowds, has given it terrible confirmations. It gives the criterion of this essay an anthropological foundation. The second storey is apologetic: the Bible and the Gospels would be the only revelation of this mechanism, and Christianity the only way out. It seems to me much more fragile. It neglects the other traditions that have thought the innocence of the victim or refused sacrifice, Greek tragedy itself, which sometimes lets the victim's lament be heard, or the refusal of blood sacrifice among the prophets, which Girard indeed ties to the Bible, but also the wisdoms of India or China, which he hardly examines. And it makes historical Christianity, which had its stakes and its Inquisitors, the vehicle of a revelation it has betrayed so often that Dostoevsky could imagine Christ condemned a second time by his Church. Girard replies that the Church betrayed the Gospels, and that betrayal presupposes revelation. So be it. But then the exit from sacrifice no longer belongs to a religion: it belongs to anyone who refuses to join the crowd, believer or not. I shall draw the consequence of this in the conclusion, against Girard's apologetics and with his anthropology.

> **En littérature.** Euripides, *The Bacchae* (405 BCE) ; Jean de La Fontaine, “Les Animaux malades de la peste” (1678) ; Shirley Jackson, “The Lottery” (1948)
>
> In *The Bacchae*, the messenger tells what the women of Thebes, possessed by Dionysus, are doing on Cithaeron: “tu aurais vu une d'elles déchirer en deux, de ses mains, une génisse aux lourdes mamelles et mugissante ; et d'autres mettaient les vaches en lambeaux ; et tu aurais vu les côtes et les pieds fourchus sauter de toutes parts, et les morceaux, suspendus aux sapins, dégoutter de sang”, you would have seen one of them tear in two, with her hands, a lowing heifer with heavy udders; and others were rending the cows to shreds; and you would have seen ribs and cloven hooves flying on every side, and the pieces, hanging from the fir trees, dripping with blood. Then it is King Pentheus, who has come to spy on them, who is torn to pieces by his own mother, Agave; she returns in triumph with the head she believes to be a lion's, and her father Cadmus slowly brings her back to reason, until the cry: “Non ! Mais je tiens la tête de Pentheus, malheureuse !”, No! But I am holding the head of Pentheus, wretched woman that I am!
>
> Why here: this is the text on which Girard built *Violence and the Sacred*, and one need only read it to see why. The unanimous crowd, the victim first royal and then a beast, the god who demands and who feeds on the lynching, the misrecognition that lets the mother carry the head as a trophy: the whole mechanism is there, and Euripides shows it at the moment when Athens is dying. “Dionysus against the Crucified” is not a formula: it is this scene against another.
>
> La Fontaine turned the scapegoat into a fable. Plague strikes the animals; the lion proposes that each confess his faults and that the guiltiest be sacrificed; the powerful absolve one another, and it is the donkey, who grazed the grass of a meadow, that is condemned: “A ces mots on cria haro sur le baudet”, at these words they all cried out against the donkey; the moral: “Selon que vous serez puissant ou misérable, / Les jugemens de Cour vous rendront blanc ou noir”, according as you are powerful or wretched, / the judgements of the Court will make you white or black. Shirley Jackson, in 1948, described the same rite in an American village, on the June morning when lots are drawn, with slips of paper in a black box, for the woman whom the whole village, its children included, will stone so that the harvest may be good; *The New Yorker* received more indignant letters than for any other story. The fable and the story show what Girard holds to be universal and what the ethnologists dispute: the victim designated by the crowd, and the crowd that does not see itself.
>
> Sources: Euripides, *The Bacchae*, trans. Leconte de Lisle (405 BCE) ; Jean de La Fontaine, *Fables*, VII, 1 (1678) ; Shirley Jackson, “The Lottery”, *The New Yorker*, 26 June 1948.

### Becker (1924-1974): religion as heroism against death

Ernest Becker was neither a theologian nor a professional philosopher, but an American cultural anthropologist who had spent his career on the margins of the university, dismissed or barely tolerated from one post to the next. *The Denial of Death* appeared in 1973; Becker died of cancer in March 1974, and the book received the Pulitzer Prize for general non-fiction two months later. This chronology made the book's legend: written by a man who knew he was dying and who drew from it a theory of the whole of culture. But the legend must not hide the thesis, which gives our question an answer that neither Feuerbach nor Freud had formulated in this form.

The thesis can be put in a few words, and I paraphrase it for want of having consulted the original text: the idea of death, and the terror it inspires, haunt the human animal more than anything else, and they are the mainspring of its activity. Man is the only animal that knows it will die; Bergson had written as much in 1932 in almost identical terms, “Les animaux ne savent pas qu'ils doivent mourir”, animals do not know that they must die, and he already drew from it a function of religion, “une réaction défensive de la nature contre la représentation, par l'intelligence, de l'inévitabilité de la mort”, a defensive reaction of nature against the representation, by the intelligence, of the inevitability of death. Becker does not cite Bergson, and the encounter is my doing; but it shows that the intuition is not peculiar to American psychology. Becker adds to it an anthropology of the hero. Man is a living contradiction: a mind capable of representing the infinite, housed in a body that decays. Unable to look this contradiction in the face, he covers it over with what Becker calls a *causa sui* project, the effort to be one's own cause, and with heroism, that is, the conviction of having a worth that outlasts death. Every culture is then a hero system: a set of roles, stories and rites that allows each person to believe himself important beyond his own disappearance.

Religion is, for Becker, the vastest of these systems, and his position is not a simple reduction. Becker starts from Freud, but he corrects him through Otto Rank, the former disciple whom Freud had rejected, and through Kierkegaard. From Rank he retains that the fear of death is more fundamental than sexuality, and that the Oedipus complex itself is a *causa sui* project, the child's desire to become his own father. From Kierkegaard he retains the analysis of anxiety as the dizziness of freedom before nothingness, and the conclusion that the only honest way out is faith, which acknowledges dependence instead of denying it. The book's last chapter is ambiguous: Becker judges there that religion in the Kierkegaardian sense, the faith that accepts creatureliness, is the highest heroism, because it alone does not lie about the human condition. He is no apologist; he says only that, if one must choose a vital lie, the one that admits itself as such is better than those that do not know themselves. This is Pascal's position, which Becker arrives at without having sought it: Pascalian *divertissement* is the mechanism of denial he describes, “les hommes n'ayant pu guérir la mort, la misère, l'ignorance, ils se sont avisés, pour se rendre heureux, de n'y point penser”, men, having been unable to cure death, wretchedness and ignorance, have taken it into their heads, in order to be happy, not to think about them.

The posthumous book *Escape from Evil* (1975) draws from this anthropology a consequence that bears directly on the criterion. People who live by hero systems cannot bear others to contest them, for contestation reopens the question the system was meant to close. Social evil then arises from the denial of death: others are sacrificed to prove to oneself that one will not die, enemies are designated so that one's own symbolic immortality remains uncontested. This is a theory of sacrifice, which meets Girard's by another path: the two men did not read each other, as far as I know, and the comparison is constructed. For the one, sacrifice protects the individual against death; for the other, it protects the community against its own violence. In both cases, religion is inseparable from a victim.

Experimental psychology has sought to put this thesis to the test. From 1986 onwards Jeff Greenberg, Sheldon Solomon and Tom Pyszczynski drew from it a terror management theory: worldviews and self-esteem would serve as a buffer against death anxiety, and being reminded of death (mortality salience) should strengthen attachment to one's worldview and hostility towards those who contest it. In the founding experiment, in 1989, judges first invited to think about their own death set heavier bonds for a prostitute: “judges recommended especially harsh bonds for a prostitute when mortality was made salient” (A. Rosenblatt et al., *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 57, 1989, p. 681-690, abstract). But a large coordinated replication, *Many Labs 4* (R. Klein et al., *Collabra: Psychology* 8, 2022), dealing with another classic experiment of the theory (Greenberg et al., 1994), did not find the effect, across seventeen laboratories and 1,550 participants. The theory is not thereby refuted, but one of its most cited effects is wavering, and it can no longer be taken as established.

Becker first gives a precise answer to the question “why do people believe?”: because we die, and we know it. Then a consequence that meets the thesis of this essay: if every culture is a hero system against death, then the exits from religion that install a new absolute, History, the Nation, Race, Civilization, are not accidents; they are replacement hero systems, which promise symbolic immortality to those who serve them and refuse it to those who contest them. The sacrifice criterion here receives a psychological explanation. But Becker leaves open a question he does not resolve: can one live without a vital lie? Lucretius answered yes, provided one understands that death is nothing to us; Becker does not believe so, and this is what leads him back to Kierkegaard. I believe he is wrong on this point, or rather that he confuses two things: the need for meaning, which is universal, and the need for immortality, which perhaps is not. The spiritualities of exercise, from Spinoza to Hadot, do not deny death; they seek to look at it without lying to themselves. They are precisely what Becker's theory holds to be impossible, and that is why they remain, in this essay, the case that puts this theory to the test.

> **En littérature.** Leo Tolstoy, *The Death of Ivan Ilyich* (1886) ; Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, “Der Gevatter Tod” (1812)
>
> Ivan Ilyich, an ordinary magistrate, has lived a respectable life and is dying of an illness the doctors do not name; the textbook syllogism, Caius is a man, men are mortal, therefore Caius is mortal, had always seemed to him right for Caius and not for himself. In the last chapter, after three days of screaming, the fear falls away: “‘And death! Where is it?’ He looked for his accustomed fear and did not find it. ‘Where is death?’ He was no longer afraid, for there was no more death. Instead of death he saw light.[…] ‘Death is finished… Death no longer exists!’ he said to himself. He drew in a breath, which remained unfinished, stiffened and died”.
>
> Why here: this is the denial of death according to Becker, and its way out. Ivan Ilyich has spent his life in a replacement hero system, his career, the drawing room, whist, and this system collapses before Caius; Tolstoy has him die in a light that the essay, with Becker, leaves undecided: is it faith regained or the end of the vital lie? The text does not say God; it says that death no longer exists, which Lucretius also said.
>
> Grimm's tale tells the same thing in a page. A poor man chooses Death as godfather to his thirteenth child, having refused God, who gives to the rich and lets the poor go hungry, and the devil, who deceives; Death presents himself: “Ich bin der Tod, der alle gleich macht”, I am Death, who makes all equal, and the man replies: “du bist der rechte, du holst den Reichen wie den Armen ohne Unterschied”, you are the right one, you take the rich as well as the poor without distinction; the child becomes a famous physician, who heals when Death stands at the sick person's feet and gives up when Death is at the head; twice he cheats Death, for a king and then for the king's daughter, whom he wants to marry; Death then leads him into his cave where the lights of all lives are burning: “„Zeige mir mein Lebenslicht“ sagte der Arzt und meinte es wäre noch recht groß. Der Tod deutete auf ein kleines Endchen, das eben auszugehen drohte”, “Show me my life's light,” said the physician, thinking it would still be quite large; Death pointed to a little stub that was just about to go out; he begs for a new one to be lit, Death pretends to do so, and lets the candle stub fall. Culture as a hero system against death, says Becker; the tale says that the hero always believes himself a tall candle.
>
> Sources: Leo Tolstoy, *Смерть Ивана Ильича* (*The Death of Ivan Ilyich*), ch. 6 and 12 (1886) ; Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, “Der Gevatter Tod”, *Kinder- und Hausmärchen*, no. 44 (1812 ; ed. of 1857).
### Berger (1929-2017) and Luckmann (1927-2016): the sacred canopy and invisible religion

Peter L. Berger and Thomas Luckmann first wrote together a book that changed sociology, *The Social Construction of Reality* (1966). What we take for reality appears in it as the product of a three-stage process: human beings externalize their activity in institutions, these institutions are objectivated and take on the appearance of a nature, and they are then internalized by each person as self-evident. The following year, in 1967, each published a book on religion on his own, and the two books say different things, almost opposite things, which still structure the sociology of religion.

*The Sacred Canopy* (*La Religion dans la conscience moderne*, in the title of its French translation) applies the theory of social construction to religion. Every society, Berger says, is an enterprise of world-building, and this world, which he calls by a Greek word, *nomos*, is an order of meanings that shields human beings from chaos. The individual torn from this *nomos*, by bereavement, exile or catastrophe, loses his bearings in experience and becomes, in a phrase Tim Knepper picks out, “anomic in the sense of becoming world-less”. Religion is the most ambitious form of this protection. It is not content to order society; it installs this order in the cosmos, and so makes it untouchable: the sacred canopy is the roof of meanings that each society stretches over its world. Religion makes people forget that the *nomos* was built; it presents it as existing since the beginning of time. This is Feuerbach's alienation, translated into sociology: man forgets that he is the author of his world, and receives it as a gift of the gods.

The chapter on theodicy is the most profound in the book. Every religion must account for suffering and death, which threaten the *nomos* at its most fragile point. Berger draws from this a thesis that overturns the Marxist critique. It is usually believed that religion consoles by promising happiness; Berger writes, on the contrary: “It is not happiness that theodicy primarily provides, but meaning”. Human beings can bear suffering, not its meaninglessness. One recognizes Nietzsche's sentence on the meaninglessness of suffering; Berger does not quote it, and the comparison is constructed. The consequence is clear: if religion provides meaning rather than happiness, it cannot be replaced by material progress, and the hope of the Enlightenment, which thought that religion would disappear along with poverty, rests on a misunderstanding.

Yet in 1967 Berger drew a prediction of secularization from his book. The canopy holds by what he calls plausibility structures: a religion is believed only if one's surroundings take it as self-evident. But modernity is pluralist; it brings everyone face to face with other beliefs, and pluralism undermines plausibility. A belief chosen among others no longer has the self-evidence of a world; it becomes a preference. Berger concluded that religion would decline; thirty years later, he publicly retracted. In the essay that opens *The Desecularization of the World* (1999), a volume he edited, he writes that the idea that we live in a secularized world is false: “The world today[…] is as furiously religious as it ever was, and in some places more so than ever”. Berger himself makes one exception, that of an “international subculture composed of people with Western-type higher education, especially in the humanities and social sciences”. The rise of militant Islam and of worldwide Pentecostalism seemed to him to refute the theory he had himself helped to establish. He later specified, in his last books, that modernity produces pluralism rather than secularization. The correction matters: Berger is right against the prophecy that religion would disappear, but he does not say that religion has remained the same. It has become a choice, and a choice does not have the same authority as a world.

Luckmann, the same year, had proposed another reading, subtler and closer to our spiritualities without God. *The Invisible Religion* (1967, a revised version of a German book of 1963) starts from a very broad definition of religion: religious is everything by which the human organism transcends its biological nature and gives itself a world of meaning. In this sense, no society is without religion, and the question of secularization is wrongly posed. What has changed, according to Luckmann, is not the presence of religion but its location. The Churches have lost their monopoly, and religion has moved into the private sphere, where each person composes his own system of ultimate meanings around new themes: self-expression, self-realization, autonomy, family and emotional life. This religion is invisible because it no longer passes through institutions that a sociologist could count; privatized, it has not disappeared.

Luckmann's contribution is to show that the “spiritual but not religious” of Part Twelve is not a contemporary curiosity but the modern form of an anthropological function: self-realization is the sacred of individualist society. The danger of his definition is that if everything that gives meaning is religion, the question of our essay becomes empty: one never leaves religion, since even the exit is one. This definition has the weakness of Durkheim's without its strength: a definition that encompasses everything no longer allows anything to be distinguished. Luckmann's private sacred, self-realization, does not ordinarily demand anyone's sacrifice; it can do so, when self-realization becomes a limitless imperative, but it does not do so by nature. Berger and Luckmann, read together, therefore give our question its two sociological terms: religion as a shelter of meaning, which does not disappear, and religion as an institution, which can recede. The exit from religion, in the sense of this essay, concerns the second; the need of which the first speaks does not condemn it in advance.

> **En littérature.** Miguel de Cervantes, *Don Quixote* (1615) ; Luigi Pirandello, *Così è (se vi pare)* (1917) ; Hans Christian Andersen, “The Emperor's New Clothes” (1837)
>
> In the last chapter of *Don Quixote*, the knight wakes from a fever and renounces: “J'ai été fou, et je suis raisonnable ; j'ai été Don Quichotte de la Manche, et je suis à présent Alonzo Quijano-le-Bon”, I was mad, and now I am sane; I was Don Quixote of La Mancha, and I am now Alonso Quixano the Good; he makes his will, receives the sacraments, curses the books of chivalry, and dies, the chronicle noting that “ce qui assura sa félicité, ce fut de mourir sage et d'avoir vécu fou”, what assured his happiness was to die sane after having lived mad.
>
> Why here: Berger's sacred canopy is a world of meaning that holds as long as a plausibility structure supports it; Don Quixote's was made of books and held thanks to Sancho, and it collapses in a single night. But Cervantes adds what Berger does not say: the man who leaves his world survives it only a few days, and those close to him mourn the madman more than the sane man. One does not leave a canopy for a neutral void; one leaves it for another, here that of the sacraments, and it is that one which buries him.
>
> Pirandello, in *Così è (se vi pare)*, has a small town investigate a veiled woman of whom no one will ever know whether she is old Signora Frola's daughter or Signor Ponza's second wife; in the last scene she appears and answers: “Per me, io sono colei che mi si crede”, for myself, I am whoever I am believed to be. This is the social construction of reality played out in three acts, fifty years before the book: a person's truth is what a world of meaning decides it is. And Andersen, in “The Emperor's New Clothes”, had shown what happens when a child, who does not yet have a plausibility structure, says that the emperor is naked: the world does not collapse, the emperor carries on with the procession, and that is perhaps the most Bergerian lesson of the tale.
>
> Sources: Miguel de Cervantes, *Don Quixote*, II, 74, French trans. Louis Viardot (1615) ; Luigi Pirandello, *Così è (se vi pare)*, III (1917) ; Hans Christian Andersen, “Keiserens nye klæder” (1837).

### Hervieu-Léger (b. 1947): religion as memory, believing without a lineage

Danièle Hervieu-Léger, a sociologist of religion and director of studies at the École des hautes études en sciences sociales, proposed in 1993 a definition of religion that shifts the question of Durkheim and Luckmann. She defines religion neither by its content, God or the supernatural, nor by its function, meaning or social cohesion, but by a particular mode of believing. In *La Religion pour mémoire*, she calls it “un dispositif idéologique, pratique et symbolique par lequel est constituée, entretenue, développée et contrôlée la conscience (individuelle et collective) de l'appartenance à une lignée croyante” (p. 119), an ideological, practical and symbolic apparatus by which the consciousness (individual and collective) of belonging to a believing lineage is constituted, maintained, developed and controlled. Everything hangs on the word lineage. To believe religiously is to believe in the name of a chain, invoking the authority of a tradition that goes back to founding witnesses and that one takes on the task of transmitting. What distinguishes a religion from a philosophy or a morality is not its object; it is this authority of memory.

The definition makes it possible to say what is happening to European societies without speaking either of disappearance or of return. Modernity, Hervieu-Léger explains, is structurally amnesiac: it values innovation, mobility, the present, and it undoes the chains of memory that transmitted belief. Believing does not disappear for all that; it comes loose from the lineage. People still believe, and a great deal, but without invoking the authority of a tradition, composing their belief from borrowed fragments. This is what she calls, in *Le Pèlerin et le converti. La religion en mouvement* (1999), a deregulation of believing. She draws from it two typical figures of contemporary religiosity. The pilgrim is the one who journeys on, who has experiences without stopping anywhere, who judges a belief by what it gives him and leaves it when it gives him nothing more. The convert is his apparent opposite: the one who chooses a strong belonging, often after a crisis, and who finds in a demanding community the identity that society no longer gives him. These two figures are the two faces of a single world: both choose, and it is this choice that makes them modern, even when the convert chooses the most rigid tradition.

These two figures replace a third. The religion of traditional societies had as its central figure the practitioner, the one who regularly performs the gestures prescribed by an institution, in a parish where he was born and where he will die. This figure has not disappeared, but it has ceased to be the norm, and Hervieu-Léger described its decline in France in *Catholicisme, la fin d'un monde* (2003), where she shows that the Catholic Church has lost not only adherents but the capacity to organize the common culture. What fades with the practitioner is religion as shared self-evidence, what Berger called the canopy. What replaces it is not unbelief but a religiosity of trajectory, judged by the authenticity of experience rather than by conformity to a rule. One recognizes here, transposed into sociology, the distinction the essay draws from Foucault and Hadot between religion as obedience and spirituality as exercise, except that the sociologist does not judge. It is the convert who touches on the criterion. He seeks a lineage because he did not receive one, and he is all the more demanding for having chosen it: it is in him that chosen religion can become once more a religion that demands sacrifices, and the recent religious radicalizations in Europe have shown this in a way the sociologist had anticipated without foreseeing its violence.

This analysis converges with that of the British sociologist Grace Davie, who had described post-war Britain as a society of *believing without belonging*, and with that of Marcel Gauchet, whom Part Eleven will examine. But Hervieu-Léger is more precise than Gauchet on one point. She does not say that structuring religion has disappeared and that private beliefs remain; she says that the need for a lineage survives the disappearance of lineages, and that it seeks substitutes. Hence the importance she gives to secular forms of collective memory, national, political, familial, which can take on a religious colouring when they present themselves as the continuation of a sacred chain. Here, through sociology, we meet the question of refoundations again. Barrès's Nation, the militants' Revolution, the Civilization that Onfray defends in *Décadence*, are substitute believing lineages: they authorize belief through fidelity to ancestors, and they can demand, like religions, that something be sacrificed to them.

This definition is useful because it distinguishes what the others conflate. The need for meaning, described by Berger and Becker, can be satisfied by a philosophy; the need for connection, described by Durkheim, by an association; but the need for a lineage, for an authority that precedes us and that we transmit, is specifically religious, in Hervieu-Léger's sense. And it is this need that the spiritualities without God of Part Twelve find hardest to satisfy. Hadot could invoke the lineage of the ancient schools, and that is his strength; Comte-Sponville invokes Spinoza and Epicurus, but by a personal choice, not by a transmission. The modern pilgrim has no lineage; he has a library. Is this a loss? Hervieu-Léger, as a sociologist, is right not to say. For our question, the answer is clear: a spirituality without a lineage escapes the risk of refoundation, since it has no ancestors in whose name to demand a sacrifice; it pays for this freedom with a fragility, since it is not transmitted. That is perhaps the price of every exit that does not refound.

> **En littérature.** Marcel Proust, *Swann's Way* (1913) ; Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, *Il Gattopardo* (1958)
>
> The church at Combray, in *Swann's Way*, is not first of all a place of worship; it is, for the child, “un édifice occupant, si l'on peut dire, un espace à quatre dimensions, la quatrième étant celle du Temps, déployant à travers les siècles son vaisseau qui, de travée en travée, de chapelle en chapelle, semblait vaincre et franchir non pas seulement quelques mètres, mais des époques successives d'où il sortait victorieux”, a building occupying, so to speak, a four-dimensional space, the fourth dimension being Time, extending through the centuries its nave which, from bay to bay, from chapel to chapel, seemed to conquer and cross not merely a few yards but successive epochs from which it emerged victorious.
>
> Why here: this is Hervieu-Léger's believing lineage described by someone who no longer believes in it but descends from it. The church holds by the generations it has seen pass, not by what is said in it; and the narrator, who does not pray, receives its memory as an inheritance. The essay's “modern pilgrim”, who no longer has a lineage but a library, was born in this nave: Proust turned the chain of believers into a chain of memories, and the novel is the place where the lineage survives belief.
>
> *The Leopard* tells of the end of a Sicilian lineage in 1860 and the old age of its prince, Don Fabrizio, who sees Garibaldi, the plebiscite and his nephew's marriage to the daughter of an upstart pass by, and dies in a hotel in Palermo; Father Pirrone, the household's Jesuit, explains to the peasants that the nobles do not change because they do not understand what is happening to them; in the last part, in 1910, the prince's daughters keep a chapel of relics which the archdiocese comes to declare false. The religion of the house of Salina is a memory that dies out with it; when the lineage has no more heirs, its relics are nothing but bones. Hervieu-Léger described what Lampedusa buried.
>
> Sources: Marcel Proust, *Du côté de chez Swann*, “Combray”, I (1913) ; Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa, *Il Gattopardo* (*The Leopard*, 1958).

### Boyer: why gods are easy to think

Pascal Boyer, a French anthropologist trained in Paris and Cambridge, who teaches at Washington University in St. Louis, published in 2001 *Religion Explained*, which became the manifesto of a field of research born in the 1990s: the cognitive science of religion. His question is not that of our nineteenth-century authors. He does not ask whether religion is true, nor what it is for, nor what desire it satisfies; he asks why certain religious ideas are so easy to acquire, to remember and to transmit, while others, just as conceivable, never appear. And his answer shifts the whole debate: religion rests neither on a special faculty nor on a special need, but on the ordinary functioning of the human mind.

The argument starts from inference systems. The human mind is neither a blank slate nor a general reasoner; it has specialized devices, shaped by evolution to deal with distinct domains: physical objects, living beings, persons and their intentions, social relations, contamination and danger. They work without our knowing it, which is why their products seem obvious to us. Religious concepts, Boyer shows, are concepts that violate on one precise point the expectations of one of these categories while respecting all the others: a spirit that has no body but sees, hears and remembers; a statue that listens to prayers; a dead ancestor who gets angry. These minimally counterintuitive concepts are better remembered than ordinary concepts, because they surprise, and better than concepts that are too bizarre, because they remain usable: one can reason about a jealous god, one cannot reason about a god who would be at once everything and nothing. Religion is neither a stroke of genius nor an aberration, but a by-product of mental devices that serve other purposes.

The subtlest point of the theory concerns the gods themselves. Why are supernatural beings almost always persons, who see, will and judge? Because the human mind is first of all a social mind, which spends its time wondering what others know about it and what they are going to do. Gods, for Boyer, are agents who have access to all strategic information: they know what we have done, what we have hidden, what others think of us. This is what makes them relevant to morality and social life, and it explains why one does not pray to a god to reveal the structure of the atom, but to see our distress or punish our enemy. The psychologist Justin Barrett added to this theory a device he calls the *hyperactive agent detection device*: our ancestors had an advantage in seeing a predator behind every rustle of leaves, even at the cost of being often wrong, rather than missing the one that was real, and we have inherited this tendency to detect agents where there is only chance. The idea goes back to the anthropologist Stewart Guthrie's book on faces in the clouds (1993), and its ancestry is older than its authors say, since Hume had formulated it in 1757: “We find human faces in the moon, armies in the clouds”, and by a natural propensity we ascribe malice or good will to everything that hurts or pleases us.

This theory explains very well what our authors explained badly: why religion is universal, why it takes similar forms everywhere, why it resists arguments so well. It also answers, in its own way, the question of Bergson, who held religion to be “coextensive à notre espèce”, coextensive with our species, and concluded that it “doit tenir à notre structure”, must be bound up with our structure: Boyer gives this structure a precise content, which Bergson could not have known. Finally, it contains a consequence that Boyer formulates, according to Anthony Campbell, with a certain relish: “science is every bit as 'unnatural' to the human mind as religion is 'natural'”. The Enlightenment's faith in the spontaneous disappearance of religion was therefore doubly naive: it misjudged the ease of belief and the difficulty of science.

But the theory is often credited with more than it claims. First, explaining why a belief is easy to acquire says nothing about its truth. This is what philosophy calls the genetic fallacy, and it works both ways: that our devices incline us to see agents everywhere does not prove that there are none, just as our natural aptitude for counting does not prove that numbers do not exist. Daniel Dennett, who popularized this research in *Breaking the Spell* (2006), sometimes forgets this; Boyer is more cautious. Feuerbach, on this point, was more lucid than his naturalist successors: he did not claim that religion was false because it came from man; he said that it told the truth about man. Next, the theory explains religious representations, spirits, gods, rites, but it poorly explains what interests our essay most: the experience of the mystics, spiritual exercise, conversion. The reviewer Joseph Bulbulia, in the Australian journal *Eras*, reproached it for this reason with a misleading title: religion is not a single cognitive dimension, and only some of its aspects are explained. Finally, and this is the most important point for us, the theory says why gods are easy to think, not why we need them. Boyer in fact rejects the notion of a religious need: there is, in his view, no need for God, but a disposition to conceive him when a culture offers him. This is the lasting contribution of the cognitive sciences to our question. They do not refute religion; they refute the idea that there exists in man an empty place, of exactly the shape of God, which the exit from religion would leave gaping.

> **En littérature.** Gustave Flaubert, “A Simple Heart” (1877) ; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* (8 CE) ; Lewis Carroll, *Through the Looking-Glass* (1871)
>
> Félicité, the servant in “A Simple Heart”, has nothing left at the end of her life but her parrot Loulou, dead and stuffed. “À l'église, elle contemplait toujours le Saint-Esprit, et observa qu'il avait quelque chose du perroquet”, in church she always gazed at the Holy Ghost, and noticed that it had something of the parrot about it; and as she dies, while the Corpus Christi procession passes by, “quand elle exhala son dernier souffle, elle crut voir, dans les cieux entr'ouverts, un perroquet gigantesque, planant au-dessus de sa tête”, when she breathed her last, she thought she saw, in the half-opened heavens, a gigantic parrot hovering above her head. Why here: Flaubert wrote Boyer's theory in twenty pages. Félicité did not learn the Trinity; she inferred it with what she had, a bird that talks, that is, a minimally counterintuitive agent; and Flaubert, who does not believe, does not mock: the representation is false, the attachment is true, and the tale judges only goodness.
>
> Ovid opens the *Metamorphoses* with a programme: “In nova fert animus mutatas dicere formas / corpora”, my mind moves me to tell of forms changed into new bodies; and he has man born as “sanctius his animal mentisque capacius altae”, an animal holier than the others and more capable of lofty thought, to whom the creator “os homini sublime dedit caelumque videre / iussit”, gave an upturned face and bade him look at the sky. The poem is a world in which anything can be someone, a laurel a girl, a rock a mother; it is the “world full of agents” that the cognitive sciences describe as the natural bent of the mind, and Ovid had made fifteen books of it.
>
> Carroll's White Queen practises believing: she has sometimes believed, she tells Alice, “as many as six impossible things before breakfast”. Boyer would say that she has the wrong method: one does not believe in gods by exercise, but because they are easy to think; and that science, for its part, demands precisely the Queen's exercise.
>
> Sources: Gustave Flaubert, “Un cœur simple”, *Trois contes* (1877) ; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I, 1-2, 76-78, 85-86 (8 CE) ; Lewis Carroll, *Through the Looking-Glass*, ch. 5 (1871).

### Norris and Inglehart: existential security, the empirical arbiter

All the preceding authors make hypotheses about the causes of belief; two political scientists set out to measure them. Pippa Norris, of Harvard University, and Ronald Inglehart (1934-2021), of the University of Michigan, founder of the great international survey of values, the *World Values Survey*, published in 2004 *Sacred and Secular. Religion and Politics Worldwide* (Cambridge University Press, second edition 2011). The book draws on surveys conducted in nearly eighty societies and proposes to revise the classical theory of secularization rather than abandon it, as Berger had done in 1999.

The thesis comes down to one notion, *existential security*. Religiosity depends, in their view, neither on the religious supply, as economists of religion maintain, nor on the progress of scientific knowledge, as the Enlightenment believed, but on the degree of vulnerability in which people live. Where the death of a child, famine, untreated illness, old age without resources, violence without recourse are daily threats, religion remains strong, because it provides insurance against what cannot be mastered. Where the welfare state, medicine and prosperity have made existence predictable, religiosity recedes from one generation to the next, without anyone having been convinced by an argument. The most secularized societies in the world are the most egalitarian and best protected, the Scandinavian countries; the most religious are the poorest and most exposed. And the case of the United States, long invoked against the theory of secularization, confirms it in their view: it is the most unequal and least protected of rich societies, and it is also the most religious.

The thesis has a second half, less often cited, which forbids reading it as a prophecy of the end of religions. Religious societies have more children than secularized societies. The result is a demographic paradox: rich societies are becoming secularized, but the share of the world's population living in religious societies is growing, so that the world, taken as a whole, is not becoming less religious. Berger, who saw the world as “furiously religious”, and the theorists of secularization, who saw Europe emptying, were therefore both right, each about one half of the world.

In *Religion's Sudden Decline. What's Causing It, and What Comes Next?* (Oxford University Press, 2021), published in the year of his death, Inglehart notes that the decline of religiosity accelerates from the end of the 2000s, the United States included. He explains it by the same security: religious norms favouring high fertility, indispensable when infant mortality was high, have lost their usefulness, and the religions that presented them as absolutes have been weakened by this.

This work has real limits. First, these are opinion surveys: they measure what people declare, the importance of God in their lives, the frequency of their prayer, not what they experience. Next, the correlation is very strong between countries but much weaker between individuals within the same country, and the authors had to respond on this point in their second edition: the poorest in a rich society are not always the most religious. Finally, the notion of religion they measure is Durkheim's more than James's: it captures practice and adherence, it poorly captures the diffuse spirituality that Luckmann and Hervieu-Léger describe. A society where no one goes to church any more but where everyone meditates could appear, in these surveys, perfectly secularized.

These limits do not take away from Norris and Inglehart their role as arbiters: their data decide between the explanations of belief. They prove Lucretius and Hume, Freud and Becker right, who derived religion from fear and distress: when distress recedes, religion recedes. They prove the Enlightenment wrong, which expected the exit from religion from the progress of ideas: it is not critique that secularizes, it is health insurance. But they also raise an uncomfortable question: if the exit from religion is the effect of security, it is not an act of freedom; a protected society no longer needs heaven, but it remains exposed to the return of insecurity, and the history of the twentieth century shows that substitute religions thrive precisely in crises.

Norris and Inglehart's thesis is opposed to another sociological explanation, from the United States. The so-called religious market school, associated with the names of Rodney Stark, Roger Finke and Laurence Iannaccone, explained American religious vitality by competition between Churches: where the state protects no denomination, the Churches must attract their faithful, and supply stimulates demand; where a state Church enjoys a monopoly, as in Scandinavia, it falls asleep and its faithful leave it. Norris and Inglehart reply that religious demand is not constant, as this theory supposes, but varies with security. The disagreement bears on our very question: is there a stable religious need, which supply alone causes to vary, or a disposition whose intensity depends on living conditions? The data argue rather for the second answer. The American sociologist Phil Zuckerman, in *Society without God* (2008), carried out fieldwork in Denmark and Sweden, among populations largely detached from any belief, and found there societies that seem to suffer from no lack that could be attributed to the absence of religion. This is, as we shall see, the strongest argument against the thesis of need.

> **En littérature.** Knut Hamsun, *Sult* (1890) ; Charles Dickens, *Hard Times* (1854)
>
> The narrator of *Hunger* (*Sult*), a penniless young man of letters in Christiania, looks for work, positions, a publisher, and hunger gnaws at his head; on a bench, he turns on God: “Supposing God Almighty simply intended to annihilate me?[…] The thought of God began to occupy me. It seemed to me in the highest degree indefensible of Him to interfere every time I sought for a place, and to upset the whole thing, while all the time I was but imploring enough for a daily meal”.
>
> Why here: Hamsun shows Norris and Inglehart's correlation in a single brain. God interests the narrator only when he is hungry; he prays to him, accuses him, attributes every refusal to him; when he eats, he no longer thinks of him. Existential insecurity produces belief, not as a conviction, but as an interlocutor of distress, and this is exactly the mechanism the two sociologists measure on the scale of nations.
>
> Dickens, in *Hard Times*, describes Coketown, the coal town: “If the members of a religious persuasion built a chapel there, as the members of eighteen religious persuasions had done, they made it a pious warehouse of red brick”, and the workers do not go to them, which astonishes the notables in session. Religion there is an abundant supply facing an absent demand: this is Norris and Inglehart's argument against the religious market school, written by a novelist in 1854. It is not the competition of Churches that makes faith; it is the hunger of Hamsun's narrator.
>
> Sources: Knut Hamsun, *Sult* (*Hunger*, 1890), in the English translation by George Egerton (1899) ; Charles Dickens, *Hard Times*, I, 5 (1854).
### Why do people believe? A constructed debate

The answers gathered so far do not overlap, and they must now be brought to meet. None of the authors called upon had read all the others: most of these encounters are constructed confrontations, and I point out those that are attested. The question is simple to state and hard to settle: why have nearly all known human societies had gods, spirits, rites and sacred stories? I distinguish four families of answers, which appeared in a roughly chronological order: fear and desire, meaning, society, cognition.

The oldest answer is fear, from Lucretius and Hume to Freud, and then to Becker, who traces it back to its root: the fear of death, which man alone knows. Among these four authors, two lines of descent are attested: Hume discusses Lucretius in the *Natural History of Religion* (sections 5 and 12), and Becker starts explicitly from Freud; for the others, the kinship is my own doing. What unites them is a strong thesis: religion answers a threat, and would disappear with it.

Feuerbach gave this first answer a deeper version, because he speaks not only of fear but of desire. In his Heidelberg lectures, he grants that the thesis may seem paradoxical, the thesis that derives religion from human desires, and even holds the deity to be “als eins mit dem Wunsche”, one and the same thing as desire. He defines desire precisely: “Der Wunsch ist das Verlangen, daß Etwas sei, was nicht ist”, desire is the demand that something be which is not. And he draws from it the consequence that matters most to this essay. If the god owes his existence solely to the human drive for happiness, the *Glückseligkeitstrieb*, and if religion satisfies this drive only in imagination, then, Feuerbach writes, it necessarily follows “daß der Mensch auf andere Weise als religiöse, durch andere Mittel als religiöse diesen Trieb zu befriedigen sucht”, that man seeks to satisfy this drive in a way other than religious, by means other than religious. The sentence holds in germ the whole question of this essay: the need survives religion, and it looks for other objects. Feuerbach believed these objects would be nature, politics, the love of human beings; we know they can also be History, the Nation or the Race.

Marx shifted this first answer without leaving it. Religion, for him, is not only a fear or a desire, it is the lament of a real condition, the sigh of the oppressed creature (Part Six). The response to Feuerbach is attested: if religion is born of real distress, one does not dissolve it by explaining its psychological mechanism, one dissolves it by abolishing the distress. Norris and Inglehart, a hundred and sixty years later, gave this intuition a confirmation Marx would not have disowned, but which changes its meaning: it was not revolution that secularized Northern Europe, it was the welfare state.

The second family no longer speaks of fear but of meaning. Nietzsche formulated it at the end of the third essay of *On the Genealogy of Morality*. Man, he writes, does not deny suffering, he even seeks it out, provided he is shown its meaning: “Die Sinnlosigkeit des Leidens, nicht das Leiden, war der Fluch, der bisher über der Menschheit ausgebreitet lag”, the meaninglessness of suffering, not suffering itself, was the curse that until now lay spread over humanity. The ascetic ideal was accepted because it gave a meaning, any meaning at all: “irgendein Sinn ist besser als gar kein Sinn”, some meaning or other is better than no meaning at all; and man, Nietzsche concludes, would rather will nothingness than not will (Part Seven). Berger rediscovers this thesis as a sociologist in his theory of theodicy, Becker as a psychologist when he makes culture a hero system. The difference from the first family lies in the consequences. If religion answered only to fear, it would recede with security; if it answers the need for meaning, security is not enough, and a protected society can be a desperate one. According to Nietzsche, European nihilism was born not of poverty but of comfort.

The third family is sociological, and its chief representative is Durkheim: religion is neither a fear nor an individual search for meaning, it is the figurative form in which a society represents its own strength to itself. Bergson gave this thesis a biological version in *The Two Sources*: static religion was born of a “fonction fabulatrice”, a fabulating function, which nature placed in intelligence to keep it from dissolving social cohesion. Bergson's response to Durkheim is attested: he accepts the existence of collective representations, but refuses to see in them the essential, which he locates in the dynamic religion of the mystics. Berger, Luckmann and Hervieu-Léger extend this family into the twentieth century: religion provides a world, an identity, a lineage. Girard, finally, gives it its darkest version: society does not merely represent its strength to itself in the sacred, it protects itself there from its own violence by designating a victim; the question of whether one can leave religion without founding another then becomes the question of whether people can live together without a scapegoat.

The fourth family is the most recent, and it partly dissolves the question. For Boyer and the cognitive sciences, there is no religious need, only mental mechanisms shaped by evolution for other tasks. People do not believe because they are afraid, nor because they seek a meaning, nor because society demands it; they believe because gods are concepts that suit the way our mind works, and the other reasons, fear, meaning, society, merely select, among these easy concepts, the ones that will survive. This answer has two great merits: it explains the universality of religion without assuming some mysterious faculty in man, and it explains why arguments have almost no hold on it: one does not refute an inclination. Its limit, as I have said, is that it explains beliefs, not exercises; gods, not mystics.

These families did not merely follow one another, they clashed, and one attested exchange shows what is at stake better than any classification. In 1927, Romain Rolland responded to *The Future of an Illusion* by reproaching Freud for having explained the religion of the crowds without saying anything about its true source, a feeling of eternity, of the unbounded, of union with the whole, which he called oceanic; Freud answered him in 1930, in the first chapter of *Civilization and Its Discontents*, that he could not find this feeling in himself, and traced it back to the narcissism of the infant, while maintaining that the source of the religious need is infantile helplessness. The exchange sets the first family, that of fear and desire, against what the second would become in James and Bergson: a positive experience, which answers no threat and which no security makes disappear. Freud won the debate on instituted religions, which existential security makes recede as he predicted. Rolland perhaps won it on experience, since the most secure societies are also those in which the spiritual quests without a Church that Luckmann and Hervieu-Léger describe are multiplying. Both are right, because they are not talking about the same thing.

We must then return to the word need. A need, in the strict sense, is that whose deprivation causes harm: we need to eat, to sleep, to be loved. If religion were a need in this sense, the societies that have detached themselves from it ought to suffer for it in some visible way. Yet the Scandinavian societies, which Norris and Inglehart rank among the most secularized in the world and which Phil Zuckerman has observed at close quarters, show none of the symptoms one would expect of a lack: they are among the most trusting, the least violent and the most satisfied with their lot. The argument is not decisive: one could reply with Durkheim that they live on a secular sacred, equality, trust, the welfare state, which takes the place of religion; or with Nietzsche that their comfort is merely a nihilism unaware of itself. It is enough, however, to establish what seems to me the most solid conclusion of this debate: religion is not a need, in the sense of being irreplaceable; it is an answer, long the most readily available, to needs that can receive other answers.

One voice is still missing, that of a believer who had formulated as early as the seventeenth century the thesis this debate puts to the test. Pascal does not deny the mechanism that Lucretius, Hume and Becker describe; he described it himself. Diversion, he writes, comes from the fact that “tout le malheur des hommes vient d'une seule chose, qui est de ne savoir pas demeurer en repos, dans une chambre”, all the unhappiness of men comes from a single thing, which is not knowing how to stay quietly in a room; and the reason for this unhappiness is “le malheur naturel de notre condition faible et mortelle”, the natural unhappiness of our weak and mortal condition. But he draws from it the opposite conclusion to that of the explainers. Human dissatisfaction is for him not the cause of religion but its sign: it cries out, he says, that there was once in man a happiness of which there remains only “la marque et la trace toute vide”, the mark and the wholly empty trace, which he vainly tries to fill with everything around him, “parce que ce gouffre infini ne peut être rempli que par un objet infini et immuable, c'est-à-dire que par Dieu même”, because this infinite abyss can be filled only by an infinite and immutable object, that is to say, only by God himself. And he adds an observation that this essay confirms without sharing his conclusion: since man lost his true good, there is nothing in nature “qui n'ait été capable de lui en tenir la place”, that has not been capable of taking its place for him. The confrontation is constructed. Pascal and the refounders say the same thing, that the place of God does not remain empty; they interpret it in opposite directions. For Pascal, it proves that the place has the shape of God; for Feuerbach, it proves that God had the shape of human desire. Boyer, who denies that there is a place shaped like God, and Norris and Inglehart, who show that it shrinks with security, prove Pascal wrong on the interpretation. But they prove him right on the fact, which the exits from religion of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries never ceased to illustrate: what comes to occupy the place can be anything at all, and sometimes the worst.

What is to be done with these four families? Each discipline chooses its own: the psychoanalyst fear, the philosopher meaning, the sociologist society, the cognitive scientist the mind. On the contrary, I believe, they must be held together, for they do not answer the same question. The cognitive sciences say why religious beliefs are possible and easy. Fear, desire and the need for meaning say why they are desirable. Sociology says why they are transmitted and imposed. And the data of Norris and Inglehart say when they grow stronger and when they weaken. The disposition to believe is therefore universal in its springs, which are cognitive, existential and social, and variable in its intensity, which depends on existential security and on the solidity of lineages. It is real; but it is not a need for God. It is a need for meaning, for bonds and for protection, to which gods were long the easiest answer, because they were also the easiest to think.

This conclusion changes the question of this essay, but not in the expected direction. One might think that the natural explanation of belief settles the problem: if we know why we believe, we can stop believing, and the exit from religion becomes a matter of lucidity. That was the hope of Lucretius, Hume, Feuerbach and Freud. The history of our series shows that it was naive, and the analysis of the four families shows why. If the need is not a need for God, it survives God and looks for other objects. These may be substitute absolutes, History, the Nation, the Race, Civilization, which offer meaning, bonds and protection at the price of sacrificing those who do not belong to them: these are the refoundations. They may also be spiritualities without God, exercises, friendships, protective institutions, which offer the same thing without demanding any sacrifice: these are the successful exits, or at least the candidates. The natural explanation of belief therefore does not settle the essay's question, it sharpens it: the place religion occupied does not remain empty, and the whole problem is to know what will come to occupy it.

There remains what this debate contributes to the sacrifice criterion, and this is perhaps its main result. Becker and Girard, as we have seen, make sacrifice not an accident of certain religions but a spring of belief itself. If this is true, the refoundations are not perversions of the exit from religion, they are its natural drift, and the exits that do not refound are costly exceptions, which must be willed, built and maintained. Norris and Inglehart add a material condition: these exceptions are possible, on the scale of a society, only where existence is secure enough for fear no longer to look for a victim. Leaving religion without refoundation is therefore not only a matter of philosophy: it presupposes a wisdom, which the spiritualities of exercise offer, and a security, which only institutions can guarantee.

> **En littérature.** Gustave Flaubert, *Madame Bovary* (1857) ; Alphonse de Lamartine, *Méditations poétiques* (1820)
>
> After Rodolphe's flight and the illness that follows, Emma Bovary turns to God: “Il existait donc à la place du bonheur des félicités plus grandes, un autre amour au-dessus de tous les amours, sans intermittence ni fin, et qui s'accroîtrait éternellement ![…] Elle voulut devenir une sainte. Elle acheta des chapelets, elle porta des amulettes ; elle souhaitait avoir dans sa chambre, au chevet de sa couche, un reliquaire enchâssé d'émeraudes, pour le baiser tous les soirs. Le Curé s'émerveillait de ces dispositions, bien que la religion d'Emma, trouvait-il, pût, à force de ferveur, finir par friser l'hérésie”, so there existed, in place of happiness, greater felicities, another love above all loves, without intermission or end, and which would grow eternally! […] She wanted to become a saint. She bought rosaries, she wore amulets; she wished to have in her room, at the head of her bed, a reliquary set with emeralds, to kiss every evening. The priest marvelled at these dispositions, although Emma's religion, he thought, might, through sheer fervour, end by verging on heresy.
>
> Why here: Flaubert wrote the debate of this section in a single page. Emma believes out of lack, exactly as Feuerbach and Freud say, “à la place du bonheur”, in place of happiness; her devotion has the shape of her love affairs, with objects to kiss; it ends when Léon returns. But Father Bournisien is right to worry: this need, which is not a need for God, produces a religion that is not his, and he will later keep vigil over Emma's body with Homais, arguing. The essay's four families of explanation can all be found in the character, and none exhausts her, because Flaubert does not judge: he describes a need for meaning, for bonds and for protection that has found a reliquary.
>
> Lamartine, forty years earlier, had given this same need its sincere form in the *Méditations*: “Le Désespoir” addresses to the creator God the lament of the creature delivered over to evil, and “La Providence à l'homme” answers it, in God's name, that the lament is the childhood of faith. The diptych is Part Nine in verse: fear, desire, the demand for meaning, and an answer that comes only if one has already decided where it comes from.
>
> Sources: Gustave Flaubert, *Madame Bovary*, II, 14 (1857) ; Alphonse de Lamartine, *Méditations poétiques*, VII and VIII (1820).
### Do we have the right to believe? Clifford, James and analytic philosophy

Another question has accompanied this one since the nineteenth century, more unsettling because it bears no longer on causes but on rights: do we have the right to believe what we believe? Explaining a belief by fear, desire, society or the structure of the mind leaves wholly open the question whether the person who holds it is at fault. Hume had given this second question its soberest maxim, at the beginning of the section on miracles in the *Enquiry concerning Human Understanding* (1748, under the title *Philosophical Essays concerning Human Understanding*, which became *An Enquiry* in 1758): “A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.” But Hume was speaking of prudence, not of duty. It was an English mathematician who, in 1877, turned this maxim into a moral obligation, and an American psychologist who answered him, by name, twenty years later. The exchange is an attested response, and it founded what analytic philosophy now calls the ethics of belief.

William Kingdon Clifford (1845-1879) was a geometer of the first rank, who died of tuberculosis at thirty-three. His article “The Ethics of Belief” appeared in the *Contemporary Review* in January 1877. It opens with a parable that has remained famous. A shipowner is about to send an emigrant ship to sea; he knows that the vessel is old, that it has often needed repairs, and doubts about its soundness have been put to him. These doubts make him unhappy; yet he rids himself of them: the ship has come through so many storms, Providence will protect these poor families, and it would be ungenerous to suspect the builders. He thus acquires, Clifford writes, “a sincere and comfortable conviction that his vessel was thoroughly safe and seaworthy”; he watches her depart with a light heart, and he collects the insurance money when she goes down in mid-ocean and tells no tales. Clifford adds that even if the ship had reached port safely, the owner would be no less guilty, because he had no right to believe on such evidence. The fault lies not in the outcome but in the way the belief was acquired.

The thesis that follows concedes nothing. Belief is not a private matter. It is, Clifford writes, “ours not for ourselves, but for humanity”, because no belief, however humble, is without effect on others: each prepares actions, each sustains a climate. It is therefore sacred, and it can be profaned: “It is desecrated when given to unproved and unquestioned statements, for the solace and private pleasure of the believer.” Whoever wishes to deserve well of his fellows “will guard the purity of his belief with a very fanaticism of jealous care”. And if a belief has been accepted on insufficient evidence, even if it turns out to be true, the pleasure it gives is stolen, and guilty, “because it is stolen in defiance of our duty to mankind”, a duty that consists in guarding ourselves from such beliefs “as from a pestilence”, which may shortly master our own body and then spread to the rest of the town. The first section sums itself up in a formula that has become the coat of arms of what would be called evidentialism: “it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.”

Clifford does not soften the consequences of this principle. Whoever sets aside his doubts, avoids the books and the people who might feed them, and regards as impious the questions that disturb his belief, leads in his view a life that is one long fault: the sentence ends on “one long sin against mankind”. To the man too busy to examine, he answers in a word: “Then he should have no time to believe.” The second section, on the weight of authority, bears directly on our subject. Clifford allows that one may take a chemist at his word, because one could in principle verify what he says; he does not allow that one should believe a prophet, because a man's moral greatness does not guarantee that he knows what he asserts. He takes the example of the founders of religions: the Prophet teaches that there is one God, whereas “The Buddha says that there is no God”, and that we shall be annihilated if we are good enough; they cannot both be infallibly inspired. The argument from the diversity of revelations, which Hume had used against miracles, becomes in Clifford a rule of hygiene: where the authorities contradict one another, none has any standing. He ends the article with a sentence that hardens the maxim further still: “It is wrong in all cases to believe on insufficient evidence; and where it is presumption to doubt and to investigate, there it is worse than presumption to believe.”

Read in the light of this essay's criterion, Clifford is instructive. His vocabulary is religious through and through: belief is a “sacred faculty”, one profanes it, one sins, one steals, one guards its purity with fanaticism, and the duty that binds the believer is a duty towards humanity, in whose name, he writes, we shall be strong, “not for ourselves, but in the name of Man and in his strength”. One recognizes Comte's religion of Humanity and Feuerbach's human species, and one may wonder whether Clifford's evidentialism is not one more cult, that of scientific Truth, with its priests and its sins.
