> Rubashov, an old Bolshevik arrested in *Darkness at Noon*, reasons in his cell with the logic he has served: the Party cannot be mistaken, since History is right and the Party is its organ; therefore, if he has doubted, he is guilty; his second interrogator, Gletkin, no longer even needs to convince him, and Rubashov confesses to imaginary crimes in order to render History one last service, before the bullet in the back of the neck. In Orwell, O'Brien explains to Winston, under torture, that the Party seeks power for its own sake, that God is power, and that reality exists only in the mind of the Party, which is immortal; the torture ends when Winston loves Big Brother.
>
> Why here: the two novels are Aron's secular religion described from within, in its liturgy, confession, and in its dogma, the infallibility of an authority that occupies the place of God and demands the lives of its faithful. Koestler shows the believer who sacrifices himself, Orwell the priest who demands; Rubashov and O'Brien are the two faces of the criterion. And Orwell has O'Brien say what Voegelin said of Gnosticism: the Party no longer promises a paradise, it is itself the immanent eschaton.
>
> Silone, lastly, a former communist leader, brings back in *Bread and Wine* a hunted revolutionary, Pietro Spina, in the cassock of a false priest, to the villages of the Abruzzi; the peasants take him for a saint, and he discovers that his socialism was a faith that had merely changed Churches. The disguise says it all: secular religion recognizes itself only by putting back on the habit of the religion it has left.
>
> Sources: Arthur Koestler, *Darkness at Noon* (1940) ; George Orwell, *Nineteen Eighty-Four*, III (1949) ; Ignazio Silone, *Pane e vino* (1936).

### Leo Strauss (1899-1973): Athens and Jerusalem

All the authors of this part argue about the way in which we left religion. Leo Strauss disputes that we left it at all. He disputes it not as a believer, which he never claimed to be, but as a philosopher, and that is why he is, I believe, the most serious adversary of the very thesis of the exit.

Strauss was born in 1899 in Kirchhain, a small rural town near Marburg, into an Orthodox Jewish family; he studied at Marburg, defended in 1921, under the supervision of Ernst Cassirer, a dissertation on Jacobi, and spent 1922 in Freiburg, where he attended Husserl's lectures and fell, like Levinas, Gadamer, Arendt and Karl Löwith, whose friend and correspondent he would remain, under the sway of Heidegger. His first book, written between 1925 and 1928 and published in 1930, is devoted to Spinoza's critique of religion, that is, to the very book that our third part made one of the founding acts of modern critique. In the preface to the English edition of 1965 he would present it as the work of a young Jew in Germany caught “in the grip of the theologico-political predicament”. This theologico-political problem, the question whether a society can be founded on reason alone or whether it rests on a revealed law, would be, he says elsewhere, “the theme of my studies”.

The book's thesis, as the 1965 preface restates it, reverses the story this essay has followed. Spinoza, and with him the whole Enlightenment critique, did not refute revelation. He could not, for belief in an omnipotent God who reveals himself when he wills and hides himself when he wills rests on a premise that, according to Strauss, can be refuted neither by experience nor by the principle of contradiction. And the indirect proof of this is the very means the critics used: “Spinoza and his like owed such success as they had in their fight against orthodoxy to laughter and mockery”; they tried to drive orthodoxy out by laughing at a position from which no proof drawn from Scripture or from reason could dislodge it. The modern critique of religion would thus not have won its case; it would have won a battle of opinion. And a genuine refutation would demand more than any philosopher has ever supplied: “The genuine refutation of orthodoxy would require the proof that the world and human life are perfectly intelligible without the assumption of a mysterious God”; it would require at the very least the completion of the philosophical system.

This sentence says that the exit from religion, in the strong sense in which the Enlightenment understood it, would have presupposed that reason become a total knowledge, master of the world and of life. Now that is what I have called a refoundation. The only possible refutation of revelation would be the installation of another absolute, completed reason, man the master of everything; and we know what secular religions made of that ambition. Strauss thus closes the door on both sides: one does not refute revelation without making oneself god, and if one gives up making oneself god, one does not refute it.

Conversely, and Strauss insists on this with the same rigour, revelation does not refute philosophy either. In *Natural Right and History* (1953), he formulates this impasse in the harshest terms for philosophy itself: “Philosophy has to grant that revelation is possible”, which amounts to granting that the philosophic life is not necessarily the right life; and further on, “the mere fact that philosophy and revelation cannot refute each other would constitute the refutation of philosophy by revelation”. For philosophy claims to be a life grounded on evidence; if it itself rests on a choice that no evidence grounds, it confirms what faith said of it. It is this conflict without an arbiter that Strauss calls Athens and Jerusalem, a title he gave to several lectures, in 1946, in 1950 and in 1967, the last published the same year in *Commentary*.

One recognizes here, displaced by eight centuries, the question of Averroes and of Maimonides, and it is no accident: it was by reading them that Strauss formed his thesis. *Persecution and the Art of Writing* (1952) maintains that the philosophers before modernity, under the threat of persecution, wrote in such a way as to convey one teaching to the majority of their readers and another to a few; Maimonides, Judah Halevi and Spinoza himself are said to be among these writers. Strauss took seriously the warning Maimonides places at the head of the *Guide*, not to explain his secret teaching, to the point of writing that no historian possessed of a sense of decency could lightly disregard the entreaty of a superior man such as Maimonides. We find again Averroes' division between those who demonstrate and those who are persuaded, which the first part set out; Strauss makes of it, rather than a prudence of circumstance, a permanent truth about the relation between philosophy and the city: the city lives on opinions, and in particular on opinions about the gods, which philosophy can neither share nor destroy without danger.

This thesis, hotly debated, seems to me partly fragile: it is unverifiable by construction, since the absence of signs of a hidden teaching can always be read as proof of its skill, and it has fostered among some disciples a way of reading texts in which suspicion takes the place of philology. One must also recall a letter Strauss wrote from Paris to Löwith in 1933: in it he asserted that one could protest against what he called the “shabby abomination” of the Hitler regime only on the basis of the principles of the right, “from fascist, authoritarian, and imperial principles”. The correspondence with Löwith, partly published under the title “Correspondence Concerning Modernity” (*Independent Journal of Philosophy*, 4, 1983, and 5/6, 1988, trans. G. E. Tucker), is one of the places where his position takes shape: the two former pupils of Heidegger, so close in their critique of historicism, diverge there over the possibility of a return to the Ancients.

His relations to the other protagonists complete his placing. As early as 1932, he wrote a review of Carl Schmitt's *The Concept of the Political*, in which he argued that Schmitt, despite all his efforts, remained a prisoner of the liberal horizon he was fighting, for want of being able to give reasons for his commitment to the political. The critique joins ours by another path: Strauss sees in a sovereign decision that cannot say in the name of what it decides the very symptom of the modernity Schmitt claimed to overcome. With Löwith he shares the rejection of progress and the gaze turned towards the Greeks; but where Löwith withdraws into the Stoic contemplation of nature, Strauss reopens the political question, that of the best regime, which classical philosophy posed and which modernity is said to have abandoned. With Blumenberg, finally, no dialogue is attested, but the disagreement is total: Blumenberg defends the legitimacy of the modern age as self-assertion, Strauss sees in it a break with ancient wisdom, of which Machiavelli is said to be the author and which the critique of religion is said to have made possible.

Strauss also strikes at our reading of Spinoza. The third part presented the *Theological-Political Treatise* as one of the acts by which modern philosophy emancipated itself from Scripture, and Spinoza as one of the rare exceptions in the series, the one who keeps the name of God without refounding a cult. Strauss does not dispute that Spinoza wanted to free philosophy; he disputes that he refuted what he was freeing it from. And he adds a suspicion our reading had not considered: that Spinoza himself wrote so as to be read in two ways, and that his apparent piety, the piety that made him a God-intoxicated man in the eyes of the Romantics, is in part an art of writing. I do not believe this suspicion undoes the reading of the *Ethics* that this essay has defended, for the intellectual love of God is demonstrated there, not suggested; but it obliges us to acknowledge that the Spinozist exception rests on a philosophical decision, that of holding the world to be intelligible without remainder, which Spinoza could no more prove than orthodoxy could prove revelation.

There remains from Strauss an objection I do not believe I can lift, and which I want to give in its best form. This essay's criterion says that one refounds a religion when one installs an absolute that demands sacrifice. Strauss accepts it, I believe, but he draws from it a more radical consequence. If the total exit from religion would presuppose the completion of reason, then every exit that believes itself total is already a refoundation, and the only honest position left is one that acknowledges that the question is not settled. It resembles that of the recognized exceptions, Spinoza, Hume, Nietzsche, Camus, in that it sacrifices no one to anything; it differs from them in that it does not claim to have found, in a spirituality of exercise or in a solidarity without a heaven, a peaceful way out. It keeps open, between Athens and Jerusalem, a tension it judges constitutive of the West and which it refuses to resolve.

> **En littérature.** Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, *Nathan der Weise* (1779) ; Boccaccio, *Decameron* (1353) ; Xenophon, *Memorabilia* (4th century BCE)
>
> Asked by Saladin about the true religion, Nathan answers with the parable of the three rings: “Vor grauen Jahren lebt' ein Mann in Osten, / Der einen Ring von unschätzbarem Wert / Aus lieber Hand besaß”, in hoary years there lived a man in the East who possessed, from a beloved hand, a ring of priceless worth, which made whoever wore it in confidence pleasing to God and to men; the father, loving his three sons equally, had two copies made, and no one could any longer tell the true one. The judge to whom the dispute is brought sends the brothers away: “Es eifre jeder seiner unbestochnen / Von Vorurteilen freien Liebe nach!”, let each of them strive to emulate his father's love, uncorrupted and free of prejudice, and let the ring's virtue show itself in works, and in a thousand thousand years a wiser judge will speak.
>
> Why here: the parable states exactly the position Strauss holds against the idea of an exit, and with the same reservations. Neither revelation nor reason has refuted the other, and judgment is deferred to a judge who does not come; but Lessing, unlike Strauss, draws from it a moral of tolerance that is already an answer, and Strauss, who read Lessing all his life, reproached him precisely for having written so as to be heard by two audiences. The authentic ring is not lost, it is undecidable; this is the difference between Athens and Jerusalem made livable, and perhaps too livable.
>
> Lessing had the parable from Boccaccio, who has it told by the Jew Melchizedek to Saladin as early as the third tale of the first day of the *Decameron*, with the same conclusion: the question of the true law remains pending. And Strauss himself, in his last years, was reading Xenophon, whose Socrates in the *Memorabilia* sacrifices to the gods of the city and philosophizes all the same, without the reader ever knowing which of the two he prefers [résumé]. Three texts, three readers who do not decide: the adversary of the exit has a library.
>
> Sources: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, *Nathan der Weise*, III, 7 (1779) ; Boccaccio, *Decameron*, I, 3 (1353) ; Xenophon, *Memorabilia*, I, 1 (4th century BCE).
### Marcel Gauchet (b. 1946): Christianity, the religion of the exit from religion

With Marcel Gauchet, the quarrel leaves Germany and changes its object. Blumenberg asked whether modernity owed anything to Christianity; Gauchet asks what a religion is, and answers that it is not first of all a belief. *The Disenchantment of the World: A Political History of Religion* (1985) is one of the most ambitious books French thought has devoted to our question, and its central formula seems written for this essay: Christianity is defined there as “la religion de la sortie de la religion”, the religion of the exit from religion.

The formula presupposes a definition of religion that is political before it is theological. A religion, for Gauchet, is a way of instituting the social: society receives its order from a source that is external, prior and untouchable. The rules of common life are not made by human beings; they are given to them by the gods, the ancestors, the time of origins. This is what Gauchet calls heteronomy, and he sees in stateless societies, those that ethnologists study, the purest form of religion: not the most mystical, but the one in which dispossession is most complete, in which the present has no power over a law fixed once and for all in the mythical past. Religion is not an illusion about heaven, as in Feuerbach; it is a way for human beings to divest themselves of their own instituting power.

The history of religions becomes the history of the loosening of this dispossession. The appearance of the State, by separating the powerful from the rest, already opens a breach: the law now has human representatives, and what has been established can be transformed. The great religions of the Axial Age, and above all monotheism, move the divine away from the world: a single God, transcendent, separate from creation, leaves the world to human beings in a way that gods mingled with nature did not allow. Christianity carries this movement to its end. Through the incarnation, God becomes man and consecrates the dignity of the human world; through the separation of the two realms, rendering unto Caesar what is Caesar's, it withdraws the political order from immediate divine law. It thus carries within its structure the possibility of a world that will do without it in order to organize itself. Gauchet also says that Christianity was “la religion possible d'une société d'après la religion”, the possible religion of a society after religion.

Gauchet himself had to correct a misreading: the exit from religion does not mean the disappearance of believers. In *La Religion dans la démocratie* (1998), he writes: “Sortie de la religion ne signifie pas sortie de la croyance religieuse, mais sortie d'un monde où la religion est structurante[…] et où elle définit l'économie du lien social”, the exit from religion does not mean an exit from religious belief, but an exit from a world in which religion is structuring and in which it defines the economy of the social bond. One may believe in God in a society that has left religion; one simply believes there as an individual, and faith becomes a matter of personal identity and choice, not the foundation of the common order. Democracy is the regime of a society that gives itself its own law, and that must therefore live without an external guarantor: it is autonomy after heteronomy.

Gauchet touches several figures of this essay. First, he proves the Nietzsche of the *Genealogy* (III, 27) and of § 357 of *The Gay Science* right on a level Nietzsche had not explored. Nietzsche said that Christian truthfulness had turned against Christianity; Gauchet says that the very structure of Christianity produced the world that makes it useless. The two theses converge: the exit from religion is a *Christian* event. Next, he ruins Onfray's position in *Décadence*: what Onfray describes as a death, the exhaustion of an organism, Gauchet describes as a fulfilment. Christianity does not die like a living thing that has exhausted its strength; it realizes itself in a world that no longer needs it in order to stand. I present this opposition as a constructed confrontation: I have found no text in which Gauchet discusses *Décadence*.

The strongest objection to Gauchet came from Quebec, and it is attested. The sociologist Fernand Dumont, relayed by Cantin, refuses to confine Christianity to the private sphere: to reduce religion to its instituting function is to decide in advance that faith has nothing more to say to the common world once that function is lost. I believe the objection is sound, but it bears less against Gauchet's history than against his definition. Gauchet defined religion by heteronomy, which can by definition recede: he built his concept in such a way that an exit from it is possible. What he does not say is what becomes of the demand for meaning when it no longer has an instituted form: Gauchet is the historian of the exit, not the thinker of what remains. He confirms, finally, what the prologue drew from Lactantius: the question “can one leave religion without founding another?” is first of all a Christian question.

Gauchet in fact debated this very question with Luc Ferry: a public debate is said to have brought them together in January 1999, and their exchange produced a book, *Le Religieux après la religion* (2004). The title states what is at stake: if religion has ceased to structure the social, what remains of the religious, of the dimension of existence that found expression in it? Not having read the book, I do not report their arguments; but their other works make it possible to say where the line runs. Gauchet describes an exit whose end point is autonomy, and he distrusts any attempt to reinject the sacred into democracy, which he judges destined to live without an ultimate guarantor. Ferry maintains that modern humanism has kept a form of transcendence, displaced from heaven to man. The one thinks the exit, the other what survives it, and this disagreement announces the passage from religion as institution to spirituality as experience.

> **En littérature.** Victor Hugo, *Religions et religion* (1880) ; Gustave Flaubert, *Madame Bovary* (1857) ; Matthew Arnold, “Dover Beach” (1867)
>
> Hugo's title is already Gauchet's thesis. *Religions et religion* sets the Churches, “talmuds, korans et bibles”, talmuds, korans and bibles, which it rejects, against the religion that remains, the God read “au fond du ciel tonnant”, in the depths of the thundering sky; and the conclusion ends as a creed: “Il est ! il est ! Regarde, âme. Il a son solstice, / La Conscience ; il a son axe, la Justice ; / Il a son équinoxe, et c'est l'Égalité ; / Il a sa vaste aurore, et c'est la Liberté.[…] Il est ! il est ! il est ! sans fin, sans origine, / Sans éclipse, sans nuit, sans repos, sans sommeil. / Renonce, ver de terre, à créer le soleil”, He is! he is! Look, soul. He has his solstice, Conscience; he has his axis, Justice; he has his equinox, and it is Equality; he has his vast dawn, and it is Liberty. He is! he is! he is! without end, without origin, without eclipse, without night, without rest, without sleep. Earthworm, give up creating the sun.
>
> Why here: “sortie de la religion ne signifie pas sortie de la croyance religieuse”, the exit from religion does not mean an exit from religious belief, Gauchet writes in 1998; Hugo had put it into verse in 1880, from the believer's side, with a God whose attributes are Conscience, Justice, Equality and Liberty, that is, the motto of the Republic. The religion of the exit from religion has its poet, and he shows what the essay points out: heteronomy recedes, and the need to consecrate remains, now consecrating the principles of autonomy.
>
> Flaubert had described the exit in the provinces. During the wake for Emma, the pharmacist Homais and the curé Bournisien quarrel: “Homais attaqua la confession. Bournisien la défendit ; il s'étendit sur les restitutions qu'elle faisait opérer. Il cita différentes anecdotes de voleurs devenus honnêtes tout à coup”, Homais attacked confession. Bournisien defended it; he dwelt on the restitutions it brought about. He cited various anecdotes of thieves suddenly turned honest; then they fall asleep one after the other before the body, and wake up to eat. Religion and its opposite, the priest and the Voltairean, equally drowsy before the dead woman: this is the disenchantment of the world seen from Yonville, and neither of the two comes out the winner. Arnold, in England, heard the same night on the beach at Dover: “The sea of faith / Was once, too, at the full, and round earth's shore / Lay like the folds of a bright girdle furled. / But now I only hear / Its melancholy, long, withdrawing roar”; and nothing remains to the poet but the faithfulness of two lovers “as on a darkling plain / Swept with confused alarms of struggle and flight, / Where ignorant armies clash by night”.
>
> Sources: Victor Hugo, *Religions et religion*, “Conclusion” (1880); Gustave Flaubert, *Madame Bovary*, III, 9 (1857); Matthew Arnold, “Dover Beach”, *New Poems* (1867).

### Charles Taylor (b. 1931): against subtraction stories

Charles Taylor, a Canadian and Catholic philosopher, published in 2007 *A Secular Age*, a book of nearly nine hundred pages that takes up the question from what he calls the conditions of belief. He distinguishes three senses of the word “secular”: public spaces emptied of all reference to God, where politics, the economy and science function without him; the decline of religious belief and practice that sociologists measure; and finally, the subject of the book, a change in the very conditions of belief: the shift, Taylor writes, “from a society where belief in God is unchallenged and indeed, unproblematic, to one in which it is understood to be one option among others, and frequently not the easiest to embrace”.

The polemical heart of the book targets a way of telling the story of modernity that Taylor calls “subtraction stories”. These are the accounts that explain modernity “by human beings having lost, or sloughed off, or liberated themselves from certain earlier, confining horizons, or illusions, or limitations of knowledge”. Modern man would be what remains once religion has been removed, as one strips a layer of paint to uncover the wall. Taylor argues that this is false: what remains when God is removed is not a bare nature; it is a new historical construction, with its own ideals, its own moral demands, its own imaginary.

Taylor describes this construction under several names. The immanent frame is the order that can be understood entirely without transcendence, a natural, social and moral order that holds up by itself. Exclusive humanism is the possibility, available on a wide scale for the first time, of a life oriented towards human flourishing with nothing beyond it: according to Taylor, “a purely self-sufficient humanism came to be a widely available option”, defined as “a humanism accepting no final goals beyond human flourishing”. Taylor finally describes what he calls the nova effect: not a retreat of religion before unbelief, but an explosion of intermediate positions, deisms, spiritualities, humanisms, religions of art, which proliferate between faith and atheism. I have not found an exact formula of Taylor's for these last three terms; I give them in paraphrase.

The kinship between Taylor and this essay is great, and the difference instructive. Taylor rejects subtraction stories as I reject the idea of a total exit: one does not leave religion as one leaves a room, with a neutral void left behind. But he draws from this a conclusion I do not draw: exclusive humanism is one construction among others, and Christian faith remains a living option, which the secular age makes more difficult but not less true; he speaks of a fullness that everyone seeks, believer or unbeliever, and that exclusive humanism struggles to name. Taylor is a loyal believing adversary of modern critique: he does not deny the legitimacy of unbelief, he denies that it is the simple result of a lucidity at last achieved. The objection he makes to Feuerbach, to Marx, to Freud is the same as Stirner's, turned around: you think you have subtracted God, but you have built something else, and you must answer for what you have built. This comparison with Stirner, which Taylor does not make to my knowledge, is a constructed confrontation.

> **En littérature.** Evelyn Waugh, *Brideshead Revisited* (1945) ; François-René de Chateaubriand, *René* (1802)
>
> *Brideshead Revisited* tells, through the voice of an agnostic painter, Charles Ryder, the story of the Catholic Flyte family, whom he loves and does not understand: Sebastian who drinks, Julia who gives up Charles so as not to live in sin, Lord Marchmain who, dying after thirty years of apostasy, makes the sign of the cross; Cordelia explains to Charles that God lets each person wander to the ends of the earth, then brings him back with a twitch upon the thread; the epilogue shows Charles, in 1944, kneeling in the chapel at Brideshead before a lamp that burns once more. Why here: this is Taylor's faith as an option, told by someone for whom it was not one. No one in Waugh is a believer by default; each chooses, renounces, returns, and the narrator himself ends up choosing without our knowing what he has come to believe. Taylor would say that the nova effect produced this novel: a faith available among others, and all the more demanding because it no longer goes without saying.
>
> Chateaubriand had described the moment before. René, in 1802, neither believes nor doubts; he is bored, and his boredom is a religion without an object: “Qu'il fallait peu de chose à ma rêverie ! une feuille séchée que le vent chassait devant moi, une cabane dont la fumée s'élevait dans la cime dépouillée des arbres[…] Levez-vous vite, orages désirés qui devez emporter René dans les espaces d'une autre vie !”, How little my reverie needed! a dry leaf the wind drove before me, a hut whose smoke rose into the bare tops of the trees… Rise up quickly, longed-for storms that are to carry René off into the spaces of another life! This is what *The Genius of Christianity*, of which *René* was a chapter, calls the *vague des passions*, the vagueness of the passions: a heart made for the infinite in a world that no longer offers it, and which Chateaubriand wanted to bring back to the Church. Taylor describes the secular age as a world in which this fullness seeks its names; René is the first hero who does not find them, and Father Souël, at the end, scolds him for it.
>
> Sources: Evelyn Waugh, *Brideshead Revisited* (1945); François-René de Chateaubriand, *René* (1802).

### Jürgen Habermas (1929-2026): translation and the post-secular society

The last great actor in the quarrel is Jürgen Habermas, long the philosopher of modernity as an unfinished project, who was expected to defend secular reason against the religions. On 14 October 2001, a month after the attacks of 11 September, he received in Frankfurt the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade and delivered a speech entitled “Glauben und Wissen”, *Faith and Knowledge*, which surprised his readers. In it he introduced an expression that would become famous: one must ask, he said, what secularization means “in unseren postsäkularen Gesellschaften”, in our post-secular societies.

A post-secular society is not a society in which religion returns in force, but a society that acknowledges that religious communities are not disappearing, contrary to what secularization theory predicted, and that must learn to live with them without renouncing the neutrality of the State. Habermas proposes a rule of reciprocity. The believing citizen must agree to translate his reasons into a language accessible to all, so that his convictions can enter public deliberation without requiring those who do not believe to adhere to his faith. But the secular citizen, for his part, must keep “einen Sinn für die Artikulationskraft religiöser Sprachen”, a sense of the articulating power of religious languages. He must not presume that religious languages say nothing that reason does not already know how to say, but admit that they have perhaps preserved moral intuitions, about dignity, suffering, guilt, reparation, that secular language has not yet managed to formulate.

Hence the central sentence of the speech: “Eine Säkularisierung, die nicht vernichtet, vollzieht sich im Modus der Übersetzung”, a secularization that does not annihilate is accomplished in the mode of translation. Habermas gives an example of it, taken from Genesis: man created in the image of God (Gn 1, 27). Faced with the possibilities of genetic engineering, this idea of creatureliness says something that secular ethics struggles to say: that a human being must not be the product of another human being's design. To translate is neither to keep the religious content as it is nor to throw it away; it is to carry it over into a language that all can understand. And Habermas gives this operation an illustrious model: Kant provided, he says, “das erste große Beispiel für eine säkularisierende und zugleich rettende Dekonstruktion von Glaubenswahrheiten”, the first great example of a deconstruction of the truths of faith that is at once secularizing and redemptive. One recognizes the Kant of Part Four, the Kant of *Die Religion innerhalb der Grenzen der bloßen Vernunft*: to reduce religion to morality, but to save in morality what was rational in religion.

In January 2004, Habermas debated at the Catholic Academy of Bavaria with Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, who the following year would become Pope Benedict XVI, on the pre-political foundations of the constitutional State; the dialogue is attested under the title “Dialektik der Säkularisierung”, but I have read none of its formulas and I do not quote it. He then took up the whole question again in a vast genealogy, *Auch eine Geschichte der Philosophie* (2019), which I have not consulted.

Habermas opens a third way between Löwith and Blumenberg. Against Löwith, he does not think that modernity merely repeats religion under another name; against Blumenberg, he does not think it owes religion nothing. It owes it contents, but these contents are not stolen: they are *translated*, and translation is a labour that transforms what it transmits. This is the most reasonable position in the quarrel, and I believe it is true for a large part of our moral heritage. But it leaves our question intact, for Habermasian translation bears only on the *normative contents* of religion, what can enter public deliberation, and says nothing about what, in religion, does not allow itself to be translated into reasons: prayer, worship, the experience of presence, the relation to death, consolation. Habermas himself takes up Weber's phrase: in *Glauben und Wissen* (2001), he speaks of a biblical intuition “die in unserem Zusammenhang auch dem religiös Unmusikalischen etwas sagen kann”, which in our context can say something even to one who is religiously unmusical; that he applied the expression to himself is often reported, but I have not found the primary source. What does not translate is what Part Twelve will call spirituality: Habermas said how reason can inherit from religion; he did not say how the individual can live without it.

> **En littérature.** Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, *Faust* (1808) ; Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, *Die Erziehung des Menschengeschlechts* (1780)
>
> Faust, in his study, opens the New Testament to translate the beginning of the Gospel of John, and cannot leave the word alone: “Geschrieben steht: Im Anfang war der Sinn.[…] Es sollte stehn: Im Anfang war die Kraft![…] Mir hilft der Geist! Auf einmal seh ich Rat / Und schreibe getrost: Im Anfang war die Tat!”, it is written: in the beginning was the Sense; it ought to read: in the beginning was the Force; the Spirit comes to my aid, at once I see my way, and confidently write: in the beginning was the Deed.
>
> Why here: this is Habermas's thesis in a single scene, and it has two sides. The secularization that does not annihilate is accomplished in the mode of translation: Faust translates, and his translation transforms what it transmits, the Logos become deed, which Marx will say again in the eleventh thesis on Feuerbach. But Goethe also shows what happens while one translates: the poodle growls, and it is Mephistopheles who steps out from behind the stove. Habermasian translation retains only the normative contents; the scene reminds us that what does not allow itself to be translated does not disappear for all that.
>
> Lessing had proposed, thirty years earlier, the model of all translations to come: “Erziehung giebt dem Menschen nichts, was er nicht auch aus sich selbst haben könnte: sie giebt ihm das, was er aus sich selber haben könnte, nur geschwinder und leichter. Also giebt auch die Offenbarung dem Menschengeschlechte nichts, worauf die menschliche Vernunft, sich selbst überlassen, nicht auch kommen würde”, education gives man nothing that he could not also have from himself: it gives him what he could have from himself, only more quickly and more easily. So revelation, too, gives the human race nothing that human reason, left to itself, would not also arrive at. Revelation as the pedagogy of reason: Habermas is its direct heir, and the essay's objection holds for both, what reason cannot give itself, prayer, worship, experience, remains outside the school.
>
> Sources: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, *Faust. Der Tragödie erster Teil*, “Studierzimmer” (1808); Gotthold Ephraim Lessing, *Die Erziehung des Menschengeschlechts*, § 4 (1780).

### Assessment of the quarrel

The quarrel over secularization does not settle our question; it reformulates it and forces me to correct myself. Schmitt showed that one can want refoundation: political theology, openly assumed, is refoundation without a mask. Löwith gave the thesis its historical support: philosophies of history are soteriologies without God, and that is why they were able to demand sacrifices. Voegelin and Aron gave the criterion its most massive cases, the secular religions of the twentieth century. Blumenberg showed that the thesis, taken in its extensive version, proves too much, and forced it to make its criterion precise: there is refoundation only when an absolute demands the sacrifice of the individual. Strauss recalled that the exit itself has not been demonstrated, and that the question remains open. Gauchet showed that the exit from religion is itself a religious event, and that our question is a Christian one. Taylor showed that exclusive humanism is not what remains when God is subtracted, but a construction that must answer for itself. Habermas showed that an exit that does not destroy is a translation.

These authors nonetheless have one thing in common: all of them speak of religion as an institution, an order, a collective structure of meaning, a set of normative contents. None really speaks of what the individual lives through when he prays, meditates, recollects himself, or seeks to transform his own existence. It is perhaps there that the possibility of an exit without refoundation is decided. One can leave a Church without leaving the demand it answered; one can stop believing without ceasing to seek a way of life that engages one's whole existence. At the end of the twentieth century this demand received a name that is today travelling around the world: spirituality. We must now ask whether this word designates a real way out or a new shadow of God in the cave.
## Part Twelve: spiritualities without God

The word “spirituality” has a shorter history than one might think, and that history is itself an argument. In Christian language, *spiritualitas* designated life according to the Spirit, as opposed to life according to the flesh, and then, in the modern period, the whole body of practices and schools of the inner life: people spoke of Ignatian, Carmelite, Salesian spirituality. Spirituality was a region of religion, the region of experience and exercise, distinct from doctrine and institution. What is new, since the second half of the twentieth century, is that the region has broken away from the continent. People now say “spiritual but not religious”, and they mean by this that they keep the experience while leaving the Church, the exercise while leaving dogma, the search for meaning while leaving the answer given in advance.

Part Eight showed how this detachment was prepared: James defined religion by the experience of individuals in their solitude, Bergson set the dynamic religion of the mystics against static religion, and Freud encountered, in Romain Rolland's oceanic feeling, an experience he admitted he could not find in himself. Spirituality without God inherits these three gestures, and it raises a question. If spiritual experience can be separated from instituted religion, the exit without refoundation is perhaps possible: one would leave religion while keeping spirituality, which, being neither a dogma nor a Church, would refound nothing. But spirituality might also be the subtlest form of refoundation, the one that keeps the sacred while excusing itself from answering for it.

Four French thinkers, who read, criticized and sometimes insulted one another, gave this question its most elaborate forms: Pierre Hadot and Michel Foucault, who open the part, make spirituality an exercise of the subject upon itself; André Comte-Sponville and Luc Ferry, further on, set a spirituality of immanence against a horizontal transcendence, and their quarrel is that of two wisdoms. Between the two pairs, four stages. Karl Jaspers, whom Camus took as a target, had as early as 1948 given the name of philosophical faith to a belief without revelation or Church. A question older than all religions, why there is something rather than nothing, serves as a test for every spirituality without God, in a constructed debate in which Leibniz, Hume, Kant, Schelling, Bergson, Heidegger, Carnap and Wittgenstein answer one another. Iris Murdoch keeps an absolute without God, the Good. Buddhism, as European philosophers have read it, finally offers the model of a religion without a creator God. After the quarrel of the two wisdoms, Mohammed Arkoun and Abdennour Bidar raise the question from within Islam, and the contemporary militant atheists show what becomes of the critique of religion when it ignores this whole path.

### Pierre Hadot (1922-2010): philosophy as spiritual exercise

Pierre Hadot was a Catholic priest before leaving the priesthood in 1952; he became one of the great historians of ancient philosophy, a specialist in Plotinus, Marius Victorinus and Marcus Aurelius, and professor at the Collège de France from 1982. His major work is not a treatise but a collection of articles, *Exercices spirituels et philosophie antique* (1981, enlarged several times up to 2002), complemented by a synthesis, *What Is Ancient Philosophy?* (1995), and by a book of interviews whose title sums everything up, *La Philosophie comme manière de vivre* (2001).

Hadot's thesis is first of all historical, and solid. In Antiquity, philosophy was not primarily a system of propositions about the world, to be adopted or refuted like a scientific theory, but a choice of life. To become an Epicurean, a Stoic, a Platonist, a Cynic was to convert to a way of existing, to enter a school, to adopt a daily discipline. Philosophical discourse, treatises, demonstrations, commentaries, served this conversion: it transformed the existence of the one who studied it, instead of constituting a knowledge detached from him. Hadot readily contrasted this conception with what he called the mere accumulation of knowledge. The Epicureans recalled to mind the fourfold remedy; the Stoics practised the view from above, the premeditation of evils, attention to the present; the Platonists practised dying, in the sense of the *Phaedo*, detaching the soul from the body through thought. These practices Hadot calls spiritual exercises.

Why “spiritual”? The word comes straight from the Christian tradition: the *Spiritual Exercises* of Ignatius of Loyola (1548) are the model of the method. But the debt is reversed, and that is the meaning of all Hadot's work: it was the Christians who inherited the philosophical exercises of Antiquity, when Christianity presented itself, from the second century onwards, as the true philosophy. Monastic Christianity took over the Stoics' attention to oneself, the Pythagoreans' examination of conscience, the Platonists' meditation on death. Philosophy therefore does not borrow the word “spiritual” from religion; it was religion that had borrowed the thing from philosophy. I have not found Hadot's justification for his choice of the word in a primary text; a summary indicates that he saw no difficulty in the expression, and Ossola surmises that Barthes's *Sade, Fourier, Loyola* (1971) had made it available.

Hadot thus makes available, to a modern reader who no longer believes, a model of spiritual life that owes nothing to faith in the Christian sense. One can practise Marcus Aurelius's view from above without believing in Stoic providence; one can train oneself, with Epicurus, not to fear death, without believing in atoms. Spirituality becomes a practice, not a belief: it asks for no dogma, no Church, no sacrifice, but for work on oneself.

Hadot does not, however, stop at the self, and it is on this point that he opposed Michel Foucault, in an attested response. Foucault, who had read Hadot and made use of him in his lectures of the 1980s, turned Antiquity into the site of a “culture of the self”, a “care of the self”, in which the subject constitutes itself as a work. Hadot, in two texts written after Foucault's death, expressed both his esteem and his disagreement. He regrets that this death interrupted a dialogue, “dans lequel nous aurions pu sans doute profiter mutuellement de nos accords, mais aussi et surtout de nos désaccords”, in which we could no doubt have profited from each other's agreements, but also, and above all, from our disagreements. Testa sums up the disagreement in three points. Foucault recentres ancient spirituality on the self, whereas it aimed at a going beyond the self towards the universal, nature and the human community. He confuses Stoic joy, *gaudium*, which is found in the best part of oneself, with pleasure. Finally, he makes the culture of the self an aesthetics of existence, which risks, Hadot writes in the English version of his text, being “too aesthetic” and becoming “a new form of Dandysm”.

This disagreement is more than a quarrel among historians: it bears on the criterion. A spirituality that aims only at the construction of the self refounds no absolute, but it risks making the self itself the absolute: Stirner's Unique turned into a work of art. Hadot replies that there is something other than the self: the awareness of being part of the Whole, the cosmic feeling, the demand for justice towards other human beings. The question then shifts: this Whole to which the sage rises, this nature of which he feels himself a part, is it not a new name for the divine? The Stoics, for their part, said so without embarrassment: nature was God, the *logos* was Zeus. Hadot keeps the exercise while setting aside Stoic theology. One can, I believe, keep the one without the other, on one condition: that the Whole be not an object of adoration but a horizon of lucidity, and that the exercise demand not that one sacrifice oneself to it, but that one see more truly within it. This is what Spinoza already called knowing things under the aspect of eternity, and Hadot is, without being a Spinozist, one of the contemporary thinkers closest to Spinoza (a constructed comparison).

> **En littérature.** Rainer Maria Rilke, “Archaïscher Torso Apollos” (1908) ; Horace, *Odes* (23 BCE) ; Henry David Thoreau, *Walden* (1854)
>
> Rilke's sonnet describes a headless torso, in the Louvre, whose stone still seems to see: “denn da ist keine Stelle, / die dich nicht sieht. Du mußt dein Leben ändern”, for there is no place that does not see you. You must change your life. Why here: this is the spiritual exercise in Hadot's sense, reduced to a single line. A Greek statue, godless since the god has been beheaded, is enough to produce the conversion of the gaze that the *Republic* called *periagôgê*; and the imperative comes from no law, it comes from what one has looked at. Peter Sloterdijk made it the title of a book on exercises.
>
> Horace, in the ode to Leuconoe, teaches the same exercise in the future tense: “Tu ne quaesieris, scire nefas, quem mihi, quem tibi / finem di dederint, Leuconoe, nec Babylonios / temptaris numeros”, do not ask, it is forbidden to know, what end the gods have given to me, to you, Leuconoe, and do not try the Babylonian calculations; and the ending: “carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero”, seize the day, trusting as little as possible to the morrow. Hadot showed that *carpe diem* is not a hedonism but the concentration on the present that Epicureans and Stoics practised, each in their own way; the ode is a manual in eight lines, with the gods left in their place, out of reach.
>
> Thoreau, finally: “I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.” Two years in a cabin as an exercise, without Church, without master and without doctrine: the American version of what Hadot describes among the Ancients, and the proof that the thing has survived the name.
>
> Sources: Rainer Maria Rilke, “Archaïscher Torso Apollos”, *Der neuen Gedichte anderer Teil* (1908) ; Horace, *Odes* I, 11 (23 BCE) ; Henry David Thoreau, *Walden; or, Life in the Woods*, ch. 2 (1854).

### Michel Foucault (1926-1984): philosophy and spirituality

Michel Foucault never wrote a book on religion, and one must not make him say more than he said. But his lecture course at the Collège de France in 1981-1982, published in 2001 under the title *The Hermeneutics of the Subject*, contains a definition of spirituality that is precise and useful to our question. In the lecture of 6 January 1982, he calls spirituality “la recherche, la pratique, l'expérience par lesquelles le sujet opère sur lui-même les transformations nécessaires pour avoir accès à la vérité”, the search, the practice, the experience through which the subject carries out on itself the transformations necessary for gaining access to the truth.

This definition has one merit: it says nothing about God. Spirituality here is neither belief in the supernatural, nor experience of the sacred, nor relation to a transcendent being, but a thesis on the relation between the subject and truth: truth does not give itself to the subject as he is; he must transform himself in order to gain access to it. Conversion, ascesis, purification, exercise are not ornaments of the philosophical life, but the very conditions of knowledge. In Antiquity, Foucault says, philosophy and spirituality were not separate: the Delphic precept “know thyself”, γνῶθι σεαυτόν (*gnôthi seauton*), was subordinate to another, more fundamental one, the care of the self, ἐπιμέλεια ἑαυτοῦ (*epimeleia heautou*). One could know the truth only by taking care of oneself, that is, by transforming oneself.

Then came what Foucault calls the “Cartesian moment”. I do not quote his formula, which I have not found on a reliable page; I paraphrase it. From Descartes onwards, access to truth comes through knowledge alone: a subject who reasons well and follows the method is enough to reach the truth, whatever the way he lives. The subject no longer has to be transformed, only to be correctly directed. Modern philosophy then separates from spirituality; it becomes knowledge, and spirituality, driven out of philosophy, takes refuge in religion, where it merges with faith. Foucault does not say that this moment is a catastrophe; he says that it took place, and that it made what the ancient philosophers were doing almost incomprehensible to us.

This framework sheds light on the debate of this essay. It explains why the modern critique of religion has almost always targeted religion as *belief*, as a set of true or false propositions: since the Cartesian moment, truth has been a matter of propositions. Spinoza is the exception: the *Ethics* is a book of geometrical demonstrations, but its title and its end are an ethics, that is, a transformation of life leading to beatitude, and Foucault could have seen in it the last great treatise in which philosophy and spirituality remain united. Nietzsche, for his part, never stops asking what truth does to the one who seeks it, and what type of human being the will to truth presupposes; against the Cartesian moment, he recovers the question of spirituality. These two comparisons are constructed confrontations; Foucault does not make them in the passages I have been able to read.

But Foucault's definition has a limit, which Hadot saw: centred on the subject, it says that he must transform himself in order to reach the truth, not what this truth is, nor whether it surpasses him. If truth is only a historical construction, as the Foucault of the 1970s tended to think, then spirituality risks closing in on the aesthetics of the self for which Hadot reproached it. If truth surpasses the subject, one must say how, and the question of the Whole returns. Foucault died in June 1984 without having settled this alternative, and the dialogue with Hadot broke off on this point.

> **En littérature.** Oscar Wilde, *The Picture of Dorian Gray* (1890) ; Oscar Wilde, *De Profundis* (1905) ; André Gide, *The Immoralist* (1902)
>
> Lord Henry, in the second chapter of *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, teaches Dorian the doctrine that will be his undoing: “The aim of life is self-development. To realize one's nature perfectly, that is what each of us is here for”; and: “The only way to get rid of a temptation is to yield to it.” Dorian makes his life a work of art and entrusts to the portrait the traces of his deeds; he dies stabbing the canvas.
>
> Why here: this is Hadot's objection to Foucault, “a new form of Dandysm”, turned into a novel by the dandy himself, and judged by him. The ancient culture of the self, Hadot says, was not an aesthetics of existence but a relation to the Whole that went beyond the self; Wilde shows what becomes of the care of the self when it has nothing but the self as its object: a portrait rotting in an attic. *De Profundis*, the letter from Reading prison, is the author's answer to his character: Wilde discovers in it, in suffering, the one thing he had not lived, and in Christ the first artist of existence: “And above all, Christ is the most supreme of individualists. Humility, like the artistic acceptance of all experiences, is merely a mode of manifestation. It is man's soul that Christ is always looking for.” The dandy, to get out of dandyism, had to remake Christ into a dandy.
>
> Gide, in *The Immoralist*, has Michel, cured of tuberculosis in North Africa, tell of his discovery of naked life, his barely veiled reading of Nietzsche, the sacrifice of his wife Marceline to his new health, and, at the end, a freedom he no longer knows what to do with: “Il me semble parfois que ma vraie vie n'a pas encore commencé. Arrachez-moi d'ici à présent, et donnez-moi des raisons d'être”, it sometimes seems to me that my real life has not yet begun; tear me away from here now, and give me reasons for being. The novel shows the spirituality of exercise turned into an exclusive care of the self, and its price: Marceline is the individual sacrificed to an absolute which, this time, is the self. Foucault, who read Gide, did not write this chapter; Hadot read it for him.
>
> Sources: Oscar Wilde, *The Picture of Dorian Gray*, ch. 2 (1890) ; Oscar Wilde, *De Profundis* (written in 1897, published in 1905) ; André Gide, *The Immoralist* (1902).

### Jaspers (1883-1969): philosophical faith, or transcendence without revelation

Karl Jaspers came to philosophy through psychiatry. His *Allgemeine Psychopathologie* (*General Psychopathology*, 1913) is a classic of the discipline; the *Psychologie der Weltanschauungen* (*Psychology of Worldviews*, 1919) marks the transition; the three volumes of *Philosophie* (1932) form his major work. In 1910 he married Gertrud Mayer, from a devout Jewish family; he was removed from university administration after 1933, dismissed from his chair at Heidelberg in 1937, banned from publishing, and he learned indirectly that a plan to deport him, together with his wife, was in place in the spring of 1945. Settled in Basel in 1948, he gave there the lectures published under the title *Der philosophische Glaube* (*Philosophical Faith*, 1948), the book that brings him into this debate.

Hadot and Foucault proposed a spirituality of exercise, which asks one to believe in nothing. Jaspers answers the simplest question that the man without a Church asks today: can one *believe* without belonging, believe in something without believing in a dogma? His answer is yes, and it bears a deliberately paradoxical name, philosophical faith. Since Kant, faith and knowledge have divided the ground between them; since Kierkegaard, faith has been the opposite of philosophy; since Heidegger, a Christian philosophy has been a wooden iron. Jaspers maintains that there is a faith which is not that of the Church and which is nonetheless the very condition of philosophy.

To understand it, one must start from the limit situations, the *Grenzsituationen*, which the *Psychologie der Weltanschauungen* introduced and the *Philosophie* developed: death, suffering, struggle, guilt. One can neither change nor evade them, and in them consciousness meets its walls. The Stanford Encyclopedia describes them as moments, usually accompanied by dread, guilt or acute anxiety, in which the mind experiences the narrowness of its forms and becomes disposed to go beyond them. In his *Einführung in die Philosophie* (*Introduction to Philosophy*, 1950), Jaspers drew from them a genealogy of philosophy with three sources: wonder, which he takes from Plato and Aristotle, doubt, which he takes from Descartes, and the shaking of the human being before limit situations, which is his own contribution. The constructed debate that follows starts from the first; Jaspers holds it together with the third.

At the edge of its limits, consciousness does not find an object. Everything we know, we know in a relation of subject to object, within a horizon; and each horizon is itself enveloped by a vaster horizon, which never becomes an object. This ultimate envelope Jaspers calls *das Umgreifende*, the Encompassing, a notion he sets out above all in *Von der Wahrheit* (*On Truth*, 1947). Transcendence is not a supreme being, in the sense in which Heidegger reproached metaphysics for making it one; it is the Encompassing of all encompassings, what can be neither known nor denied. It gives itself only in *ciphers*, *Chiffern*: nature, the work of art, the religious symbol, metaphysics itself are ciphers of transcendence, which designate it by withdrawing. The peculiarity of the cipher is that it refuses knowledge at the very moment it points; and the attitude that answers it is not possession, but failure, *Scheitern*, in which consciousness experiences its absolute insufficiency.

This philosophy does not refute religions, it translates them. Dogmas, myths, rites are ciphers; they are not false, they become false when they are taken for knowledge. Philosophical faith therefore holds between two refusals: that of orthodoxy, which freezes the cipher into doctrine and demands obedience, and that of dogmatic atheism, which takes the refusal of dogma for a knowledge of the absence of all transcendence. The Stanford Encyclopedia sums up the notion in three senses: authentic philosophy is guided by a faith in the transcendent origin of existence; it cannot for all that abdicate rationality before revealed contents; and the certainties of faith remain paradoxical and uncertain, so that whoever seeks them must accept a philosophical relativism and the exchange of reasons. Jaspers adds to this framework a word that sets him apart from all the mystics of this essay: *Kommunikation*. The truth of philosophical faith is tested in discussion, and is lost as soon as it dispenses with it.

This programme underwent two great public tests, both attested. The first is the demythologization controversy. Rudolf Bultmann had proposed, as early as 1941, to free the kerygma of the New Testament from its mythical envelope, so as to keep its existential core. Jaspers was expected to approve; he attacked him in *Die Frage der Entmythologisierung* (*The Question of Demythologization*, 1954), the small book that gathers the documents of the debate. He reproaches him with a false rationalism, an arbitrary contempt for the spiritual experiences laid down in the myths of ancient times, and, under cover of liberalism, the imposition of a new orthodoxy that reduces all transcendence to a single scheme. The reversal is clear: the philosopher without a Church defends myth against the theologian. Myth, for him, is not an error of physics to be corrected, as it is for Lucretius or d'Holbach; it is a cipher, and to demythologize it is to reduce it to silence. The second test is the book of 1962, *Der philosophische Glaube angesichts der Offenbarung* (*Philosophical Faith in the Face of Revelation*). In it Jaspers rejects a revelation's claim to be exclusive, that is, to make a historical event, the Incarnation, the single truth binding on all. He comes to read the Trinity itself as a set of ciphers of human possibilities, and Christ as the cipher of the human possibility of inner turning; the Stanford Encyclopedia notes that this reading echoes Feuerbach's anthropological analysis. Karl Barth denounced in Jaspers a transcendence without any objective content. Barth was right about the fact and wrong in the judgement: the absence of objective content is precisely what Jaspers lays claim to.

The third item in the file, a historical one, gives Jaspers his place in an essay that seeks to move beyond Christianity alone. In *Vom Ursprung und Ziel der Geschichte* (*The Origin and Goal of History*, 1949), Jaspers proposes the notion of the axial period, *Achsenzeit*. Between roughly 800 and 200 before our era, and above all around 500 BCE, comparable spiritual events occur independently of one another in China, India, Iran, Palestine and Greece: Confucius and Laozi, the Upanishads and the Buddha, Zarathustra, the prophets of Israel, the Greek philosophers. Everywhere human beings become aware of being as a whole, of themselves and of their limits, and the categories with which we still think are born. The thesis runs counter to a Christian conception, which Hegel had taken up, according to which the appearance of Christ is the axis of universal history. For Jaspers, the axis is not a particular revelation, but a common breakthrough of humanity towards reflection and transcendence. If spirituality has a birthplace, it is neither Sinai nor Golgotha, but this constellation of five centres, none of which holds a monopoly. Philosophical faith is the modern form of this breakthrough, freed from all the orthodoxies that emerged from it.

It remains to let the adversaries speak. The sharpest is Camus, and the response is attested. In *The Myth of Sisyphus* (1942), Jaspers is cited from the first chapter, as one of those who recognized “l'impossibilité de constituer le monde en unité”, the impossibility of constituting the world as a unity, and Camus immediately adds: “combien pressés d'en sortir !”, how eager to get out of it! The chapter “Le suicide philosophique” (“Philosophical suicide”) makes him the textbook case: “Jaspers va nous fournir, poussé jusqu'à la caricature, un exemple type de cette attitude”, Jaspers will provide us, pushed to the point of caricature, with a typical example of this attitude. Camus then quotes a sentence of Jaspers: “L'échec ne montre-t-il pas, au-delà de toute explication et de toute interprétation possible, non le néant mais l'être de la transcendance”, does not failure reveal, beyond every possible explanation and interpretation, not nothingness but the being of transcendence? And he concludes: “Ainsi l'absurde devient dieu (dans le sens le plus large de ce mot) et cette impuissance à comprendre, l'être qui illumine tout. Rien n'amène en logique ce raisonnement. Je puis l'appeler un saut”, thus the absurd becomes god (in the broadest sense of the word) and this inability to understand becomes the being that illuminates everything. Nothing logically leads to this reasoning. I can call it a leap. Camus calls Jaspers “cet apôtre de la pensée humiliée”, this apostle of humiliated thought.

The objection hits home. Jaspers starts from the failure of reason, from *Scheitern*, and draws from it the being of transcendence; between the two there is no inference, only a trust. Camus, who refuses the leap, asks that one hold to the failure. But the objection leaves something intact. Jaspers's leap ends in no Church, no dogma, no commandment; the transcendence it reaches has no objective content, as Barth objected. Kierkegaard's leap ended in Christ, and in the obedience of Abraham; Jaspers's ends in a cipher, which it is forbidden to take for knowledge. Camus's objection therefore holds in logic, not with regard to the criterion: a leap that ends in no obedience refounds nothing.

With Heidegger, the second adversary, the debate is first of all biographical. The two men were friends in the 1920s, and they were long classed together under the label of the philosophy of existence, which both of them rejected. Heidegger had written, already in the years of their friendship, a critical review of the *Psychologie der Weltanschauungen*, in which he reproached Jaspers for remaining caught in the metaphysics of subjectivity; the break came with the commitment of 1933, which Jaspers, married to a Jewish woman, experienced as a personal threat; and, after the war, consulted by the Freiburg denazification commission, Jaspers recommended that Heidegger be suspended from teaching. On the substance, Heidegger awaits a god without saying which; Jaspers believes in a transcendence without saying which. The structure is similar, and the objection I addressed to Heidegger, that of an empty absolute available to whoever wishes to occupy it, could be turned against Jaspers. A single word protects him from it: communication. Heideggerian waiting is solitary, reserved for the thinker and the poet; Jaspersian faith is subject to the discussion of all with all, and it denies itself as soon as it claims to impose itself. That is why Jaspers, as early as 1946, published *Die Schuldfrage* (*The Question of German Guilt*) and addressed his compatriots publicly on the responsibility of each.

In the Groningen lectures published under the title *Vernunft und Existenz* (*Reason and Existence*, 1935), Jaspers placed Kierkegaard and Nietzsche at the threshold of contemporary philosophy, as two exceptions who shattered systematic reason and of whom no one can be the disciple. He wrote a *Nietzsche* (1936). The one is the believer, the other the impious one; Jaspers holds them together because both lived a limit situation through to the end. His own position is to remain between them, without a leap towards Christ and without proclaiming the death of God.

With regard to the criterion, Jaspers does not refound: his transcendence demands no sacrifice, no obedience, no belonging, and it forbids anyone to put it at the service of a historical cause. But neither does he leave, nor does he claim to. He deliberately keeps transcendence, as Spinoza kept the name of God, and so belongs to the family of exceptions who keep something of the religious knowingly; and he brings to it what Spinoza lacked, a positive recognition of the plurality of ciphers, Chinese, Indian, Jewish, Greek, Christian, which shifts the question of religion towards that of human spirituality. My reservation is Camus's, displaced: Jaspers's danger is not the leap, it is inflation. A faith that welcomes every cipher and holds on to none risks no longer saying anything, and the infinite tolerance of the Encompassing can become an elegant way of never deciding. Jaspers answered in advance through his practice: he decided, in 1933, in 1945, in 1946, each time history demanded it, and his philosophical faith was never confused with indifference.

> **En littérature.** William Shakespeare, *King Lear* (1606) ; Friedrich Hölderlin, “Hälfte des Lebens” (1804)
>
> Lear, stripped by his daughters, goes out into the storm with his fool and discovers, in the rain, what a man without a kingdom is; Gloucester, his eyes torn out, concludes: “As flies to wanton boys are we to the gods, / They kill us for their sport”; and when Cordelia dies, the old king enters with her body in his arms: “Thou'lt come no more, / Never, never, never, never, never! / Pray you undo this button. Thank you, sir. / Do you see this? Look on her: look, her lips, / Look there, look there!” Why here: Jaspers wrote on the tragic in 1947, and the play is his chapter on failure. The limit situation, death, suffering, guilt, is traversed in it to the end, and what shows itself is not an answer but a cipher: Lear does not know whether Cordelia is breathing, and Shakespeare does not say. Jaspers's transcendence is that lip one looks at; Barth's objection, a transcendence without content, is the same scene seen by a man who would like to be told.
>
> Hölderlin, in the poem of 1804 that shortly precedes his madness, sets an image of summer, the swans “trunken von Küssen” dipping their heads “ins heilignüchterne Wasser”, drunk with kisses, into the holy-sober water, against the question of winter: “Weh mir, wo nehm ich, wenn / Es Winter ist, die Blumen, und wo / Den Sonnenschein, / Und Schatten der Erde? / Die Mauern stehn / Sprachlos und kalt, im Winde / Klirren die Fahnen”, alas, where shall I find, when it is winter, the flowers, and where the sunshine and the shade of the earth? The walls stand speechless and cold; in the wind the weathervanes clatter. The poem does not answer; it sets fullness and the wall side by side, and that is exactly what Jaspers calls a cipher: a writing of transcendence that does not let itself be read, and whose reading is failure itself. The clattering weathervanes are the last thing the half of life says.
>
> Sources: William Shakespeare, *King Lear*, III, 2, IV, 1 and V, 3 (c. 1606) ; Friedrich Hölderlin, “Hälfte des Lebens”, *Nachtgesänge* (1804).
### Why is there something rather than nothing? A constructed debate

We must carry the widening of religion into spirituality to its end, and ask the question that precedes all religions and outlives them all: why is there something? It belongs to no Church. A child can ask it, and so can a physicist, and most of those who say today that they “believe in something” without believing in God mean, by that vague word, the emotion it arouses. It therefore allows us to test the criterion: is the question of being the door to a spirituality without God, or the back door through which theology returns? The debate is constructed; I indicate which of its exchanges are attested.

The starting point is Greek, and it is not yet the question. It is wonder. Socrates tells the young Theaetetus: “μάλα γὰρ φιλοσόφου τοῦτο τὸ πάθος, τὸ θαυμάζειν· οὐ γὰρ ἄλλη ἀρχὴ φιλοσοφίας ἢ αὕτη”, this affection is very much a philosopher's, to wonder; for there is no other beginning of philosophy than this (*Theaetetus*, 155d). Aristotle takes up the word at the beginning of the *Metaphysics*: “διὰ γὰρ τὸ θαυμάζειν οἱ ἄνθρωποι καὶ νῦν καὶ τὸ πρῶτον ἤρξαντο φιλοσοφεῖν”, it is through wonder that men, now as at the beginning, began to philosophize (A 2, 982b12-13). And he adds a remark precious for our purpose: “διὸ καὶ ὁ φιλόμυθος φιλόσοφός πώς ἐστιν· ὁ γὰρ μῦθος σύγκειται ἐκ θαυμασίων”, this is why the lover of myths is also in some way a philosopher, for myth is made of wondrous things (982b18-19). Wonder is the common root of myth and of philosophy, and therefore of religion and of its critique. But Greek wonder bears on phenomena, the phases of the moon, the generation of the whole; it does not ask why there is a whole rather than nothing. The Greeks had no idea of an absolute nothingness from which being would have been drawn; it took creation *ex nihilo* for the question to take its modern form. A first clue: the question that seems the most secular of all was born in a biblical world.

The modern form, perfectly sharp, is Leibniz's. In the *Principles of Nature and Grace, Based on Reason*, written in 1714, Leibniz first lays down the principle of sufficient reason, then, in § 7, quoted in Part Three, the first question we have the right to ask: why is there something rather than nothing, since nothing is simpler and easier than something? The answer follows: the sufficient reason of the universe cannot be found in the series of contingent things, where each state refers back to the previous one without end; it must lie outside that series, in a necessary substance, “portant la raison de son existence avec soi”, bearing the reason of its existence within itself, and “cette dernière raison des choses est appelée Dieu”, this ultimate reason of things is called God (§ 8). Three things should be noted. The question is not a wonder but a demand: “on a droit”, we have the right, to ask it, because reason requires it. It assumes that nothingness is the default state, “plus simple et plus facile”, simpler and easier, and that being calls for an explanation. And its answer does not stop at an abstract first principle: three paragraphs further on, this God has chosen the best of all possible worlds (§ 10), and, in § 18, read in Part Three, he is the object of a love that gives a foretaste of future felicity. In Leibniz, the question of being leads without a break to a piety: this is the back door.

The sceptical answer comes from Hume, and it is attested in its form, if not in its addressee. In Part IX of the *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion* (published in 1779), Demea defends the argument he calls “the common one”, which asks what determined the existence of this series of causes rather than any other: “What was it, then, which determined Something to exist rather than Nothing, and bestowed being on a particular possibility, exclusive of the rest?” This is Clarke's argument, which has the same structure as Leibniz's; Hume names Clarke in a note a few lines further on, he does not name Leibniz. Cleanthes answers him with two blows. The first bears on necessity: “Whatever we conceive as existent, we can also conceive as non-existent. There is no being, therefore, whose non-existence implies a contradiction.” The second bears on the whole: each part of the series has its cause in the preceding one, and to demand in addition a cause of the whole is to forget that the unity of this whole “is performed merely by an arbitrary act of the mind, and has no influence on the nature of things”. Hume does not say that the question is absurd, but that it does not lead where Leibniz wanted to go. The whole needs no reason outside itself, because “the whole” is only a manner of speaking.

Kant takes up the difficulty from within and gives it the tone no longer of demand but of vertigo. In the *Critique of Pure Reason*, as he refutes the cosmological proof, he writes: “Die unbedingte Nothwendigkeit, die wir als den letzten Träger aller Dinge so unentbehrlich bedürfen, ist der wahre Abgrund für die menschliche Vernunft”, unconditioned necessity, which we so indispensably need as the ultimate bearer of all things, is the true abyss for human reason. And he imagines the supreme being speaking to itself: “Ich bin von Ewigkeit zu Ewigkeit, außer mir ist nichts ohne das, was bloß durch meinen Willen etwas ist; aber woher bin ich denn?”, I am from eternity to eternity, outside me there is nothing except what is something merely through my will; but whence then am I? “Hier sinkt alles unter uns”, here everything gives way beneath us. By putting the question to God himself, Kant shows that Leibniz's answer merely pushes it back, and he adds that we can neither dismiss this thought nor bear it. With Kant, the question of being becomes an affect, an experience of the abyss, and no longer a problem.

Schelling, half a century later, drives it to despair, and the question then changes its source. In the lectures of the *Philosophie der Offenbarung* (*Philosophy of Revelation*, delivered in Munich from 1831-1832, then in Berlin from 1841, published in 1858 by his son), it is not the spectacle of the universe that prompts it, it is man. Everything moves restlessly without aim, he writes, and, “wie ein altes Buch sagt”, as an old book says, everything under the sun is full of toil and labour: this is Qoheleth. Man, far from making the world intelligible, is “selbst das Unbegreiflichste”, himself the most incomprehensible thing of all. And Schelling concludes: “Gerade Er, der Mensch, treibt mich zur letzten verzweiflungsvollen Frage: warum ist überhaupt etwas? warum ist nicht nichts?”, it is precisely he, man, who drives me to the last, the despairing question: why is there anything at all? why is there not nothing? The passage goes on to say so: that there should exist a science which answers these questions and tears us from this despair is a need of human nature itself. This science, for Schelling, is a positive philosophy that culminates in a philosophy of revelation, that is, in Christianity thought through. The despairing question opens, as in Leibniz, onto a theology; but it opens onto it through anguish and not through sufficient reason.

Bergson, in 1907, declares the question a false problem. Chapter IV of *Creative Evolution* begins by describing from within the very movement of Leibniz and Schelling: “L'existence m'apparaît comme une conquête sur le néant. Je me dis qu'il pourrait, qu'il devrait même ne rien y avoir, et je m'étonne alors qu'il y ait quelque chose.”, existence appears to me as a conquest over nothingness; I tell myself that there could, that there even should, be nothing, and I am then astonished that there is something. He adds: “je ne puis me défaire de l'idée que le plein est une broderie sur le canevas du vide, que l'être est superposé au néant, et que dans la représentation de ‘rien’ il y a moins que dans celle de ‘quelque chose’. De là tout le mystère.”, I cannot rid myself of the idea that the full is an embroidery on the canvas of the void, that being is superimposed on nothingness, and that there is less in the representation of “nothing” than in that of “something”; hence the whole mystery. This is Leibniz's premise, the nothing “plus simple et plus facile”, simpler and easier; Bergson does not name Leibniz in these two sentences, but he names him at the end of the following paragraph, together with Spinoza, as the culmination of this movement: the connection is therefore his own. To think the absence of one thing is always to represent the presence of another; to suppress is to substitute. The idea of an abolition of everything is therefore “une idée destructive d'elle-même, une pseudo-idée, un simple mot”, a self-destroying idea, a pseudo-idea, a mere word, as absurd “que celle d'un cercle carré”, as that of a square circle. And the conclusion falls: the question of knowing “pourquoi quelque chose existe”, why something exists, is “une question dépourvue de sens, un pseudo-problème soulevé autour d'une pseudo-idée”, a question devoid of meaning, a pseudo-problem raised around a pseudo-idea. Once nothingness is dispelled, one can posit an absolute that acts freely and endures, the one Bergson would find again, twenty-five years later, in the mystics of the *Two Sources*. He dissolved the question, but he did not dissolve wonder: he moved it from existence to creation.

In Heidegger, the reply is attested twice. In 1929, the Freiburg inaugural lecture, *Was ist Metaphysik?*, ends on the question; in 1935, the lecture course published in 1953 under the title *Einführung in die Metaphysik* (*Introduction to Metaphysics*) opens with it, and Heidegger declares it the first of all questions, the broadest, the deepest, the most originary. Above all, in 1949, in the introduction added to the fifth edition of *Was ist Metaphysik?*, he answers Leibniz explicitly: he acknowledges that the final question of his lecture, “Warum ist überhaupt Seiendes und nicht vielmehr Nichts?”, why are there beings at all and not rather nothing?, is “offenbar die Frage, die der Metaphysiker Leibniz in seinen Principes de la nature et de la grace gestellt hat”, evidently the question that the metaphysician Leibniz asked in his *Principles*, and he wonders why, if that is so, Leibniz's name was not mentioned. The question is asked there, he replies, “in einem ganz anderen Sinne”, in an entirely different sense. It does not ask for the first cause of beings; it asks how it comes about that beings everywhere take precedence, while nothingness, understood as being itself, remains forgotten. And Heidegger turns Leibniz's own premise against him: if being were not forgotten, Leibniz could not have written, by way of explanation, “Car le rien est plus simple et plus facile que quelque chose”, for nothing is simpler and easier than something. Leibniz's question is the question of metaphysics; the same question, asked otherwise, would be the exit from metaphysics.

One might side with Heidegger: he wrested the question from Leibnizian theology and gave it back to wonder. But one must read the postscript to the same small volume, written in 1943. The thinking of being, Heidegger says there, is a thanking, *Danken*, for the favour by which being has given itself to man, and this thanking is accomplished in sacrifice: “Das Opfer ist der Abschied vom Seienden auf dem Gang zur Wahrung der Gunst des Seins”, sacrifice is the farewell to beings on the way to safeguarding the favour of being.
