Mahfouz, finally, wrote in 1959 the novel that Cairo banned: in *Children of the Alley*, the inhabitants of a quarter descend from an invisible ancestor, Gabalawi, whose successive sons, Adham, Gabal, Rifaa, Qasim, are the prophets; the last, Arafa, the magician, science, enters the great house, and Gabalawi dies of his intrusion. The death of God in an Arabic novel, and the reason why the essay judges the exit “first of all Christian, not only Christian”.
>
> Sources: Omar Khayyam, *Rubáiyát*, trans. Edward FitzGerald, fifth edition (1889; first edition 1859), XII, LXXI, XCIX ; Abu l-ʿAla al-Maʿarri, *Luzûm mâ lâ yalzam* (11th century) ; Naguib Mahfouz, *Awlâd hâratinâ* (*Children of the Alley*, 1959).

### Contemporary militant atheists: Onfray and the “new atheists”

A last atheism occupied public debate at the beginning of the twenty-first century without belonging to the same category as the preceding authors. Neither Michel Onfray (b. 1959) in France nor the “new atheists” of the English-speaking world are the peers of Spinoza or Nietzsche. But they form a useful test case: they show what becomes of the critique of religion when it ignores this whole path. Their books are under copyright; I quote from them only what is published by the publisher or by the author, and I indicate what is known only through third parties.

The *Traité d'athéologie. Physique de la métaphysique* (Grasset, 2005) belongs to the first regime, that of error, in the version of the militant Enlightenment. The back cover, signed by the author, sums up the thesis: “Les trois monothéismes, animés par une même pulsion de mort généalogique, partagent une série de mépris identiques : haine de la raison et de l'intelligence ; haine de la liberté ; haine de tous les livres au nom d'un seul ; haine de la vie ; haine de la sexualité, des femmes et du plaisir ; haine du féminin ; haine des corps, des désirs, des pulsions.”, the three monotheisms, driven by one and the same genealogical death drive, share a series of identical contempts: hatred of reason and intelligence; hatred of freedom; hatred of all books in the name of one alone; hatred of life; hatred of sexuality, of women and of pleasure; hatred of the feminine; hatred of bodies, of desires, of drives. Religion here is neither a misunderstood human truth, as in Feuerbach, nor a symptom, as in Marx, but a harmful lie. According to quotations reported by third parties, Onfray writes there that he despairs that believers “préfèrent les fictions apaisantes des enfants aux certitudes cruelles des adultes”, prefer the soothing fictions of children to the cruel certainties of adults (p. 27). Engels's objection, formulated in 1882, struck him in advance: one does not get rid of a religion that subdued the Roman Empire by declaring it a tissue of absurdities forged by impostors; explanation by hatred of life is hardly any better. A historian of antiquity, Jaime Alvar, entitled his review “Un tratado fracasado: la ateología como discurso del ateísmo cristiano”, a failed treatise: atheology as the discourse of Christian atheism. The word atheology Onfray takes from Bataille, reversing its meaning: where the *Somme athéologique* sought an experience of the sacred without God, the *Traité* critiques religion through knowledge, which is what Bataille fought against. The mythicist thesis, which the *Traité* sketches and *Théorie de Jésus* (2023) radicalizes, is examined in Part Two.

With *Décadence. Vie et mort du judéo-christianisme* (Flammarion, 2017), the regime changes. The book traces the history of Judeo-Christian civilization as that of an organism, birth, vigour, exhaustion, and its central thesis is that “c'est la religion qui produit une civilisation”, it is religion that produces a civilization (p. 575). Religion is no longer an error, but a power, and Onfray claims the neutrality of the diagnosis: “Mon propos n'est ni optimiste ni pessimiste, ni conservateur ni réactionnaire”, my purpose is neither optimistic nor pessimistic, neither conservative nor reactionary. Then the position shifts. In 2020, the magazine he founded, *Front populaire*, placed itself on the ground of the “défense de la civilisation judéo-chrétienne”, the defence of Judeo-Christian civilization. On 18 July 2021, he wrote in *Le Figaro*: “Je suis athée, on le sait, mais la vie de l'Église catholique m'intéresse parce qu'elle donne le pouls de notre civilisation judéo-chrétienne bien mal en point. Car si Dieu n'est pas de mon monde, mon monde est celui qu'a rendu possible le Dieu des chrétiens.”, I am an atheist, as is well known, but the life of the Catholic Church interests me because it takes the pulse of our Judeo-Christian civilization, which is in a very poor state. For if God is not of my world, my world is the one that the God of the Christians made possible.

The diagnosis of *Décadence* makes Onfray an inverted Marx. Marx wanted to abolish the need for opium by abolishing the misery that made it necessary; he thought religion would disappear of its own accord when the world no longer needed that sigh. *Décadence* observes that the weaning has taken place, that the West no longer believes, and this observation, far from being an emancipation, is called decline. Marx's prognosis is verified, his evaluation reversed: the end of religion is no longer the liberation of men, it is the death of a civilization. Gauchet's reading, which describes the same event as a fulfilment, seems to me more accurate; but Onfray has the merit of making visible what the madman of § 125 announced to the atheists of the marketplace: the death of God is not good news to be celebrated, it is an event whose weight we have not finished measuring.

This is usually seen as a contradiction. I see in it rather the passage from one regime to the other without the first ever being refuted. Religion remains false, and it is necessary. Now this conjunction has a name in our corpus: it is the position of the Grand Inquisitor, for whom faith is a lie men cannot do without. Onfray does not govern a Church, but he defends the Latin Mass without believing in God, in the name of what it holds together: in the same column, against the motu proprio *Traditionis custodes*, he makes it a “patrimoine liturgique”, a liturgical heritage. The irony is complete if one recalls the reproach he is said to have addressed to Comte-Sponville in 2005: he has in turn become a Christian atheist, but differently. Comte-Sponville keeps from Christianity an inner fidelity, a spirituality without a Church; Onfray keeps from it an outer civilization, a Church without spirituality. By the criterion, the first refounds nothing, since he demands no sacrifice; the second, by making the defence of a civilization the ground of his combat, refounds a collective absolute. It is a contemporary case of Stirner's law, not its culmination.

The new atheists of the English-speaking world offer its other side. Richard Dawkins (b. 1941), a biologist, published *The God Delusion* in 2006; Sam Harris (b. 1967), *The End of Faith* in 2004; Daniel Dennett (1942-2024), *Breaking the Spell* in 2006; Christopher Hitchens (1949-2011), *God Is Not Great* in 2007. I do not quote them; their common position is simple. Religion is a hypothesis about the world, the God hypothesis, false or indemonstrable, and harmful, since it justifies violence, hinders science and oppresses consciences. It must therefore be fought with reason and with science.

This current does not deserve the contempt sometimes shown it in Europe: it had the courage to say in public what many thought in private, in societies where unbelief remained suspect. Dennett, in particular, proposed an explanation of religion grounded in evolutionary biology, a serious research hypothesis. But for our question they bring nothing new: they return to the regime of error, in its poorest form, the one Spinoza had already gone beyond in 1670 by asking not whether superstition was false, but why men clung to it. They ignore Feuerbach, who had shown that religion speaks a human truth; Marx, who had shown that it is a symptom; Nietzsche, who had shown that science itself rests on a faith; Durkheim, who had shown that the sacred is social; Taylor, who would soon show that unbelief is not a subtraction. They refute the God hypothesis like a physical theory, which neither Feuerbach nor Nietzsche had judged sufficient, and they fall back, without knowing it, under the objection Stirner addressed to the atheists of 1844: they fight religion in the name of Reason and Science, essences to which the individual must submit, and their crusading tone has something pious about it. This comparison is constructed.

Onfray and the new atheists thus fail in two symmetrical ways. The latter remain in error; the former has left it by the high road, towards a civilization to be defended. The new atheists are the men of the marketplace of § 125, who did not believe in God and laughed at the madman: they are right about the existence of God, and have not understood what his death means. Onfray has understood it, and concluded that the Church must be kept without God.

> **En littérature.** Thomas Mann, *Der Zauberberg* (1924) ; Anatole France, *La Révolte des anges* (1914)
>
> Settembrini, the Italian humanist of *The Magic Mountain*, a Freemason, a Carbonaro through his grandfather, Hans Castorp's pedagogue, preaches against illness, death, the Church and Naphta; Mann sums up his faith: “er sprach vom „Worte“, vom Kultus des Wortes, der Eloquenz, die er den Triumph der Menschlichkeit nannte. Denn das Wort sei die Ehre des Menschen, und nur dieses mache das Leben menschenwürdig”, he spoke of the Word, of the cult of the Word, of eloquence, which he called the triumph of humanity; for the word is the honour of man, and it alone makes life worthy of human beings.
>
> Why here: Settembrini is the new atheist a hundred years ahead of time, and Mann loved him while portraying him. His cult of the Word, of Reason and of Progress has every mark of a cult, down to the encyclopedia of human sufferings he is compiling for an international league; and Naphta has no trouble showing him that his religion of Humanity is a religion. It is the objection of Stirner that the essay addresses to the atheists of the marketplace, put into the mouth of a Jesuit; and the final duel, in which Settembrini fires into the air and Naphta kills himself, says that militant reason has no answer to terror, except not to shoot.
>
> Anatole France, in *The Revolt of the Angels*, brings down to Paris guardian angels who, from reading the libraries of their charges, have lost their faith; they prepare a revolt against Ialdabaoth, the demiurge whom men call God, and go to offer the command to Satan, who refuses: victorious, he says in substance, he would become God, and the revolt would serve only to change masters. The fable is Stirner's law, “our atheists are pious people”, told by the most Voltairean of novelists: the science that overthrows God refounds a throne, and the only consistent atheist in the book is the one who refuses to take it.
>
> Sources: Thomas Mann, *Der Zauberberg*, IV (1924) ; Anatole France, *La Révolte des anges*, ch. XXXV (1914).

### Towards the conclusion

The landscape has become clearer: there are those who refound deliberately, those who refound without meaning to and whom their successor unmasks, those who refute without understanding, and a few figures who seem to escape the trap because they knowingly keep something of what they criticize, without demanding of anyone that he sacrifice himself to it. It remains to be seen whether these exceptions form a position or only a family of attitudes, and whether they answer the question Marx's *Protestation* left open: what becomes of the complaint of the oppressed creature when it no longer has a heaven to address? That is for the conclusion to say.
## Conclusion: who leaves, and for what?

### Assessment of the refoundations

Can one leave religion without founding another? At the end of this journey, from Plato to our contemporaries, the series answers first in the negative, and with a regularity that ends up resembling a law. Refoundation does not even wait for the exit to take place. Plato, who was leaving nothing, had already shown what a religion founded by reason costs: a demonstrated theology, then a law, then prison for the impious and death for the repeat offender. Rousseau, in leaving the Church, refounds a civil religion and gives it back the death penalty. D'Holbach, who believed he was opposing nothing but physics to religion, ends the *Système de la nature* with a prayer to Nature. Leibniz justifies the evil of the part by the beauty of the whole, and asks the individual to sacrifice his complaint. Feuerbach leaves God by deifying Man, and Comte, who draws all the consequences of this gesture, organizes the cult of the Great Being with its sacraments and its calendar. Stirner leaves Man by absolutizing the Self. Marx leaves religion by promising an emancipation that has its form, and Löwith had only to trace Christian eschatology onto the philosophy of history to show it. Durkheim leaves the Churches by discovering that Society is the god of all gods, which is a way of sacralizing what one thought one was explaining. Freud leaves illusion by entrusting our future to “unser Gott Λόγος”, and he names this new god himself. Heidegger leaves the god of the philosophers by waiting for a god who saves. The twentieth century, finally, gave the law its most massive cases: the secular religions that Voegelin and Aron named, the deified People of 1938, the social order to come in whose name present generations were sacrificed, had their police, their camps and their trials. Closer to us, and in an altogether different register, Ferry leaves vertical transcendence by calling sacred whatever in the human surpasses us, and Onfray leaves faith by sacralizing the civilization that faith produced. Each time the dismissed absolute returns under another name, and each time the next critic denounces it. “Unsere Atheisten sind fromme Leute”: Stirner formulated the law of the whole series, and he did not escape it himself.

This law is not an accident in the history of ideas, and the inquiry into the causes of belief has shown why. What anthropologists, psychologists and sociologists have described is not a need for God, but a broader and more tenacious disposition: a need for meaning, for bonds and for protection, universal in its springs, variable in its intensity. This need survives God, as Feuerbach had seen, and it seeks other objects. Explaining why people believe, through fear, desire, society or the structure of the mind, therefore does not tell us whether one can stop believing without believing in something else; the explanation makes the question sharper, since the disposition that produces gods is also the one that produces refoundations. Becker and Girard, by two different paths, have even shown that sacrifice is not a late perversion of certain religions, but a spring of belief itself: one sacrifices to deny death, one sacrifices to appease violence. Refoundations are the natural slope of the exit, and the exits that do not refound are costly exceptions, which have to be willed, built and maintained. Norris and Inglehart add a condition that philosophers readily forget: these exceptions are possible, on the scale of a society, only where existence is secure enough for fear to stop looking for a victim.

We must, however, take seriously the three objections that threaten the thesis itself, and not this or that author. The first, already announced in the prologue, is Durkheim's. If every society lives on something sacred, if “le dieu n'est que l'expression figurée de la société”, the god is merely the figurative expression of society, then the question is idle: one never leaves religion, one only changes the sacred, and the series I have just drawn up is not a sequence of failures but the description of a necessity. The second, the other objection announced in the prologue, is Blumenberg's. If what modernity inherits from Christianity is not a content but a place, if the questions left open by theology have merely been “reoccupied” by heterogeneous answers, then speaking of “refoundation” is an abuse: Marx does not found a religion because he answers the question of the meaning of history, but because the question was posed once and for all and one can no longer fail to answer it. Durkheim says the thesis is too weak, because refoundation is inevitable; Blumenberg that it is too strong, because it sees gods wherever there are only places. The third objection is more disturbing, for it bears on the criterion itself. If Girard is right, the sacred is born of sacrifice: a community in crisis recovers its unity by discharging its violence onto a victim, then deifies that victim. The criterion of this essay would then not be one criterion among others, it would name the very origin of the religious; and Girard draws from it a consequence the modern critics had not foreseen, since the Gospels, by taking the side of the innocent victim, would have unveiled the mechanism, so that the exit from sacrifice would be the work of Christianity itself.

I believe that the first two objections neutralize each other, and that the third forces us to deepen the criterion rather than abandon it. Blumenberg is right against the lazy version of the secularization thesis, the one that sees a salvation in every promise and a Church in every institution: such a thesis is unfalsifiable, and it makes it possible to discredit any modern thought by finding it a theological ancestor. This is, moreover, the reproach Kelsen addressed to Voegelin's notion of political religion, when it becomes a genealogy of the whole of modernity. But Durkheim is right against the optimistic version of the exit, the one that believes a society can live without holding anything untouchable. Between the two, the notion of secular religion, understood in Aron's functional sense rather than in Voegelin's genealogical sense, provides the distinction Blumenberg lacked: not all reoccupations are equal. There are those that answer an inherited question with a modest hypothesis, and those that answer it with an absolute that demands. The criterion set out in the prologue, and refined in connection with Feuerbach, thus comes through Blumenberg's test, and I can formulate it one last time: one refounds a religion, in the sense that matters here, not when one occupies a place that theology left empty, but when one installs in that place **an absolute in whose name the sacrifice of the individual can be demanded**, and whose critique becomes a sacrilege; freely consented self-offering does not fall under it. This last point settles cases the journey had left undecided: Justin dying for having refused a cult, Clifford's scientist who renounces a consoling belief, Ferry's man ready to die for freedom refound nothing by their devotion alone; what refounds is the authority that demands this devotion of others. The criterion also has two degrees. Refoundation in the strict sense installs an absolute that demands: Plato's law, Rousseau's civil religion, Comte's Great Being, which requires the individual to efface himself (the disciple of the *Catéchisme* says so herself), the secular religions of the twentieth century with the History of the revolutionaries whom Camus accuses, which demanded victims, and Schmitt's political theology. Soft refoundation confines itself to consecrating without demanding: Feuerbach sacralizes the relation, Ferry calls sacred that for which some men agree to die; they immolate no one, but they feel the need to consecrate that Engels named, and it is through this need that consecration can become demand in their successors. Onfray's Civilization has already taken the step: it demands that one defend a liturgy in which one does not believe. By contrast, the question of the meaning of history that Blumenberg raises, or the social sacred that Durkheim describes, refound nothing as long as they demand no sacrifice and tolerate their own critique. As for Girard, I keep his anthropology and leave his apologetics: Christian history has known the stake, and Dostoevsky could imagine Christ condemned a second time by his Church. The lesson I draw from it is that no exit can avoid refounding if it does not refuse the scapegoat, and that this refusal needs no god in order to be demanded, even if it needed a religious history in order to be discovered. This refusal is the criterion seen from the other side: it is the condition of any exit without refoundation, not yet its form. The criterion has, finally, the advantage of not depending on the presence or absence of God. It allows us to say that some believers have left religion, in the sense in which Barth, Bonhoeffer and Weil denounce it, and that some atheists have remained in it.

The dispute over the right to believe gives this criterion its translation into the order of knowledge, and it has the advantage of addressing unbelievers as much as believers. Clifford held that it is always wrong to believe on insufficient evidence; James replied that one has the right to believe, at one's own risk, when the option is living, forced and momentous and reason cannot decide. I believe both must be kept. One has the right to believe where reason leaves the question open: that is James. This right ends where belief engages the lives of others without their having chosen it: that is Clifford, and it is the lesson of his shipowner. A belief that asks its believer only to risk his own life is a faith, or a wisdom; a belief that asks others to risk theirs, or that sacrifices them when they refuse it, is a refoundation. The rule holds against the Inquisitor, and it also holds against those who invoke Clifford to wage a crusade against the beliefs of others: Russell reproached believers for believing without reason, but what he chiefly believed was Lucretius, and the new atheists kept Clifford's maxim while forgetting his shipowner.

There remains the most serious adversary, not of this or that exit, but of the very idea of an exit. Leo Strauss grants the critics of religion everything one could wish, except the essential: neither philosophy nor revelation has refuted the other, and modern critique contented itself with mocking what it could not refute. If a total exit presupposed the completion of reason, then every exit that believes itself total is already a refoundation, and the only honest position left is one that acknowledges that the question is not settled. I do not believe Strauss is right to make the tension between Athens and Jerusalem an eternal return of the same: the history this essay has traversed shows that the question shifts, that it changes ground, and that faith itself has learned from its critics. But he is right on the essential point, and his lesson joins that of the whole series: leaving religion is not an accomplished event, it is a question that remains open, and those who believe it closed are the most exposed to giving themselves a god without knowing it. The inquiry into the birth of Christianity confirms this in another way. The religion the West seeks to leave was already an alloy: the God of the Greek philosophers had taken on the face of a crucified man in it, through Philo, through Justin, through Augustine, and it is this alloy that Pascal, Feuerbach, Nietzsche and Heidegger tried to undo, each from one end. The mythicist thesis, which thinks it settles everything by denying the existence of Jesus, misses precisely this object: it goes back to the regime of error, whereas the question is that of the construction of a figure. And the question raised from within Islam, by Arkoun and by Bidar, recalls that the exit from religion, Christian first, is not only Christian, that no tradition leaves religion by the same path, and that the Christian exit described by Weber and Gauchet is not the measure of the others.

> **En littérature.** Franz Kafka, “In der Strafkolonie” (1919) ; Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, *Vol de nuit* (1931)
>
> In the penal colony, an officer shows a traveller around the machine of the old commandant, which for twelve hours inscribes with needles on the body of the condemned man the law he has broken, “Ehre deinen Vorgesetzten!”, honour your superiors; the officer sets out his principle: “Der Grundsatz, nach dem ich entscheide, ist: Die Schuld ist immer zweifellos”, the principle by which I judge is: guilt is always beyond doubt. When the traveller refuses to support the machine before the new commandant, the officer frees the condemned man, sets the apparatus to “Sei gerecht!”, be just, and lies down in it himself; the machine breaks down and pierces him through without granting him the promised transfiguration.
>
> Why here: the story is the assessment of this section in twenty pages. The old commandant is dead, his grave lies under a café table, and his law goes on demanding bodies; the officer is its priest, who ends up immolating himself to the absolute he serves, without the absolute giving him anything back. It is strict refoundation seen from inside its clergy: an authority that demands sacrifice, whose critique is a sacrilege, and which outlives the faith of those who administer it. The broken machine is Onfray's Civilization, Comte's Great Being and Rubashov's Party, after the believers have gone.
>
> Saint-Exupéry wrote the admiring version. Rivière, director of the airmail lines of Buenos Aires in *Vol de nuit*, demands that the pilots fly at night, punishes delays, refuses excuses, and when Fabien is lost in a cyclone while his wife waits, he sends the Europe mail off on time, because the work is worth more than men. Gide, in his preface, admired this hardness; the essay reads in it the absolute that demands: not the self-offering of Fabien, who chose, but the authority that demands the offering of all, and that has an office.
>
> Sources: Franz Kafka, “In der Strafkolonie” (written in 1914, published in 1919) ; Antoine de Saint-Exupéry, *Vol de nuit* (1931).

### What the exceptions have in common

The exceptions are more numerous than one would have thought at the outset. Spinoza and Nietzsche, first; Simone Weil, who leaves consoling religion without leaving faith; Hadot, Camus, Wittgenstein, Murdoch; Jaspers and Ricoeur; and, on the borderline, Levinas. Hume, whom I place apart, refounds nothing either; Blumenberg and William James, finally, seem to be among them and are rather allies of the thesis. I do not believe they are all of the same rank, and a decision must be made.

What unites them first is a **genealogical lucidity**: they know what they owe to what they criticize. Spinoza keeps the name of God, and he does not keep it out of prudence; Nietzsche admits that he borrows his fire “von dem Brande[…], den ein jahrtausendealter Glaube entzündet hat”; Hadot's “spiritual exercises” bear a Christian name, that of Ignatius of Loyola's *Exercises*, and Hadot turns the debt around: it was the Christians who inherited the philosophical exercises of Antiquity; Camus knows that his Ivan does not deny God but judges him, and that he “inaugure l'entreprise essentielle de la révolte qui est de substituer au royaume de la grâce celui de la justice”, inaugurates the essential undertaking of revolt, which is to substitute for the kingdom of grace the kingdom of justice. This lucidity is what the atheists of the marketplace lack, from the militant materialists to the new atheists, who believe that religion is an error to be got rid of like a superstition, and who for that reason do not see the shadows of God in their own faith in science. Western Buddhism, as we have seen, offers the counterproof.

What unites them next is the **absence of a sacrificial absolute**. None of them asks the individual to immolate himself to a higher authority. Spinoza's beatitude is not a reward purchased by sacrifice: “Beatitudo non est virtutis præmium, sed ipsa virtus”, beatitude is not the reward of virtue, but virtue itself. Nietzsche's amor fati is not obedience to fate but a consent that transforms the one who consents. Camus's measure is expressly directed against the deification of history: “Au midi de la pensée, le révolté refuse ainsi la divinité pour partager les luttes et le destin communs”, at the noon of thought, the rebel thus refuses divinity in order to share the common struggles and the common fate. The case of Murdoch is more instructive, because she unambiguously installs an absolute, the Good, sovereign and transcendent. But this absolute demands that no one be immolated to it; it demands that we stop immolating ourselves to our own fantasies: “We cease to be in order to attend to the existence of something else.” One does not govern men in the name of a sun that commands nothing. The criterion therefore does not condemn every absolute: it condemns the absolute that demands the sacrifice of others and has priests to speak in its name.

What unites them, finally, is a **practice** rather than a doctrine. What Spinoza, Nietzsche, Hadot, Camus or Murdoch propose is not a new belief, it is a way of transforming oneself: knowledge of the third kind, the incorporation of the heaviest thought, the exercise of the view from above, the revolt that never ceases to measure itself, patient attention to what is. This is what Foucault called spirituality, the practice by which the subject carries out on himself the transformations necessary to gain access to the truth, and it is, transposed outside Christianity, what Bergson called dynamic religion, as opposed to static religion (a constructed comparison: for Bergson, dynamic religion is Christian mysticism). Spirituality so understood is not a weakened religion, nor the refuge where religion survives its critique; it is what remains when religion has been stripped of its two functions of power, the guarantee of meaning and submission to the absolute.

But we must now distinguish, among these exceptions, a **position**, a **family of attitudes**, and a few neighbouring figures who belong to neither. The position articulates an ontology and a practice, and it has three versions. Spinoza and Hadot give the version of immanence: the Whole, and exercises that make it possible to relate to it without the mediation of Church or dogma; it is, moreover, towards Spinoza that contemporary secular spiritualities tend, more or less consciously, Comte-Sponville's first of all. Murdoch gives the version of transcendence without God: a real Good that judges the world instead of blessing it, and that one reaches through attention. Wittgenstein gives the silent version: where the others offer an ontology and exercises, he offers a limit and a wonder, he holds the place left empty by the death of God without filling it, and he refuses even the name. This is, I believe, the strictest of the three versions. Nietzsche and Camus form rather an attitude, more unstable, because it has no settled ontology: Nietzsche oscillates between the lucidity of FW 344 and the prophetic temptations of Zarathustra, and it is not certain that he always resisted the latter; Camus refuses the absolute in the name of measure, but he himself acknowledges that revolt must constantly watch over itself so as not to turn into what it fights. The reservation I made about his sacred Mediterranean stands, but it bears on an aesthetic myth, not on an absolute that demands: it makes his position more unstable, it does not place it among the refoundations.

The believing exceptions form a group apart, and they are decisive for the thesis, because they show that the criterion crosses the frontier between believers and unbelievers. Simone Weil is its most radical figure, making atheism a purification of faith. Jaspers and Ricoeur join her with less radicalism and more prudence: they are the witnesses of a faith that has passed through critique, who do not refound but listen. Levinas remains in suspense. He leaves the God of the philosophers through ethics and not through being, and his absolute is the singular face of the other man, which forbids him to sacrifice an individual to an abstraction; but his responsibility without reciprocity is an infinite demand, and I am not sure it entirely escapes the criterion, even if I lean towards counting him among the believing exceptions. Plotinus and Maimonides, finally, showed that the negation of every image can be carried out from within a tradition, demanding nothing but the asceticism of thought; but they remain, the one in a school, the other in the Law, and they are precursors rather than exceptions.

Three figures, to conclude, are exceptions of none of these families. Hume leaves without refounding, but through a suspension of judgement that he himself admitted was hard to maintain outside the study, and which proposes no way of living with the Whole: he is the sceptic of the series, not its sage. Blumenberg proposes no spirituality, but an intellectual hygiene, which consists in not confusing an inherited question with an imposed answer. William James, likewise, proposes not a wisdom but a right: that of believing at one's own risk, which no one has the right to impose on others, either in the form of faith or in that of unbelief. Blumenberg and James are allies of the thesis, the one in the order of history, the other in that of belief; they are not examples of it. Several authors, finally, do not refound and yet are not exceptions for all that. Clifford and Löwith propose no way of living with the Whole: the first offers only an ethics of belief, whose absolute demands sacrifice only of oneself, the second only a Stoic withdrawal that one may doubt is habitable. Montaigne, Barth, Bonhoeffer and Arkoun remain within a tradition: Montaigne as a practising Catholic who stops speaking of salvation, Barth and Bonhoeffer within revelation, in whose name they leave religion, Arkoun within an Islam he wants to reopen to its history. Bergson escapes the deification of man only narrowly, at the price of a metaphysics of life. Comte-Sponville refounds nothing, but his wisdom renounces protest, and I return to this below. Buddhism, for its part, is neither an exception nor an ally, but a test. It shows that religion is not defined by God, since a tradition without a creator God could have a Law, monks and sometimes states; and it confirms the criterion, since its doctrine demands no sacrifice and its institutions, in contact with power, have sometimes demanded it.

My answer to the question of this essay is therefore the following. One leaves religion without refounding one only if one renounces the idea of leaving it entirely, that is, if one agrees to keep, knowingly, something of what it carried. This something is neither a belief nor an institution, it is an orientation: the relation to a Whole that surpasses us and that we do not possess, or to a Good that we possess no more. The form that makes it possible to keep this orientation without turning it into a sacrificial absolute is a spirituality of exercise, of which Spinoza gave the most coherent ontology, Hadot the most exact historical description and Wittgenstein the strictest limit. Of this exit without refoundation, the refusal of the scapegoat is the condition, the spirituality of exercise the form, and wonder without debt the barest affect: to think being is not to owe it something. This spirituality presupposes a wisdom, which these spiritualities offer, and a security, which only institutions can guarantee. And it is never possessed once and for all, Strauss is right on this point: the claim to a total exit is itself the modern form of the absolute, and whoever believes he no longer has anything religious about him is the worst equipped to recognize the gods he gives himself.

> **En littérature.** Fernando Pessoa, *O Guardador de Rebanhos* (1914) ; Hermann Hesse, *Das Glasperlenspiel* (1943)
>
> Alberto Caeiro, the “master” Pessoa invented for himself among his heteronyms, is the poet of immanence without doctrine. The fifth poem of *The Keeper of Sheep* (*O Guardador de Rebanhos*) begins: “Há metafísica bastante em não pensar em nada. / O que penso eu do mundo? / Sei lá o que penso do mundo! / Se eu adoecesse pensaria nisso”, there is metaphysics enough in thinking of nothing; what do I think of the world? how should I know what I think of the world! if I fell ill I would think about it; and further on: “O mistério das cousas? Sei lá o que é mistério! / O único mistério é haver quem pense no mistério”, the mystery of things? how should I know what mystery is! the only mystery is that there are people who think about mystery.
>
> Why here: Caeiro is the position of immanence, that of Spinoza and Hadot, written by someone who refuses even to name it. He consecrates nothing, demands nothing, consoles for nothing; he looks, and the exercise lies in that look, “a luz do sol vale mais que os pensamentos / De todos os filósofos e de todos os poetas”, the light of the sun is worth more than the thoughts of all the philosophers and all the poets. The essay says that the exceptions have in common a practice rather than a doctrine; Caeiro is that practice without the doctrine, and that is why Pessoa, who was not Caeiro, needed to invent him: one cannot be Caeiro, one can only write him.
>
> Hesse, in *The Glass Bead Game*, imagines a pedagogical province, Castalia, where an elite cultivates a game that unites all the sciences and all the arts, in a discipline of meditation without Church and without dogma; Joseph Knecht, having become Magister Ludi, ends up leaving the order to become the tutor of a single child, and drowns in a mountain lake on the first morning of his new life. Castalia is the spirituality of exercise become an institution, with its hierarchy and its renunciation of the world; and Knecht's departure is the objection the essay makes to every spirituality that institutionalizes itself: it becomes an order, and one has to leave it for the exercise to remain an exercise.
>
> Sources: Fernando Pessoa (Alberto Caeiro), *O Guardador de Rebanhos*, V (written in 1914, published in *Athena* in 1925) ; Hermann Hesse, *Das Glasperlenspiel* (1943).
### The sigh without a heaven

One question remains that neither the wisdoms nor the critiques have settled. Religion, Marx said, is also “die Protestation gegen das wirkliche Elend”, the sigh of the oppressed creature. If it were only an error, its disappearance would be pure gain. If it is also a lament, what becomes of that lament when heaven empties?

The spiritualities of immanence do not answer it well, and this is their gravest weakness. Spinoza asks us to understand necessity, and Ivan answered in advance that he did not want to understand the child's tear; Comte-Sponville proposes saying yes to everything that happens, and his critic, H. Hausemer, was right to remark that in this acceptance evil disappears. A spirituality that consoles us for injustice by making it understood refounds nothing, but it does not answer the lament: it keeps religion's function as opium, without its function as protest. Consolation is therefore not a second criterion of refoundation; it is the sign of what an exit leaves unanswered. This is where Marx remains right against the sages. Murdoch herself escapes it only halfway, as we saw with regard to her morality of vision, and corporate meditation offers its caricature.

The theologians of the twentieth century gave this question an answer that unbelievers would be wrong to ignore. Bonhoeffer conceives a God who lets himself be edged out of the world and who helps only through his weakness, that is to say a God who no longer guarantees anything and who shares the lament instead of soothing it. Simone Weil writes: “La religion en tant que source de consolation est un obstacle à la véritable foi : en ce sens l'athéisme est une purification”, religion as a source of consolation is an obstacle to true faith: in this sense atheism is a purification. These two answers take away religion's function as opium without taking away its function as protest. But they remain the answers of believers, and the question of this essay is what becomes of the lament for someone who has no God, not even a weak one.

The most just answer seems to me to be Camus's, and that is why I keep him among the exceptions despite the instability of his position. “Je me révolte, donc nous sommes”, I rebel, therefore we are. The lament that no longer has a heaven does not disappear; it changes its address. It is no longer addressed to God, it is addressed to other human beings, and it founds a community that is not a Church, because it rests on no dogma, but on the recognition of a shared suffering. Here we meet again, by an unexpected detour, the sentence of Markel that Zosima preserved: “всякий пред всеми за всех и за всё виноват”, each of us is guilty before all, for all and for everything. Dostoevsky utters it as a Christian, Camus rediscovers it as an unbeliever, and Levinas, between the two, draws from it a responsibility for the other without reciprocity. Between them there is the difference of God, and there is also the same conviction: the answer to suffering is not an explanation but a solidarity.

This answer has a price, and it must be stated in closing. Camus's solidarity is an exit from religion only if it remains horizontal, that is to say if the “we” it founds never becomes an absolute to which individuals are sacrificed. That is what the twentieth century saw fail, when the “we” of revolt became History, the Party or the Nation, and the secular religions designated their victims; it is what Camus spent his life denouncing, and what his adversaries of 1952 did not forgive him. Girard gives this demand its sharpest form: a “we” that remains a solidarity and does not become a crowd is a “we” that refuses the scapegoat. The sigh of the oppressed creature can find an addressee without a heaven: the others. But on condition that these others are never made into a god, and that no victim is ever designated for them. The question that the quarrel of the two wisdoms left open thus receives its answer: one can hold together Spinoza's acceptance and Marx's protest, if one consents to the necessity of the world without consenting to the injustice of men, and if the solidarity that carries the lament remains horizontal. The critique of religion has not abolished the need to which religion answered; at best, it has found for it an address that demands no adoration. It is little, and it is perhaps all that can be asked of an exit from religion that does not wish to found another.

> **En littérature.** Primo Levi, *Se questo è un uomo* (1947) ; John Steinbeck, *The Grapes of Wrath* (1939) ; Alfred de Vigny, “Le Mont des Oliviers” (1843)
>
> On the evening of the selection of October 1944, at Auschwitz, old Kuhn, who has not been chosen, prays aloud on his bunk, his cap on his head, rocking back and forth, and thanks God; beside him, young Beppo, who is twenty and will leave for the gas chamber the day after next, stares fixedly at the light. Levi concludes that, if he were God, he would spit Kuhn's prayer onto the ground. Why here: it is the end of this section in a single page. Kuhn's prayer is the consolation that Weil forbids and the opium that Marx denounces, and it has a scapegoat, Beppo, whose death is Kuhn's grace; Levi, an unbeliever, takes away the consolation without taking away the protest, and the protest is addressed to God for the last time, in the form of spittle.
>
> Tom Joad, at the end of *The Grapes of Wrath*, leaves his mother in the night after killing the man who killed Casy; he tells her, in substance, that he will be wherever a man is hungry, wherever a cop is beating someone, in the shouts of those who rebel and in the laughter of children who have enough to eat, because Casy taught him that a man has only a piece of a great soul that belongs to everyone. It is “I rebel, therefore we are”, spoken by an Oklahoma farmer in the words of a defrocked preacher: Camus's horizontal “we”, without God, without Party and without victim, which is the essay's answer to the sigh without a heaven.
>
> Vigny wrote, a century earlier, the lament at the moment it no longer has an addressee. On the Mount of Olives, Christ prays and the Father does not answer; the poem ends, in the lines added in 1862 under the title “Le Silence”, with this: “Le juste opposera le dédain à l'absence / Et ne répondra plus que par un froid silence / Au silence éternel de la Divinité”, the just man will meet absence with disdain, and will answer only with a cold silence the eternal silence of the Godhead. It is the sigh without a heaven at its zero point: the lament no longer has an address, and the just man chooses silence. Levi spits, Tom Joad leaves, Vigny falls silent; the essay holds that the lament must change its address, and the three texts show what each of the three answers costs.
>
> Sources: Primo Levi, *Se questo è un uomo*, ch. 13, “October 1944” (1947) ; John Steinbeck, *The Grapes of Wrath*, ch. 28 (1939) ; Alfred de Vigny, “Le Mont des Oliviers”, *Les Destinées* (1843 ; “Le Silence” added in the 1864 edition).

### Still to be checked before any circulation

Every quotation in the essay is either verified against the text, or reported by a named and consulted secondary source, or paraphrased without quotation marks. Three reservations remain. Authors still under copyright (Heidegger, Barth, Bataille, Sartre, Camus in part, Marion, Schmitt, Löwith, Blumenberg, Gauchet, Taylor, Habermas, Hadot, Foucault, Comte-Sponville, Ferry, Bidar, Onfray, Ricoeur, Levinas, Jaspers, Russell, Mackie, Plantinga, Voegelin, Aron, Leo Strauss, Murdoch, Droit, Arkoun, as well as Girard, Jung, Becker, Berger, Luckmann, Hervieu-Léger, Boyer, Norris, Dennett, Couchoud, Goguel, Bultmann, Buber, Kelsen, Carnap, Ehrman, Carrier, Sanders) are cited from secondary sources or online reproductions: their pages ought to be collated against the printed editions. Texts drawn from imperfect optical character recognition (Hegel, *Vorrede zu Hinrichs* and *Religionsphilosophie* ; Comte ; Bayle ; Eckhart ; Otto ; Averroes in Gauthier's translation ; Maimonides in Munk's translation ; Schelling ; Feuerbach for the texts of 1846 and 1851) are cited in normalized spelling, to be collated against a reliable edition. Finally, a few biographical facts presented as established consensus have not been checked against a source during the session; they are flagged in the text.



The “In literature” boxes follow the same convention: each quotation in them is marked as verified with its file, and works still under copyright (Céline, Hesse, Saint-Exupéry, Camus, Malraux, Koestler, Orwell outside Europe, Grossman, Levi, O'Connor, Waugh, Greene, Mahfouz, Beckett, Kerouac, Lampedusa, Kazantzakis, Bulgakov, Steinbeck, Hemingway, Jackson, Celan, Char, Giono, Borges, Eco, Singer, Murdoch, Brecht, Silone, T. S. Eliot, Yourcenar, Musil, Sartre, Mann for *Joseph* and *Doktor Faustus*) are summarized in them without quotation.
